230:
750. Dvīditinamisse. In a compound, the vowel 'i' of the words 'dvi' and 'ti' is changed to 'e' in some instances. (Examples:) dvebhāvo, manasāadvejjho, tecattālīsaṃ, dvecattālīsaṃ. For whichever king of swans there are two wings of golden hue, that king of swans is called 'kañcanadepiñcho'. Why is 'kvaci' (in some instances) said? (To prevent the change to 'e' in) dvibhāvo, dvirattaṃ, tirattaṃ, ticattālīsaṃ, dvecattālīsaṃ, etc.

This Saddanīti treatise is like an eye-ointment that purifies the eye of wisdom. One should always study this treatise with mindfulness, as it removes the cataract of delusion (moha).

## Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, called the Samāsakappa (Section on Compounds), in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the linguistic paths of the Tipitaka together with its Commentaries, which consist of nine factors.

## 5-Taddhitakappa

I shall now speak on this chapter named Taddhita, which brings benefit to the listeners; listen to it with a well-concentrated mind.

Taddhita is the name of suffixes such as ṇa that occur in meanings such as apacca (offspring/lineage). It is also the name of the procedure to be accomplished through ellipsis (ekasesa), etc. Only if this is so, words like 'purisā' (formed by considering 'puriso ca puriso ca'), 'vīsatī' (considering 'dasa ca dasa ca'), 'cuddasā' (considering 'ten plus four'), and 'aḍḍhuḍḍho' (considering 'the fourth with a half'), etc., which are words devoid of suffixes, should also be understood as Taddhita words; not otherwise. Some teachers, however, holding that "Taddhita is only the name of suffixes like ṇa," say that the elliptical word 'purisā' is not a Taddhita word because it is devoid of a suffix, but is merely a pure noun (suddhanāma). That view should not be accepted, because the meaning must be understood through mental conception (parikappa) even though it is devoid of a suffix. For, in order to make known that the word 'purisā' denotes many men, (one conceives) 'puriso ca puriso...'
231:
...and so on, conceiving the ellipsis (ekasesa), performing the ellipsis, and making it end in the plural. This procedure is called 'Taddhita'. This elliptical procedure is also not fixed. Why? Because if one takes it as 'pūrentīti purisā' (they are called purisā because they fulfill), without such mental conception, that word becomes a kitanta (primary derivative) noun because it is followed by the suffix isa. If that same word is taken as 'puri senteīti purisā', it becomes an upapada-samāsa (dependent determinative compound). Thus, with a different intention, the word 'purisā', which is an ellipsis formed by mental conception to denote many men, is indeed a Taddhita word, not a pure noun. Therefore, Taddhita is the name of suffixes like ṇa that occur in meanings such as apacca, and it is also the name of the procedure to be accomplished through ellipsis, elision, substitution, etc. The treatise, however, is called 'Taddhita' because it is the locus of those procedures.

In this context, the etymological meaning (vacanattha) is: since the understanding of the meaning of a word depends on the suffix, it is called 'Taddhita' because it is beneficial (hita) or suitable for those meanings such as apacca. Or, because it should arise from words denoting lineage (gotta), it is called 'Taddhita' because it is suitable for those groups of words such as Vasiṭṭha; it receives suffixes like ṇa. Or, because it accomplishes the purpose for those who have set out to understand the meaning—the noble sons (kulaputta) who are devoted to hearing, learning, and memorizing—it is called 'Taddhita' because it is beneficial. It receives suffixes like ṇa, as well as the procedures of ellipsis, elision, substitution, etc., to be performed in various words.

751. Āyo vuddhī. Ā, e, and o have the name vuddhi. What is the use of the name 'vuddhi'? The use is the designation and the accomplishment of the task in the rule: 'ayuvaṇṇānamāyo vuddhi avuddhi ca'.

752. Apacce ṇo. The suffix ṇa occurs in the sense of 'his offspring' (apacca). In this rule, 'apacca' refers to lineage (kula). The offspring of Vasiṭṭha is Vāsiṭṭho. However, in accordance with the Dispensation (Sāsana), when the vowel i is changed to e, it always becomes 'Vāseṭṭho'. Here, when 'Vāseṭṭho' is said, it refers to all men born in that lineage, such as the son, grandson, or great-grandson of Vasiṭṭha. If the feminine gender is intended, the suffix ī is added after the word Vāseṭṭha, and it becomes 'Vāseṭṭhī'. Here, when 'Vāseṭṭhī' is said, it refers to the wife of Vasiṭṭha, or the daughter...
232:
...or all women born in that lineage are obtained. If the word 'kula' (clan/family) is considered, it becomes 'Vāseṭṭhaṃ'. It is like 'Virūpakkhaṃ ahirājakulaṃ', etc., and like 'Kāḷāvakañca Gaṅgeyyaṃ', etc. This method is the same in all examples. The lineage of Bhāradvāja is Bhāradvājo. Similarly, Gotamo. The lineage of Vāsudeva is Vāsudevo. Similarly, Bāladevo, Vesāmitto, etc.

753. Manuto ussusaṇ. After the word Manu, the suffixes ussa and usaṇ occur in the sense of offspring (apacca). The offspring of Manu is manusso. Similarly, mānuso. Here, the first part is 'mana'; it is a compound word (samāsa) in the sense that 'he has an expansive or abundant mind.' Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries said: 'They are called manussā because of the expansiveness of the mind.' However, because of the meaning 'he knows (manati) what is beneficial and what is harmful,' it is a kitanta (primary derivative) word.

754. Kaccādito ṇānaṇāyana. After the Kacca group of lineages (gotta), the suffixes ṇāna and ṇāyana occur in the sense of offspring (apacca). The offspring of Kacca is Kaccāno. Similarly, Kaccāyano. In another way, it becomes Kātiyāno. If the feminine gender is spoken, they become 'Kaccānā, Kaccāyanī, Kātiyānī'. The offspring of the Brahmin woman named Moggallā is Moggallāno. Similarly, Moggallāyano, Vacchāno, Vacchāyano, Sākaṭāno, Sākaṭāyano, Kaṇှāno, Kaṇှāyano, Aggivessāno, Aggivessāyano, etc. Here also...
233:
The form *Aggivessana* is also desired. This is because of the Pāḷi evidence: "Aggivessana, three similes have certainly become clear to me." (M 1.304).

755. The suffix *ṇeyya* is applied after words beginning with *Kattikā*. The descendant (offspring) of *Kattikā* is called *Kattikeyya*. Likewise, *Venateyya* (the son of Vinatā, the Garuda), and so forth.

756. The suffixes *ṇi*, *ṇika*, and *ṇiya* are applied as appropriate after words beginning with *Dakkha*. The descendant of *Dakkha* is called *Dakkhi*. Likewise, *Doṇi*, *Vāsavi*, *Sakyaputti*, *Jenadatti*, *Anuruddhi*, *Nāṭaputtiko*, *Nāṭaputtiyo*, *Jenadattiko*, *Jenadattiyo*, *Sakyaputtiko*, *Sakyaputtiyo*, and so forth.

757. The suffix *ṇava* is applied after words beginning with *Upaku*. The descendant of *Upaku* is called *Opakava*. Likewise, *Māṇava*, *Bhaggava*, and so forth.

758. The suffix *ṇera* is applied after the group of words beginning with *Vidhavā*. In the sense of "the descendant of that person," the suffix *ṇera* occurs after the group of words beginning with *Vidhavā*. The descendant of a woman whose husband has died (a widow) is called *Vedhavera*. The descendant of a *samaṇa* (ascetic) is called *sāmaṇera*, and so forth.

759. (The suffix *ṇera* is also applied) in the sense of "desiring" (*atthika*). When referring to a person who desires women such as a widow with the intention of engaging in unrighteous conduct, the suffix *ṇera* occurs after words beginning with *Vidhavā*. One who desires a *vidhavā* (widow) is called *vedhavera*. Likewise, *kaññera* and *vesiyera*. Here, the Pāḷi text along with the Commentary is the evidence: "The *vedhaveras* (those who desire widows) of fair complexion..." (Kh 6.327).

760. The suffix *ṇeyya* is also applied in the senses of "a certain state" (*bhāva*), "flowing from something," "being in something," "growing in something," and so forth. The suffix *ṇeyya* does not only occur in the sense of "descendant" (*apacca*); indeed, it also occurs in the senses of "a certain state," "flowing from something," "being in something," "growing in something," and so forth. The state of a pure person is called *soceyya*. A deer that exists on a mountain is called *pabbateyya*.
234:
A river that flows from a mountain is called *pabbateyya* (a mountain-river). Thread produced in the cocoons of worms is called *keseyya* (silk). Likewise, cloth produced in the city of Bārāṇasī is called *bārāṇaseyya*. A dog that grows up in a family is called *koleyya*. A person who is to be disciplined is called *veneyya*, and so forth.

761. The suffixes *ṇiya* and *ṇika* are applied in the senses of "being known," "being included," and "being designated." That which is known in the world, included in the world, or designated by the world is called *lokiya*. Likewise, it is also *lokika*.

762. The suffix *ṇiya* is also applied in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*). The state of a lazy person is called *ālasiya*. The state of a wise and energetic person is called *dakkhiya*. Likewise, the state of a brave person is called *suriya*. It is found in the Pāḷi: "O king of monkeys, for whomsoever these three qualities exist as they do in you—*dakkhiya* (energy), *suriya* (bravery), and wisdom—he overcomes the enemy he sees." (Kh 5.14). The state of a brave person is called *vīriya*. When *vī* is made short (*rassa*), it becomes *viriya*. The state of a lord is called *issariya*. Other words should also be combined in this way.

763. The suffix *ṇiya* is applied after the word *Inda* in the senses of "indicating," "accomplishing," "teaching," "seeing," "cultivating," and "ruling." The suffix *ṇiya* occurs after the word *Inda* when the senses of "indicating" (*liṅga*), "accomplishing" (*siṭṭha*), "teaching" (*desita*), "seeing" (*diṭṭha*), "cultivating" (*juṭṭha*), and "ruling" (*issariya*) are to be expressed. In the word "*indriyāni*," the Fully Enlightened Buddha is called "*Inda*" because of His supreme lordship, and wholesome and unwholesome kamma is also called "*Inda*" because no one else has lordship over kammas. Therefore, the eye and so forth, which are produced by kamma, are called "*indriyāni*" because they indicate (make known) that wholesome or unwholesome kamma, and because they are accomplished by that kamma. Furthermore, all twenty-two faculties are called "*indriyāni*" because they were taught according to reality by the Blessed One, who is called *Inda*. Likewise...
235:
The faculties are called 'indriya' because they are seen by the Blessed One (who is Indra, the Lord) [in terms of their characteristics, functions, etc.]. They are also called 'indriya' because some of them are resorted to by the Blessed One (Indra) through the practice of sense-object association, and some through the practice of mental development. They are also called 'indriya' in the sense of 'indriya' meaning lordship or predominance. Alternatively, they are called 'indriya' because they exercise rule or governance. In this regard, the following should also be noted: In the word-analysis (viggaha) 'indassa bhāvo indiyaṃ', the word 'indiya' refers only to the state of Sakka (Indra). However, when the letter 'da' in that same word is changed to 'dra' [becoming indriya], it refers only to the eye and so forth. This is because words are established in their meanings through conventional usage.

764. The suffix -ṇika is applied in the senses of: being born in a place, living in a place, studying a subject, being mixed with something, being made by something, crossing by means of something, traveling by means of something, or carrying by means of something; and also in the senses of being situated in, being engaged in, a craft, goods, livelihood, and so forth. The suffix -ṇika is not only applied in the senses of offspring, things to be known, or inclusion; rather, it also occurs in such senses as: where one is born, where one lives, what one studies, what [such as sesame] it is mixed with, what [such as the body] it is made by, what [such as a boat] one crosses with, what [such as a cart] one travels with, what [such as the head] one carries with, where [such as the body] it is situated, where [such as a door] one is engaged, what is one's craft, what is one's goods or articles, and what is one's livelihood.

One born in the city of Rājagaha is called 'Rājagahika'. Or, one who lives in Rājagaha is 'Rājagahika'. Likewise, 'Māgadhika', 'Sāvatthika', 'Kāpilavatthika', and so forth. One who studies the Vinaya is called 'Venayika'. Likewise, 'Suttantika', 'Ābhidhammika', and 'Veyyākaraṇika' (one who studies grammar). Food mixed with sesame (tila) is called 'Telika'. Likewise, 'Goḷika' (food mixed with molasses) and 'Ghātika' (food mixed with ghee). Kamma performed by the body is 'Kāyika'. Likewise, 'Vācasika' (performed by speech) and 'Mānasika' (performed by the mind). One who crosses by boat (nāvā) is called 'Nāvika'. Likewise, 'Oḷumpika' (one who crosses by raft). One who travels by cart (sakaṭa) is called 'Sākaṭika'. Likewise, 'Pādika' (one who travels on foot). One who carries on the head (sīsa) is called 'Sīsika'. Likewise, 'Aṃsika' (one who carries on the shoulder), 'Khandhika', 'Hatthika' (one who carries with the hand), and 'Aṅgulika' (one who carries with the finger). Feeling (vedanā) situated in the body is called 'Sārīrika'. Likewise, 'Mānasikā' (feeling situated in the mind). One engaged at the door (a gatekeeper) is called 'Dovārika'. Likewise, 'Bhaṇḍāgāရိက' (one engaged in the treasury), 'Nāgarika' (one engaged in the city), and 'Nāvakammika' (one engaged in new construction). If one's craft is playing the lute (vīṇā), he is called 'Veṇika'. Likewise, 'Pāṇavika' (one who plays the hand-drum), 'Modiṅgika' (one who plays the mridangam drum), and 'Vaṃsika' (one who plays the flute or wind instruments). If perfume (gandha) is one's goods, he is called 'Gandhika'. Likewise, 'Telika' (one whose goods are oil).
236:
One whose goods are molasses is called 'Goḷika'. One who lives by killing sheep is called 'Orabbhika'. Likewise, one who lives by killing wild animals is 'Māgavika', one who kills pigs is 'Sokarika', and one who kills birds is 'Sākuṇika'.

Because of the statement, 'The application of Taddhita (secondary derivation) is diverse,' the suffix -ṇika should be understood in other senses beyond those already mentioned. How? One who is worthy of being disciplined is called 'Venayika'. Or, one who teaches the Vinaya, or teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline, is called 'Venayika'. One who comes from the Anga and Magadha regions, or who is a ruler in those Anga and Magadha regions, is called 'Aṅgamāgadika'. That which is killed or caught with a net (jāla) is 'Jālika'. That which is bound or tied with thread (sutta) is 'Suttika'. One whose weapon is a bow (cāpa) is called 'Cāpika'. Likewise, one with a javelin is 'Tomarika', one with a club is 'Muggarika', and one with a pestle is 'Mosalika'. One who has a wind-disease is called 'Vātika'. Likewise, one with a phlegm-disease is 'Semhika', and one with a bile-disease is 'Pittika'. One who has faith in the Buddha is called 'Buddhika'. Likewise, one with faith in the Dhamma is 'Dammika', and one with faith in the Sangha is 'Saṅghika'. Property belonging to the Buddha is called 'Buddhikaṃ'. Likewise, 'Dhammikaṃ', 'Saṅghikaṃ dhanaṃ' (Sangha's wealth), and 'Saṅghiko vihāro' (Sangha's monastery). Goods or articles bought with cloth (vattha) are called 'Vatthikaṃ'. Likewise, goods bought with a pot are 'Kumbhikaṃ', goods bought with a ploughshare or fruit are 'Phālikaṃ', goods bought with small bells are 'Kiṅkaṇikaṃ', and goods bought with gold are 'Sovaṇṇikaṃ'. That which has the measure of one pot (or a ten-ambaṇa pot) is called 'Kumbhikaṃ'. A heap that fills a pot is 'Kumbhika'. That which is worthy of a pot is 'Kumbhika'. One who plays with dice (akkha) is called 'Akkhika'. Likewise, one who plays with bamboo splints is 'Sālākika'. One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma or follows the Dhamma is called 'Dhammika'. That which brings about the subsiding of defilements is 'Upasamika'. That which effects the total unbinding (parinibbāna) of defilements is 'Parinibbāyika'; these refer to the Dhamma.

The Noble Path (Ariya Magga) is called 'Sandiṭṭhika' because it is to be seen by oneself as one who brings about the absence of greed and so forth in one's own continuity. The ninefold supramundane Dhamma is called 'Sandiṭṭhika' because it is to be seen by oneself through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). Alternatively, praised wisdom is called 'sandiṭṭhi'; because one conquers defilements through that sandiṭṭhi (Right View), it is called 'Sandiṭṭhika'. This is like calling one who conquers by means of a chariot 'Rathika'. Alternatively, 'diṭṭha' means seeing; 'diṭṭha' itself is 'sandiṭṭha', meaning 'vision' or 'seeing'. Because it is worthy of being seen, it is called 'Sandiṭṭhika', just as one who is worthy of a cloth is called 'Vatthika'. With reference to the yielding of its own fruit, it is called 'Akālo' (timeless) because there is no fixed time such as morning, day, or night for it.
237:
The word *akāla* itself is called *akālika*. In this context, it should be noted that the suffix *ṇika* is applied in the sense of *sakattha* (its own meaning). Alternatively, it is called *kālika* because it has a time reached for giving its own fruit. What is that *kālika* dhamma? It is worldly wholesome dhamma (*lokiya kusala dhamma*). However, this Path dhamma (*magga dhamma*) is called *akālika* because it gives fruit immediately after its occurrence, without delaying for time. What is that *akālika* dhamma? It is the Path dhamma. In this sense, the word "*akālika*" is a compound word (*samāsa*).

*Ehipassika* is so called because it is worthy of the procedure "Come and see." It means it is worthy of the *ehipassavidhi* (procedure of "come and see") expressed as "Come and see this Dhamma."

Bringing near is called *upanaya*. *Opanayika* is so called because it is worthy of being brought into one's own mind by the power of meditation (*bhāvanā*). The word *opanayika* is the same as *opaneyyika*; that dhamma is the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) supramundane dhamma. *Opaneyyika* is so called because it is worthy of being approached and attached to by the power of realization (*sacchikiriyā*) with one's own mind; that dhamma is the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) supramundane dhamma (Nibbāna). Alternatively, it is called *upaneyya* because it leads to Nibbāna; that dhamma is the Noble Path (*ariya magga*). It is called *upaneyya* because it should be brought to the state of being realized; that dhamma is the Dhamma of Fruition (*phala*) and Nibbāna. The word *upaneyya* is the same as *opaneyyika*.

Wearing rag-robes is *paṃsukūla*. One is called *paṃsukūlika* because of the habit of wearing those rag-robes. Similarly, *tecīvarika* (one who wears three robes). One is called *piṇḍapātika* because of seeking alms-food. Alternatively, one is called *piṇḍapātī* because the practice of going for alms belongs to that person. That *piṇḍapātī* itself is called *piṇḍapātika* with the suffix *ṇika* applied in the sense of *sakattha*. One is called *na-ehibhadantika* because one does not come even when told, "Venerable sir, please come." One is called *na-tiṭṭhabhadantika* because one does not stop even when told, "Then, venerable sir, please stop." One is called *antarāyika* because of causing obstacles. One is called *anāthapiṇḍika* because of giving alms and food to the helpless. Other words should also be combined in this manner.

## 765. Tena rattaṃ tassidamanyatthesu ca ṇo.

Cloth dyed with astringent dye is called *kāsāva*. Similarly, *kosumbha* (cloth dyed with safflower), *hālidda* (cloth dyed with turmeric), etc. Meat that is the property of a pig is called *sokara*. Similarly, *māhiṃsa* (buffalo meat), etc.
238:
And so forth. A forest born near the city of Kapilavatthu is called *kāpilavatthava*. A mansion located not far (near) from a fig tree (*udumbara*) is called *odumbara*. That which occurs not far from the Vidisā region is called *vedisa*. One born in the city of Madhurā is called *mādhura*. The Buddha is the deity (object of devotion) of that person; therefore, that person is called *buddha*. Similarly, one who has the deity Bhadda is *bhadda*, one who has Māra is *māra*, and one who has Mahinda (Sakka) is *māhinda*, and so forth. One who enters into and studies for a whole year is called *saṃvacchara*. Similarly, one who enters into and studies for a moment (*muhutta*) is *mohutta*, and one who enters into and studies the *aṅgavijjā* treatise is *aṅgavijja*.

A place that is the domain of geomancers is called *vāsāda*. Similarly, the place of pots is *kumbha*, and the place of guests is *ātisāra*. Fig trees exist in this place; therefore, that place is called *odumbara*. It is called *sāgara* because it was dug by the Sāgara princes, who were the sons of King Sagara. It refers to the eastern part of the ocean. Because it is connected to that dug ocean, the entire ocean region also receives the name *sāgara*; this is the common parlance of worldly people. Madhurā is the residence of that person; therefore, that person is called *mādhura*. Or, the king who rules over the city of Madhurā is called *mādhura*. People born in market towns (*nigama*) and the countryside (*janapada*) are called *negamajānapada*. Similarly, those born in the eastern countryside are called *porimajānapada*.

## 766. Suvaṇṇato taṃrāsatthe ṇayo.

After the word *suvaṇṇa*, the suffix *ṇaya* is applied in the sense of "a heap of that treasure." This heap of beautiful-colored treasures is called *sovaṇṇaya*. In the Pāḷi texts, it is said: "I think it is a heap of treasures called *sovaṇṇaya*."

## 767. Jātiniyuttatthesu imiyā.

The suffixes *ima* and *ya* are applied in the senses of birth (*jāti*) and connection (*niyutta*). One born later is called *pacchima*. Similarly, one born at the end is *antima*, that which occurs above is *uparima*, that which occurs below is *heṭṭhima*, and that which occurs at the ankle is *gopphima*. One born in the lineage of the Bodhisatta is called *bodhisattajātiya*. Similarly, one born in the horse breed is *assajātiya*. One connected at the end is called *antima*. Similarly, it is also called *antiya*. By another rule, however, it also becomes *antika*.

## 768. Tadassatthīti iko ca.

In the sense "that belongs to him" (*tadassatthi*), the suffix *ika* is also applied along with *ima* and *ya*. In this sense "that belongs to him," these suffixes *ima* and *ya* occur, and the suffix *ika* also occurs. He who has a son, or in whom a son exists, is called *puttima*. Similarly...
239:
Puttiyo, puttiko. In this regard, this distinction should also be understood. How? In the Pali text, "He who is not a Sakyaputtiya (son of the Sakyan) is not a recluse (samaṇa)," the suffix 'iya' should be understood in the sense of offspring (apaccattha) as 'the son of the Blessed One who is a Sakyan prince' (Sakyaputtiyo). However, in the Pali text, "The princesses (rājaputtiyo) with many attendants have come," the suffix 'ī' should be understood. Even if the sounds are similar, words may have different suffixes and different numbers (vacana).

769. The suffix 'kiya' is applied in the sense of connection (niyutta). One who is connected with birth is called 'jātikiyo'. Similarly, one connected with the end is 'antakiyo', and one connected with blindness from birth is 'jaccandhakiyo'.

770. The suffix 'kaṇ' is applied in the sense of a group (samūhattha). A group of princes is called 'rājaputtako' or 'rājaputto'. Similarly, a group of humans is 'mānussako' or 'mānusso'. However, in the Pali text, "Musical instruments belonging to humans and those belonging to devas sounded at that time," in the word 'mānussakā', the suffix 'kaṇ' should be understood in the sense of "belonging to that human" (tassedanti). A group of peacocks is 'māyūrako' or 'māyūro', a group of buffaloes is 'māhiṃsako', a group of trainings is 'sikkho', a group of pigeons is 'kāpoto', and so on.

771. The suffix 'tā' is applied after words such as jana (people), bandhu (relative), and sahāya (companion). A group of people is called 'janatā'. Similarly, a group of relatives is 'bandhutā', a group of companions is 'sahāyatā', a group of villages is 'gāmatā', and so on.

772. The suffix 'tā' is applied after words like 'deva' in its own meaning (sakatthe). After the word 'deva', the suffix 'tā' occurs in its own meaning without regarding other meanings such as a group. A deva itself is called 'devatā'. Because of this suffix, it is called 'idappaccayatā'. A direction itself is 'disatā', and so on. In this regard, the Pali text, "Above, below, these directions are ten (dasadisatā)," is an example.

773. The suffix 'iya' is applied in the sense of "the place (or cause) of that." The cause (or object) of intoxication is called 'madaniyaṃ'. Similarly, the cause of binding is 'bandhaniyaṃ', the cause of liberation is 'muccaniyaṃ', the cause (or object) of attachment is 'rajjaniyaṃ', and so on.
240:
774. The suffix 'iya' is applied after 'upādāna' (clinging), etc., in the sense of benefit (hita), etc. Because it increases clinging, it is the benefit of clinging, or because it is the object of those clingings, it is called 'upādāniya'. Similarly, states that are objects of the floods are 'oghanīyā dhammā', states that are objects of the yokes are 'yoganīyā dhammā', and states that are not objects of the yokes are 'ayoganīyā dhammā'. That which exists in the belly is 'udariyaṃ', and that which exists in the brave is 'vīriyaṃ', and so on.

775. The suffixes 'īya' and 'eyya' are applied in the sense of worthiness (arahattha). Because it is worthy of seeing, it is called 'dassanīya', referring to form (rūpa). Similarly, there are 'dassaneyya', 'vandanīyo', 'vandaneyyo', 'namassanīyo', 'namassaneyyo', 'pūjanīyo', and 'pūjaneyyo'. Because one is worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇā), one is called 'dakkhiṇeyyo'. In this regard, Pali passages such as "The city named Amaravatī is beautiful to behold (dassaneyyaṃ) and delightful," "Having worshipped those worthy of worship (vandaneyyānaṃ)," and "Honor to those worthy of honor (pūjaneyyānaṃ)" serve as examples.

776. The suffixes 'ṇaka' and 'ṇiya' are applied in the sense of "his possession" (tassedaṃ). Because it is the possession of humans, it is called 'mānussakaṃ' (referring to kingship). Because it is the possession of poets (kavi), it is called 'kāviyaṃ'.

777. The suffix 'āyitatta' is applied in the sense of comparison (upamā). That which appears like smoke is called 'dhūmāyitatta'. Similarly, that which appears like darkness is 'timirāyitatta'.

778. The suffix 'la' is applied in the sense of being in that place or depending on that thing. A bad place is 'duṭṭhulla', the place of knowledge (veda) is 'vedalla', that which depends on the bad is 'duṭṭhulla', and that which depends on knowledge is 'vedalla'.
241:
779. Tabbahule ālu. The suffix 'ālu' is applied in the sense of abundance (tabbahula). One whose nature is to covet others' property or who has much covetousness is called 'abhijjhālu'. Similarly, one who is very cold is 'sītālu', one who has much compassion is 'dayālu', and a palace that has many banners is 'dhajālu pāsādo'.

780. Ṇyattattanabyatā bhāve. The suffixes 'ṇya', 'tta', 'ttana', 'bya', and 'tā' are applied in the sense of state or nature (bhāva). The state of being lazy is 'ālasyaṃ'. By the power of the suffix 'ṇiya', it is formed as 'ālasiyaṃ'. The state of being free from disease is 'ārogyaṃ'. By changing the 'o' to 'u', it is formed as 'ārugyaṃ'. Furthermore, in verses, by applying the suffix 'ṇiya' to the word 'ārogya' in its own meaning (sakatthe), and by making one of the dissimilar conjunct consonants similar, it is formed as 'āroggiyaṃ'. This is seen in the Pali: "āyuṃ āroggiyaṃ vaṇṇaṃ." Therefore, it should be understood that in the Dispensation (Sāsana), there are three readings: 'ārogyaṃ', 'ārugyaṃ', and 'āroggiyaṃ'. The state of being wise is 'paṇḍiccaṃ', and so on. The state of a monk who wears rag-robes is 'paṃsukūlikattaṃ'. Similarly, the state of one who does not practice overeating is 'anodarikattaṃ', and so on. The state of being a worldling is 'puthujjanattanaṃ'. The state of being a servant is 'dāsabyaṃ'. Alternatively, from the word 'dāsa', the suffix 'ṇiya' is applied in the sense of state, and by inserting the augment 'va' in the middle, it is formed as 'dāsaviyaṃ'. Or, in the word 'dāsaviyaṃ', by the rule "saralopoyamannarādīsū," the 'i' in 'vi' is elided when followed by 'ya', resulting in 'dāsabyaṃ'. The state of one who delights in sleep is 'niddārāmatā'. The state of being fit for work is 'kammaññatā'. Similarly, 'lahutā' (lightness), and so on.

781. Visamādito ṇo. The suffix 'ṇa' is applied after words such as 'visama'. The state of being uneven or unjust is 'vesamaṃ'. Similarly, the state of being a court chaplain is 'porohiccaṃ'. The state of respect is 'gāravo' or 'gāravaṃ'. The state of softness is 'maddavo' or 'maddavaṃ'.
242:
Soceyya means the state of being pure. By the power of the ᅆeyya suffix, it becomes 'soceyya'. In the Pāጷi, it is found as "Soceyyacādhigacchati."

782. The suffix kaᅆ is added after words such as ramaᅆĩya. The state of being delightful is called rāmaᅆĩyakaፁ. Similarly, the state of being pleasant is called mānuakaፁ. In the passage, "Wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful," the word ramaᅆĩya is used because it is to be delighted in. Taking the meaning that ramaᅆĩya is indeed rāmaᅆeyya, it becomes bhũmirāmaᅆeyyā. In this context, in the compound word bhũmirāmaᅆeyyakaፁ, it should be understood that the suffix ka is added.

783. The suffix ᅆya is added in the sense of "goodness" (sādhu). In that context, the suffix ᅆya occurs in the sense of being good. Being good in action (being fit for work) is called kammaaፁ.

784. After the word pura, the suffix ĩ is added in the sense of "being born there," etc. Speech that originates in a city, or speech belonging to city-dwellers, is called porĩ. It is also called porĩ because it is refined speech, like a woman raised in a city. This refers to the speech of urban residents.

785. The suffix a is added in the sense of "that which is desired." It is called saፁghādisesa because the Saፁgha is required at the beginning (the parivāsa stage) and for the remaining middle and end (the abbhān stage) of the process of rehabilitation from that offense. This is the group of offenses of that name.

786. In the sense of distinction (visesa), the suffixes tara, tama, isika, iya, and iጷጷha occur as appropriate. "This person is noble, and this person is noble; but this person is especially noble among them," thus he is called varatara. Similarly, varatama (most noble). "All these are superior and eminent; but this person is especially superior, eminent, and more exalted than these," thus he is called uttaritara. It should be understood that the 'a' is changed to 'i'. Other examples are hĩnatara (lower than the low), hĩnatama, paᅆĩtatara (more excellent than the excellent), paᅆĩtatama, assatara (a horse superior to other horses), and seጷጷhatara (a guild-leader superior to other guild-leaders). Generally, the suffixes tara, tama, etc.
243:
Generally, the suffixes tara, tama, etc., occur after qualitative words (guᅆasadda) in the sense of distinction. "All these people are wicked; but this person is especially wicked among them," thus pāpatara. Similarly, pāpatama, pāpisika, pāpiya, and pāpiጷጷha. Among these five suffixes, the distinction is clear only in tara and tama. This is because of the words: "This person's inclination is soft; this person's is softer; this person's is softest."

787. In the sense of "that belongs to him" (tadassatthi), the suffix vĩ is added after words such as māyā. One who possesses deceit (māyā) is called māyāvĩ. Similarly, medhādhĩ (one who possesses wisdom).

788. The suffix sa is added after the word sumedhā. In the sense of "that belongs to him," the suffix sa occurs after the word sumedhā. Good wisdom is called sumedhā. One who has good wisdom, or in whom good wisdom exists, is called sumedhaso. Similarly, bhũrimedhaso. The teachers, however, by applying the suffix sa, desire the formation of the word 'sumedhaso'. In the phrase "paca pacaso," they also desire 'pacapacaso', meaning "these groups have five letters each." Such a desire is not appropriate. The reason is that in the view of these teachers, 'sumedhaso' is a word ending in the singular, while 'pacapacaso' is a word ending in the plural. Thus, this suffix sa would express both singular and plural meanings. This method has never been heard of before in the nine-fold Buddha's word (the Tipiጷaka) along with its commentaries. This is our preference (khanti): that the singular forms like 'sumedhaso', 'sumedhasaፁ', the plural forms like 'sumedhasā', 'sumedhasāyo', and the neuter singular and plural forms like 'sumedhasaፁ kulaፁ', 'sumedhasāni kulāni' are acceptable. It should be understood that only this method is in accordance with the Pāጷi.

789. The suffix sĩ is added after words such as tapa. Tapassĩ, yasassĩ, tejasĩ. Here, in the first two words, the letter 's' is doubled (dvitta) for ease of pronunciation; in the last word, however, there is only a single letter 's'. Some teachers within the Dispensation who are proficient in Sanskrit...
244:
...taking the method from there (Sanskrit), they read it as 'tejassĩ', doubling the letter 's'. Even if read that way, there is no fault. However, in the original Pāጷi manuscripts, it appears only as 'tejasĩ', a word without a conjunct consonant (nissaoga).

790. After words such as daᅆጷa, the suffixes ĩ and ika occur. One who has a staff is called daᅆጷĩ. Similarly, daᅆጷiko, mālĩ (one who has a garland), māliko, etc.

791. After words such as madhu, the suffix ra occurs. Madhuro (having a sweet taste), kujaro (an elephant having a jaw), mukharo (one who has a mouth/is talkative), sarĩro (the body), etc.

792. After words such as guᅆa, the suffix vantu occurs in accordance with the Pāጷi. Guᅆavā (one who has virtue), gaᅆavā (one who has a group), paavā (one who has wisdom), vedanāvā (one who has sensation), saavā (one who has perception), rasmivā (one who has rays/reins), yasassivā (one who has attendants), massuvā (one who has a beard). Here, it should be understood that generally, the suffix vantu occurs after words ending in 'a' (akāranta).

793. After words such as sati, the suffix mantu occurs. Satimā (one who has mindfulness), jutimā (one who has radiance), atthadassimā (one who habitually sees the meaning), dhĩmā (one who has wisdom), cakkhumā (one who has eyes), āyasmā (one who has long life), gomā (one who has cows).

794. After words such as canda, the suffix imantu occurs. He is called candimā (the moon deity) because he possesses the moon-mansion known as the candavimāna. Or, candimā (the moon-mansion) is so called because the deity known as Canda resides in it. In the Pāጷi, it is found as: "Like the moon (candimā) freed from a cloud." Some people, taking the method from the Sanskrit language, read it as 'candamā'; that reading is not appropriate. One is called puttimā (the wealthy man Dhaniya who has many sons) because he has sons. Here, it should be understood that the suffix imantu is used in an intensive sense (atisaya), not just to indicate mere possession, similar to the suffix vantu in the word 'bhagavā'. One is called pāpimā (the Evil One/Māra) because he has evil. Here too, the suffix imantu is in the intensive sense. This method should be understood as appropriate in other words as well.
245:
795. The suffix ṇa is added after words such as saddhā (faith). He who has faith is called saddho (a man with faith). She who has faith is called saddhā (a woman with faith). A family that has faith is called saddhaṃ (a faithful family). Similarly: paññā, paññā, paññaṃ (a man, woman, or family with wisdom). The same applies to a mango tree with fruit (phalo ambo) and one without fruit (aphalo), etc.

796. The suffix to is added after words such as pabba in the sense of "this belongs to him/it." A mountain that has joints or ridges (pabba) is called pabbato, meaning a mountain (giri). A mountain that has a crooked shape (vaṅka) is called vaṅkato. What is this vaṅkato? It is the mountain named Vaṅkata. Referring to that mountain, the Bodhisatta Vessantara said: "The great king has banished me; I shall go to Mount Vaṅkata." Also, the Blessed One, having become the Buddha, said regarding that same mountain: "Those travelers, seeing us there, spoke pitiful words. They reported with difficulty that Mount Vaṅkata was sixty leagues away." In grammatical treatises, the suffix to is also prescribed after the word maru. He who has the gods of the two heavens is called maruto, meaning Sakka, the king of gods.

797. In the suffix mantu, the vowel u of the word āyu (life) should be changed to as. He who has life is called āyasmā, meaning one who is long-lived. This is an endearing form of address.

798. The suffix maya is used in the sense of "made of that substance." That which is made of gold is suvaṇṇamayaṃ. Similarly, rajatamayaṃ (made of silver), etc.

799. The suffix maya is also used in the sense of "originated from that" and in its own sense (sakattha). That which originates from cows is gomayaṃ (cow-dung). Giving itself is dānamayaṃ (consisting of giving). Similarly, sīlamayaṃ (consisting of virtue), etc.
246:
800. In the sense of "made by him," the suffix a is added after the word sura (with the lengthening of u and the shortening of a). The intoxicating liquor made by the forest-dwelling hunter named Sura is called surā.

801. In the sense of "made by him," the suffix ī is added after the word varuṇa (with the lengthening of the short a). The intoxicating liquor made by the immoral ascetic named Varuṇa is called vāruṇī. However, in the Kumbha Jātaka Commentary, it is said: "From the beginning, because it was seen by both the hunter Sura and the ascetic Varuṇa, that drink came to be known as both 'surā' and 'vāruṇī'." In that context, what is called surā is the same as vāruṇī, and what is called vāruṇī is the same as surā. This is because they were made by Sura and Varuṇa together. Nowadays, although that intoxicating liquor is made by others, it is still called surā or vāruṇī based on the ancient designation.

802. In the sense of completing a number (ordinal), the suffix ma is added after words such as pañca (five) and satta (seven). The completion of five is called pañcamo (fifth). Similarly, sattamo (seventh), aṭṭhamo (eighth), navamo (ninth), etc.

803. In verses (gāthā), the suffix ma is added after the word chaṭṭha (sixth) in its own sense (sakattha). In the domain of verses, for the purpose of completing the syllables of a poetic line, the suffix ma follows the word chaṭṭha in its own sense. "That sixth cause of ruin (exists)." "For the monk who is homeless and without wealth, the sixth is auspiciousness." In these instances, chaṭṭha itself is chaṭṭhamo. Why is it said "in verses"? To prevent the suffix ma from occurring in prose such as "he speaks the sixth verse" (chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamaṃ) or "the sixth sense-base" (chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ).

804. In the sense of completing a number, the substitution of the letter sa for the letter cha in the word cha (six) occurs optionally. The completion of six is called saṭṭho or chaṭṭho.

805. The suffix ī is added after words starting from ekādasa (eleven) and ending in dasa (ten). The completion of eleven is called ekādasī. Similarly, dvādasī, etc. Why is it said "in the sense of completing a number"? To prevent the suffix ī from occurring in the simple cardinal number ekādasa.
247:
806. When the word dasa follows, the substitution of so for cha is permanent. Ten exceeded by six is called soḷasa (sixteen). In the view of some teachers, "six and ten is soḷasa" is a compound (samāsa).

807. Teachers say that the niggahīta (anusvāra) character is added at the end of those numbers. Their examples are ekādasiṃ, etc. However, in the verse "Throughout the fourteenth (cātuddasiṃ), the fifteenth (pañcadasiṃ), and the eighth day of the fortnight, I shall observe the Uposatha," the terms cātuddasiṃ and pañcadasiṃ are in the accusative case (upayogavacana) used to denote a continuous period of time (accantasaṃyoga). It is not an augment of niggahīta here. Although "the eighth day of the fortnight" (yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī) is in the nominative case, the accusative case tancā pakkhassa aṭṭhamiṃ should be understood in the sense of accantasaṃyoga. This method should be carefully borne in mind.

808. The augment ti occurs after the words vīsa and tiṃsa. For example: vīsati (twenty), tiṃsati (thirty).

809. In numbers, the letters da and ra are substituted by la. For example: cattālīsaṃ (forty), aḍ္ဎtelasehi bhikkhusatehi (with twelve hundred and fifty monks), soḷasa (sixteen).

810. The word dvi (two) occurring before the words vīsati and dasa is changed to bā. For example: bāvīsatindriyāni (twenty-two faculties), bārasa manussā (twelve people).

811. The word dvi is changed to du, di, or do. For example: durattaṃ (two full nights), dirattaṃ (two nights), diguṇaṃ (twofold, double), dohaḷinī (a woman with two longings/pregnant).

812. In the sense of counting (saṅkhyāna), the letter da of the word dasa following words such as eka is sometimes changed to ra. For example: ekārasa, ekādasa, bārasa, dvādasa. Why is it said "in counting"? To prevent the substitution of ra in places like dvādasāyatanāni (the twelve sense-bases).

813. After words such as aṭṭhā, the letter da of the word dasa is also sometimes changed to ra in the sense of counting. For example: aṭṭhārasa, aṭṭhādasa. Why is it said "after aṭṭhā etc."? To prevent the substitution of ra in the word pañcadasa (fifteen).

814. The letter da of the word dasa following the word pañca becomes ra...
248:
814. The letter 'da' of the word 'dasa' following the word 'pañca' should be changed to the letter 'ra'; because of this change to 'ra', the word 'pañca' must always be changed to 'panna'. Example: pannarasa (fifteen).

815. In counting, the final letter of the words 'dvi', 'eka', and 'aṭṭha' should be changed to the letter 'ā' in some instances. Examples: dvādasa (twelve), ekādasa (eleven), aṭṭhārasa (eighteen). Why is it said "in counting"? It is to prevent the change to 'ā' in contexts that are not counting, such as dvidanto (having two tusks), ekacchanno (having one roof), aṭṭhathambho (having eight pillars), and so on.

816. When ordinal suffixes (pūrana) are applied to the words 'catu' and 'cha', the forms 'ttha' and 'ṭṭha' occur. The fourth person is called catuttha; the sixth person is called chaṭṭha.

817. The suffix 'tiya' should be applied to the words 'dvi' and 'ti'. The second person is called dutiya; the third person is called tatiya.

818. Due to the suffix 'tiya', the word 'dvi' should be changed to 'du', and the word 'ti' should be changed to 'ta'. (dutiya, tatiya).

819. Together with the preceding word 'aḍḍha', the words 'catuttha', 'dutiya', and 'tatiya' are respectively changed to aḍḍhuḍḍha, divaḍḍha, diyaḍḍha, and aḍḍhatiya. The fourth including a half (three and a half) is called aḍḍhuḍḍha. The second including a half (one and a half) is called divaḍḍha or diyaḍḍha. The third including a half (two and a half) is called aḍḍhatiya.

820. If there is a desire to indicate plurality, only one of the words with identical forms should remain (ekasesa). For example: a man and a man are 'men' (purisā); a woman and a woman are 'women' (itthiyo); a clan and a clan are 'clans' (kulāni); a mind and a mind are 'minds' (cittāni); likewise migiyo (female deer), and so on. Here, when 'purisā' is said, it is known that there are many men, such as two men, three men, four men, or many hundreds of men. Why is it said "desire to indicate plurality"? In the passage "They do not listen to the words of the servants of the servants of the Great Kings," although the words have identical forms, there is no desire to indicate plurality [as a single group], but they are spoken merely as worldly usage; therefore, ekasesa does not occur, and the word is repeated twice.
249:
In the case of words with identical sounds, it is shown that ekasesa does not occur when there is no desire to indicate the plurality of men as in "purisā" (a man and a man), because it is spoken merely by way of worldly usage. In fact, this word "purisā" is conceived by the intellect to indicate the meaning of many men. It is not spoken by way of ekasesa of identical sounds existing by nature. This is because the plural meaning is known through the derivation itself: "pūrentīti ca puri sentīti ca purisā". Why is it said "of words with identical sounds"? Elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry (being different) become hatthassarathapattiyo.

821. In the view of other teachers, ekasesa occurs for words with different sounds (virūpekasesa). In the alternative view of teachers, ekasesa occurs for dissimilar words. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are Sāriputtā (the Sāriputtas). Father and mother are pitaro (parents). Son and daughter are puttā (children). Male deer and female deer are migā (deer). One form of 'crooked' and another form of 'crooked' are kuṭilā. Here, we shall state the following decision: If virūpekasesa were desired in masculine contexts such as "Sāriputtā" and "pitaro", then in feminine contexts also, one should form the virūpekasesa "itthiyo" by analyzing it as "a woman and a man". Likewise, "mother and father" should be formed as "mātaro", and "daughter and son" as "dhītaro". If "itthiyo", "mātaro", or "dhītaro" were spoken, men etc. should also be understood. However, grammarians do not apply virūpekasesa in feminine contexts; they apply it only in masculine contexts. Both of these are inconsistent. In both places, it should occur in an exactly similar manner. But it does not happen so. Therefore, it is known that "virūpekasesa is not to be desired".

822. Due to the desire for association, the plural is used for a single meaning. In whatever instance one wishes to speak of a certain thing together with another thing, in that usage...
250:
When there is a desire to combine a certain object with another, the plural number occurs for a single meaning even without the rule of virūpeka-sesa-vidhi. How is this? It is like the Blessed One, wishing to send the Venerable Sāriputta along with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to the Kīṭāgiri district, used the plural address "Sāriputtā". Similarly, King Sañjaya, seeing his son arrive with his daughter-in-law, addressed him as "Sons" (Puttā). Likewise, people seeing a tiger coming out of the forest with a lion, call out, "Come, tigers!" (Byagghā). In this regard, there are these Pali passages:

Sāriputtas (Sāriputta and Moggallāna), you may go.
Anuruddhas (Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimila), are you keeping well?
Sons (son and daughter-in-law), are you safe?
Come, tigers (tiger and lion), turn back,
Enter the great forest once again.

## 823. When masculine nouns, excluding Brahma, Inda, Buddha, Purisa, Mātugāma, etc., are expressed in the plural, females are also included.

When masculine nouns, excluding these words such as Brahma, Inda, Buddha, Purisa, and Mātugāma, are expressed in the plural, they do not only include men; even without the rule of virūpeka-sesa-vidhi, females are also included. This is because by taking the primary (the male), the non-primary (the female) is also taken. Indeed, males are primary. This is because only Great Bodhisattas existing in the state of manhood receive the definite prophecy for Buddhahood, and because states such as Brahma-hood are seen only in men. Females, however, are not primary. This is because beings existing in the state of womanhood have never received a prophecy for Buddhahood, and because states such as Brahma-hood are not seen in women. In this regard, there are these usages:

"Sons (Puttā) are the beloved of humans."
"Swans (Haṃsā), herons, peacocks, elephants, and deer."

In these instances, by the word "Puttā", daughters are also included. By the words such as "Haṃsā", female swans and so on are also included.

Why is it said, "excluding Brahma, Inda, Buddha, Purisa, Mātugāma, etc."? In masculine nouns such as "Brahmas, Sakkas, men, male cuckoos"...
251:
It is to show that females are not included because it is not the proper place, even when indicated by the plural, and because only the meaning of the masculine word is taken. Similarly, in masculine plural terms like "Mātugāmā" and "Orodhā", it is to show that females are not included again because only the meaning of the feminine word is taken. Why say "when indicated by the plural"? [Examples:] Satto (being), Haṃso (swan), Koñco (heron).

In this context, this method should also be known: When it is said "Satto" or "Sattā", "Loko" or "Lokā", "Pajā" or "Pajāyo", both females and males are understood, because those words denote "beings". When "Naro" is said, sometimes only the male is understood, and sometimes both female and male are understood, because the word "Nara" denotes both "man" and "being". When "Devatā, Vaṭṭakā, Godhā" are said, both females and males are understood, because although words like "Devatā" are feminine in gender, they denote both male and female. When "Sīho, Byaggho" are said, the male is understood; when "Sīhā, Byagghā" are said, both female and male are understood. When "Sīhā vā Sīhiyo vā, Byagghā vā Byagghiyo vā" are said, females and males are understood separately.

824. In counting, when two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine of the word "dasa" (ten) remain as one (through eka-sesa), the substitutions Vī, Ti, Cattāra, Paññā, Cha, Satta, Asa, and Nava occur respectively due to the "yo" case-endings. For the "yo" case-endings, there are the substitutions: īsaṃ, āsaṃ, ṭhi, ri, ti, īti, and uti. [The results are:] Vīsaṃ (20), Tiṃsaṃ (30), Cattālīsaṃ (40), Paññāsaṃ (50), Chaṭṭhi (60), Sattari (70), Sattati (70), Asīti (80), Navuti (90). Why say "in counting"? It is to indicate that such substitutions do not occur in places like "dasa-dasakā purisā" (men in groups of ten). By the characteristic of this rule, words such as "Vīsaṃ" have plural endings and do not have distinct forms based on gender.

825. Furthermore, words ending in "Navuti" starting from "Vīsa" and "Tiṃsa" have singular endings and are feminine in gender. Observe also the course of other words.
252:
The words from vīsati and tiṃsati up to navuti should be understood as feminine nouns ending in the singular number. If it is asked, "How is it known that vīsati, tiṃsati, etc., are singular and feminine?"—it is known from usage (payoga) and from the nature of their designation having indistinct forms.

Twenty monks stand. He sees twenty monks. The work done by twenty monks. The man gives to twenty monks. Departed from twenty monks. The property of twenty monks. Established in twenty monks.

Thus, there are forms such as: vīsati, vīsatiṃ, vīsatiyā, vīsatiyaṃ; tiṃsati, tiṃsaṃ, tiṃsāya, tiṃsāyaṃ; cattālīsa, cattālīsaṃ, cattālīsāya, cattālīsāyaṃ; paññāsa, paññāsaṃ, paññāsāya, paññāsāyaṃ; saṭṭhi, saṭṭhiṃ, saṭṭhiyā, saṭṭhiyaṃ; sattati, sattatiṃ, sattatiyā, sattatiyaṃ; asīti, asītiṃ, asītiyā, asītiyaṃ; navuti, navutiṃ, navutiyā, navutiyaṃ. In the Pali texts, where it occurs as "vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo," vīsaṃ, tiṃsaṃ, etc., should be understood as words ending in the accusative singular.

## 826. Catūpapadassa tulopo uttarapadādicassa cuco kvaci.
In the context of counting, the elision of the syllable 'tu' of the proximate word 'catu', and the substitution of the initial 'ca' of the subsequent word with 'cu' or 'co' occurs in some instances. Ten exceeded by four (14) — cuddasa, coddasa, catuddasa.

## 827. Cattālīsāyādivaṇṇassa ca.
In the context of counting, the elision of the initial syllable of the word 'cattālīsa', as well as the substitutions 'cu' and 'co', occurs in some instances. Tālīsaṃ, cattālīsaṃ, cuttālīsaṃ, cottālīsaṃ.

## 828. Caturāsītiyā tulopo, cassa cu, rassa lo, dvittañca.
In the context of counting, the elision of the syllable 'tu' of the word 'caturāsīti', the substitution of 'ca' with 'cu', the substitution of 'ra' with 'la', and doubling occur in some instances. Eighty-four thousand (cullāsītisahassāni), caturāsītisahassāni.
253:
829. In some instances, the letter 'sa' of the word *dvāsaṭṭhi* is elided, while the 'ā' of *dvā* is changed to 'a'. (Example) *Dvaṭṭhi paṭipadā*—sixty-two practices. *Dvāsaṭṭhi manussā*—sixty-two people.

830. In the views of other teachers, those words that are not accomplished by various specific rules are accomplished by the *nipātana* rule. In the views of other teachers, those words whose characteristics are not indicated by rules concerning phonemes, words, or consonants; or by feminine, masculine, or neuter genders; or by nouns, prefixes, or particles; or by compounds such as *avyayībhāva* and *taddhita* derivatives; or by counting, numbers, time, cases, usage, and nomenclature; or by euphonic combination (*sandhi*), natural state (*pakati*), strengthening (*vuddhi*), elision, augmentation, transformation, and inversion; or by the analysis of case endings—these words should be understood as being accomplished by the *nipātana* rule.

We have previously explained the characteristics of words in various places below, in terms of phonemes, words, and consonants, etc.
Now, I shall respectfully present the characteristics that bring benefit to the wise in the *nipātana* rule, without the slightest neglect.

Thus, we have previously indicated the characteristics of certain words from the perspective of phonemes, etc., by such methods as "*saralopo yamanarādīsu*," and have shown examples such as "*khatyā*" and "*paddhānī*." Now, in this Dispensation of the Blessed One, for the sake of removing the doubts of listeners regarding words that are subtle and varied through various ingenious methods, and for the sake of generating great skill in grasping the meaning, I shall present various characteristics in the *nipātana* rule without the slightest neglect. Since characteristics that are beneficial like rain (though repetitive) are seen here, it should not be said that there is the fault of tautology.

831. The suffix '-ka' is added after words such as *dvi* in various meanings. A group of two hundreds is called *dvisataṃ* (two hundred). A group of three hundreds is called *tisataṃ* (three hundred). A group of four hundreds is called *cutusataṃ* (four hundred). A group of five hundreds is called *pañcasataṃ* (five hundred). A group of six hundreds is called *chasataṃ* (six hundred). A group of...
254:
A group of seven hundreds is called *sattasataṃ* (seven hundred). A group of eight hundreds is called *aṭṭhasataṃ* (eight hundred). A group of nine hundreds is called *navasataṃ* (nine hundred). A group of ten hundreds is called *dasasataṃ*, which becomes *sahassa* (one thousand).

832. Because of the suffix '-yo', ten groups of ten (ten times ten) are designated as '*sata*' (one hundred); ten groups of one hundred (one hundred times ten) are designated as '*sahassa*' (one thousand). In counting, ten groups of ten constitute one hundred, and ten groups of one hundred constitute one thousand. *Sataṃ* (one hundred), *sahassaṃ* (one thousand).

833. Above that [one thousand], up to *asaṅkhyeyya* (the incalculable), it should be multiplied by ten; or, according to the Pali method, starting from *abbuda*, it should be multiplied by twenty, and the numbers from *nirabbuda* up to *asaṅkhyeyya* should be understood. 

How? Multiplying ten by ten makes one hundred (*sata*). Multiplying one hundred by ten makes one thousand (*sahassa*). Multiplying one thousand by ten makes ten thousand (*dasasahassa*). Multiplying ten thousand by ten makes one hundred thousand (*satasahassa*); that is called '*lakkha*'.

Multiplying one hundred thousand by ten makes one million (*dasasatasahassa*). Multiplying one million by ten makes ten million (*koṭi*). The meaning is that one hundred of one hundred thousands is called a *koṭi*. One hundred of one hundred thousand *koṭis* is a *pakoṭi*. One hundred of one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is a *koṭipakoṭi*. One hundred of one hundred thousand *koṭipakoṭis* is a *nahuta*. One hundred of one hundred thousand *nahutas* is a *ninnahuta*. One hundred of one hundred thousand *ninnahutas* is an *akkhobhaṇī*. Similarly, there are *bindu*, *abbuda*, *nirabbuda*, *ahaha*, *ababa*, *aṭaṭa*, *sogandhika*, *uppala*, *kumuda*, *paduma*, *puṇဍarīka*, *kathāna*, *mahakathāna*, and *asaṅkhyeyya*.

This arrangement is stated by adopting the views of the teachers. However, in the Dispensation, because of the statement, "This great earth is two hundred thousand and forty thousand (*satasahassabalahā*) yojanas in thickness," and the statement, "two hundred thousands and forty thousands," ten thousand is also called '*nahuta*'. Therefore: one, ten, hundred, thousand, *nahuta* (ten thousand)...
255:
According to the words "two hundred thousand and forty thousand", ten thousand is also called "Nahuta". Therefore—

Units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands (Nahuta),
Hundred-thousands (Lakkha), likewise millions (dasa-sata-sahassa),
Beyond that, thousands (sahassa),
Koṭi, Pakoṭi, Koṭipakoṭi, and so on,
The wise should point out in order.
In this presentation, Nahuta is the fifth and also the eleventh.

Another method—Units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands, millions, Koṭi, Pakoṭi, Koṭipakoṭi, Nahuta, Ninnahuta, Akkhobhaṇī; thus counting from one, Akkhobhaṇī stands in the thirteenth position.

"Nine thousand elephants; for each elephant, a hundred chariots;
For each chariot, a hundred horses; for each horse, a hundred warriors;
For each warrior, a hundred maidens; for each maiden, a hundred slave-girls;
This is called an Akkhobhaṇī, as spoken by the former teachers."

By these words, it should be understood as standing in the fourteenth position.

Akkhobhaṇī, Bindu, Abbuda, Nirabbuda,
Ahaha, Ababa, Aṭaṭa, Sugandhika,
Uppala, Kumuda, Paduma, Puṇဍarika,
Kathāna, Mahākathāna, Asaṅkhyeyya.
This is the order in the Kaccāyana text, which contradicts the Pāḷi.

In the Pāḷi, however, the order from Nirabbuda should be understood as follows—
Ababa, Aṭaṭa, Ahaha,
Kumuda, Sugandhika, Uppala,
Puṇḍarīka, Paduma; thus the Blessed One spoke.
256:
In the Brahmasaṃyutta Sutta, the Blessed One said: "Monks, just as twenty Abbudas are the lifespan of the Abbuda hell, so is one Nirabbuda the lifespan of the Nirabbuda hell," and so on, stating that twenty Abbudas make one Nirabbuda. Likewise, twenty Nirabbudas make one Ababa, twenty Ababas make one Aṭaṭa, twenty Aṭaṭas make one Ahaha, twenty Ahahas make one Kumuda, twenty Kumudas make one Sogandhika, twenty Sogandhikas make one Uppala, twenty Uppalas make one Puṇḍarīka, and twenty Puṇḍarīkas make one Paduma.

In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) also, the meaning is taken without contradicting the Pāḷi. How? Here, the count of years should be understood thus: Just as a hundred hundred-thousands make one Koṭi, so a hundred hundred-thousand Koṭis are called Pakoṭi, a hundred hundred-thousand Pakoṭis are called Koṭipakoṭi, a hundred hundred-thousand Koṭipakoṭis are called Nahuta, a hundred hundred-thousand Nahutas are called Ninnahuta, and a hundred hundred-thousand Ninnahutas are called one Abbuda. Multiplying that Abbuda by twenty makes a Nirabbuda; this method applies to all, including Ababa and so on. Therefore, we have said: "By the Pāḷi method, multiplying the count ending in Abbuda by twenty, one should understand from Nirabbuda up to Asaṅkhyeyya." In this matter, only the Pāḷi method should be trusted as the essence, because for the Omniscient Buddha, there is no such thing as unknown or poorly known phenomena.

In this context, the distinction between the terms for calculation should be understood thus—In the Pāḷi passages "Muddhā, Gaṇanā, Saṅkhyāna", Muddhā refers to counting by bending fingers, marking the joints of the fingers. It means counting by making a sign such as "one thousand on this finger". Gaṇanā means continuous counting; it means counting without interruption using the method of nine, such as "one, two", etc. Saṅkhyāna means aggregate counting. It means counting by totaling through summation and so on. By which counting, looking at a field, they know, "In this field, there will be this much grain"; looking at a tree...
257:
By looking [at the field], they know, "In this field, this much grain will be produced"; by looking at a tree, "On this tree, this much fruit will be produced"; by looking at the sky, "In this sky, birds of such a number will appear."

## 834. Ṇavatāṃ ṇo lopaṃ.
The 'ṇa' marker of those suffixes containing the letter 'ṇa' is completely elided. For example: *Gotamo* (son of Gotama), *Vāseṭṭho* (son of Vāseṭṭha), *Venateyyo* (son of Vinatā), and so forth.

## 835. Hīḷanānukampakhuddakakucchitasakatthesu ko.
The suffix '-ka' is applied in the senses of contempt, compassion, smallness, blame, and its own meaning (*sakattha*). Among these, in the sense of contempt: *muṇḍako* (a wretched shaveling), *samaṇako* (a wretched ascetic), *itthikā* (a mere woman), and so forth. In the sense of compassion: *puttako* (dear son), *kumārako* (dear boy), and so forth. In the sense of smallness: *gāmako* (small village), *rathako* (small chariot), *dhanukaṃ* (small bow), *naṅgalakaṃ* (small plough), and so forth. In the sense of blame: *uddhūmātakaṃ* (a bloated corpse), *vinīlakaṃ* (a discolored corpse), and so forth. In its own meaning (*sakattha*): *hīnako* (low), *potako* (young), and so forth.

## 836. Ekādito vibhāge dhā.
The suffix '-dhā' is applied after words such as *eka* in the sense of division. By one division—*ekadhā*; by two divisions—*dvidhā*; similarly *dvedhā*, *duvidhā*; by three divisions—*tidhā* or *tedhā*; similarly *catudhā*, *pañcadhā*, etc., as well as *katidhā* (in how many ways) and *bahudhā* (in many ways).

## 837. Ekadvīhi jjho.
The suffix '-jjha' is applied after the words *eka* and *dvi* in the sense of division. In the sense of doing with one division (together)—*ekajjhaṃ* (meaning to do as one or together). In the sense of doing with two divisions—*dvijjhaṃ*. Because those Buddhas do not have double speech (divided speech), they are called *advijjhavacanā* (those without double speech).

## 838. Ākāra pakāra vibhāgakevalatatiyatthesu so.
The suffix '-so' is applied in the senses of manner, variety, division, and the pure instrumental sense without being mixed with manner, etc. Among these, in the sense of manner: *sabbākārena* (in every manner) becomes *sabbaso*, and so forth. In the sense of variety: *bahūhi pakārehi* (in many varieties)...
258:
These are bahuso, etc. In the sense of division (vibhāgattha), by dividing the Suttas, it is "suttaso", etc. In the pure instrumental sense (kevalatatiyattha), by way of means it is "upāyaso", by way of cause "hetuso", at that very moment "ṭhānaso", by way of reason "yoniso", etc.

839. The suffix "sa" is added after the word lahu in its own meaning (sakattha). Whatever faults there are that are slight, of minor measure, light, or considered light. In this context, "lahūni" itself is "lahusāni", meaning those that are light. However, in the passage "lomasāni brahāni ca", the meaning should be taken as "lomasāni" (having hair) because hairs (hair of the head) arise in this (head).

840. The suffix "ḷhaka" is added after the word "dvi" in the sense of state (bhāvattha). In the sense of state, the suffix ḷhaka comes from the word dvi; the state of being two is "dvebhāvo", "dveḷhakaṃ", "dveḷhakajāto" (the state of being twofold).

841. It should be known that a suffix may also be added after another suffix.

842. The suffix "ṇiya" is added after the suffix "yu" which follows the root "yā" preceded by "nī". The suffix yu which follows the root yā preceded by nī is placed before, and after that yu suffix, the suffix ṇiya occurs. Because it leads out, it is called "niyāniya". In that very word niyāniya, by making the vowel ī in nī short (rassatā), making the y double (dvibhāva), and changing the second y to k, it becomes "niyyāniko". For this reason, it is stated in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: "Because it is said 'niyyāti', where it should be said 'niyāniya', the ī is made short and the y is changed to k, thus it is called 'niyyānika'." It is further stated: "Alternatively, it is called 'niyyāna' because one leads out by means of this [Dhamma]; niyyāna itself is 'niyyānika', like 'venayika'. Here, where it should be said 'neyyānika', it is spoken without changing i to e."
259:
## 843. Tavato tassidamiccatthe iyo tassarocu.
After the word "tava", the suffix "iya" is added in the sense of "his possession" (tassedaṃ); also, the vowel 'a' of the letter 'ta' is changed to 'u'. Because of the sense "this is your possession", it becomes "tuviyaṃ". As for the meaning of this tuviyaṃ, the verse appearing in the Jayadisa Jātaka is the evidence:

"Dear son, before this time, I do not remember any fault of yours (tuviyaṃ) committed by deed or by word."

In that verse, "aparādhito" should be analyzed as "aparādhaṃ ito". "Tuviyaṃ" is called tuviyo because of the sense "this is your possession"; that possession of yours is called "tuviyaṃ". It is in apposition (tulyādhikaraṇa) with the word "aparādhaṃ". Therefore, it was said in the Commentary: "Tuviyaṃ means your possession." By saying "tava santakaṃ", it demonstrates that the word tuviya is a derivative (taddhita) ending in a suffix. Just as the word "sokaraṃ" is a taddhita derivative by the definition "this is the meat of a pig", so it is here. For just as when "sokaraṃ maṃsaṃ" is said, it means pork, even so when "tuviyo aparādho" is said, it means your fault. Herein, the summary of the meaning is: "Dear son, before this time, I do not remember any fault of mine that is unpleasant to me, caused by your bodily action or vocal action."

## 844. Sabbanāmehi thātatthāpakāravacane.
After pronouns, the suffixes "thā" and "tatthā" are added in the sense of manner (pakāra). Such a manner is "tathā". That manner is "tathā", by that manner is "tathā". Likewise: "yathā" (in which manner), "sabbathā" (in every manner), "aññathā" (in another manner), "itarathā" (in a manner other than this), "ubhayathā" (in both manners). By that manner is "tatatthā"; likewise "yatatthā", "aññatatthā". However, some teachers desire the derivation as "a manner like that is tatatthā", etc. All this should be borne in mind. The suffix "tatthā" is rarely used in the Pāḷi Canon; only the suffix "ttayuga" is well-known. For example: being in that way is "tathattaṃ" (the state of being so), likewise "aññathattaṃ" (the state of being otherwise), etc. Here also, there are examples such as: "The alteration (aññathattaṃ) of that which exists is discerned," and "He practices for the sake of truth (tathattāya)." Therein, "tathattāya" means for the sake of the state of truth (tathabhāvāya).
260:
845. After the words "kiṃ" and "ima", the suffix "thaṃ" occurs in the sense of expressing manner (pakāra). If it is asked "in what manner?", it is "kathaṃ"; "which manner?", it is "kathaṃ"; "by what manner?", it is "kathaṃ". Here also, "How (kathaṃ) shall we know you?" is the example. "This manner" is "itthaṃ"; "this manner (accusative)" is "itthaṃ". Here also, the derivation "itthambhūta" meaning "one who has reached such a state" is the example. "By this manner" is "itthaṃ". Here also, "Thus (itthaṃ) indeed did the Venerable Elder Puḷinathūpiya speak these verses" is the example. In such phrases as "itthanāmo" (having such a name), "itthanāmassa bhikkhuno" (to the monk having such a name), etc., where the meaning is "such a name as Tissa or Phussa belongs to him", the word "evaṃ" should be understood as being substituted by "itthaṃ". If it is asked, "O Teacher, since the word 'evaṃ' is an indeclinable (avyaya), how can it deserve the substitution 'itthaṃ'?", the answer is: it certainly deserves it. This is because substitutions like 'ajjha' are seen for indeclinables like 'adhi', etc. The indeclinable nature of those words consists in the absence of change due to gender and case, not in the absence of substitution (ādesa).

846. When the word "nāma" follows, "evaṃ" is changed to "itthaṃ". "Itthanāmo bhikkhu" (a monk of such a name). Why say "when nāma follows"? [Compare] "evaṃgotto" (of such a clan).

847. When a suffix with an elided 'ṇa' (saṇa) follows, there is vuddhi (strengthening) of vowels that do not end in a conjunct. One who studies the Abhidhamma is "ābhidhammiko"; the son of Vinatā is "venateyyo", etc. Why say "not ending in a conjunct"? [Compare] "bhaggavo" (son of Bhaggu).

848. In words such as "viākaraṇa", etc., vuddhi of 'i' and 'u' does not occur; instead, vuddhi [vowels e and o] appears in the appropriate place. In words such as viākaraṇa, sagga, etc., the vuddhi of the vowels 'i' and 'u' does not happen; rather, it is only the appearance of vuddhi (e, o) in the place of those vowels. Here also—
261:
The arrival of e and o strengthening (ekārokāravuddhiāgamo). Examples include veyyākaraṇiko, sovaggiko, and so forth.

849. The word "nippajjate" should be understood as governing the subsequent sutras.

850. When the suffix saṇakāra follows, the analytical form (byāsarūpa) of the word byākaraṇa, which is "viākaraṇa", is accomplished. One who knows grammar (byākaraṇa) is called "veyyākaraṇo". Similarly, "veyyākaraṇiko" is also formed.

851. When the suffix saṇa follows, the analytical form of the word sagga, which is "suagga", is accomplished. It is called "sagga" (heaven) because it is excellently noble (suṭṭhu agga) through the five strands of sensual pleasure such as visible forms. A gift that is conducive to heaven because it yields results in the heavenly realm is called "sovaggikaṃ".

852. When the suffix saṇa follows, the analytical form of the word nyāya, which is "niāya", is accomplished. One who studies the method (nyāya) is called "neyyāyiko".

853. When the suffix saṇa follows the word byāvaccha, the analytical form "viāvaccha" is accomplished. The son of Byāvaccha is called "veyyāvaccho".

854. When the suffix saṇa follows the word dvāra, the analytical form "duara" is accomplished. It is called "dvāra" (door) because two door-leaves occur (move) here. Alternatively, it is called "dvāra" because two functions, entering and exiting, occur here. One who is appointed at the door is called "dovāriko". (In the Apadāna of Elder Ekappaṭṭhiya, it is said, "At that time, I was a terrestrial demon at the southern door," thus "duvāra" also exists.)

855. When the suffix saṇa follows the word byaggha, which denotes tiger skin, the analytical form "viaggha" is accomplished. This skin of a tiger is called "veyyagghaṃ". Chariots covered with tiger skin are called "veyyagghā".

When will the horse-drawn chariots,
firmly harnessed, with hoisted banners,
covered with panther skins, and also covered with tiger skins,
adorned with all chariot ornaments, proceed?
262:
Camma means tiger skin. Chariots covered with tiger skin are meant by veyyaggha (chariots covered with tiger skin). Thus it is seen in the Pāḷi:

"When will the horse-drawn chariots,
firmly harnessed, with hoisted banners,
covered with panther skins, and also covered with tiger skins,
adorned with all ornaments,
not follow behind me?
When will that not following occur?"

856. Other analytical forms of other words are also accomplished in ways other than these.

857. In words such as isi and usabha, the state of ā occurs in place of i and u. The augment of the letter ri also occurs when the suffix saṇa follows. "The state of a seer (isi) is called ārisaṃyaṃ. The state of iṇa is called āṇyaṃ. This place of a bull (usabha) is called āsabhaṃ. The state of an upright person (uju) is called ājjavaṃ." This is stated according to the preference of teachers who contemplate on letters (akkharacintaka). However, according to the Buddha's preference (sogatamata), "The state of an upright person is called ajjawo," where the long ā becomes short. That word ajjawo is mostly in the masculine gender, like the word gāravo in the passage "gāravo ca nivāto ca". This being so, it is found in the Pāḷi as "ajjawo ca maddavo ca". According to a few preferences, it is found in some Pāḷi passages as "ajjavaṃ, gāravaṃ, maddavaṃ".

858. In some places, the initial, medial, and final vowels become long (dīgha) or short (rassa). Among these, first, regarding the initial lengthening: pākāro (wall), nīvāro (dwelling), pāsādo (palace), etc. Regarding the medial lengthening: mahākāruṇiko—one who is associated with great compassion (mahākaruṇā) or the locus of great compassion; aṅgamāgadhiko—a person from the Aṅga and Magadha regions, etc. Regarding the final lengthening: añjanāgirī, koṭarāvanaṃ, tālāvatthukatā, etc. This is called sabhāvadīghatā (natural lengthening). The chief of the Gandhabba deities; from a chasm or from a mountain; palinā (having flown)...
263:
In the phrase 'Like the king of swans flying in the sky from the Rose-apple Island (Jambudīpa),' the long vowel at the end of 'Jambudīpāto' is known as length due to meter (chanda-dīgha). O Teacher, is it not more appropriate to say 'pabbatamhā' instead of 'pabbatāto,' or 'jambudīpamhā' instead of 'jambudīpāto'? If so, why did the Omniscient Buddha and his disciples not preach it in that way? This should not be questioned. The reason is that in the context of verses, the majority of people, even those with the eye of wisdom, are unable to speak such specific linguistic variations. The Teacher is exceedingly skilled in worldly usages (lokavohāra), and the disciples who follow him are the same. Therefore, one should note it exactly as they have preached it.

O Teacher, was this phrase 'darito pabbatatāto vā' not spoken by the Bodhisatta (Prince Temiya) and not by the Blessed One? That should not be said. The reason is that although the meaning was spoken by the Bodhisatta, the Blessed One, upon becoming the Buddha, took that meaning and preached both the meaning and the Pali text. This is indeed true. In the Jātakas, the Blessed One took the meaning of words spoken by dogs, jackals, and others, composed them into verses, and delivered the teaching, saying, 'The dog spoke this verse,' and so on. This is because dogs, jackals, and the like do not have the ability to compose verses. Therefore, the words spoken by the Bodhisatta are indeed the words preached by the Blessed One.

In the Pali Canon preached by the Blessed One, there is nothing to be removed. This is because the Tathāgatas do not speak even a single syllable that is useless. However, in the words of disciples, deities, and others, there may be things that should be removed, and the Elders who were the Reciters of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka) removed them. On the other hand, there are things to be added in all parts of the Pali Canon. Therefore, they added what was appropriate to be added. What are those additions? They are merely connective phrases such as 'tena samayena' (at that time), 'tena kho pana samayena' (now at that time), 'atha kho' (then), 'evaṃ vutte' (when this was said), 'etadavoca' (said this), and so on.

In this context, initial shortening (ādi-rassa) occurs in words like 'pageva,' and so on. Medial shortening (majjhe-rassa) occurs in words like 'sumedhaso,' and so on. Final shortening (uttara-rassa) occurs in words like 'gotrabhū,' 'sukhakāri dānaṃ,' and so on. This is known as natural shortness (sabhāva-rassatā). The phrase 'suññāgāre va' (or in an empty house), and the phrase 'one should offer every sacrifice in the world,' are known as shortness due to meter (vutti-rassatā).

In those initial, medial, and final positions, strengthening (vuddhi), elision (lopa), augmentation (āgama), alteration (vikāra), inversion (viparīta), and substitution (ādesa) also occur. In those initial, medial, and final positions, without contradicting the Blessed One's Pali text, strengthening (vuddhi) occurs in some places. In doing so, first, initial strengthening (ādi-vuddhi) occurs in words like 'ābhidhammiko,' and so on. Medial strengthening (majjhe-vuddhi) occurs in words like 'sukhaseyyaṃ,' and so on. Final strengthening (uttara-vuddhi) occurs in words like 'kāliṅgo,' and so on. Initial elision (ādi-lopa) occurs in words like 'tālīsaṃ,' and so on. Medial elision (majjhe-lopa) occurs in words like 'kattukāmo,' and so on. Final elision (uttara-lopa) occurs in words like 'bhikkhu,' and so on. Initial augmentation (ādi-āgama) occurs in words like 'dubhato,' 'vanavikāse,' and so on. Medial augmentation (majjhe-āgama) occurs in words like 'samaṇamacalo,' 'etadatthā,' and so on.

Here, 'samaṇamacalo' means that the Arahant is both tranquil (samaṇa) and unshakable by the worldly winds (acala); thus, it means 'samaṇācalo' (the unshakable Arahant). O Teacher, do not say that because the word 'macala' occurs in the sense of a thief, the term 'samaṇamacalo' seems to have an unseemly meaning. The reason is that in this context, the letter 'ma' has no meaning.
264:
The term 'Bhikkhavo' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.222) and the sentence 'Whatever sacrifice or offering one might make in the world' (Khuddaka Nikāya 1.29, 35) are instances of shortness due to meter (vutti-rassatā).

859. In those (initial, medial, and final positions), strengthening (vuddhi), elision (lopa), augmentation (āgama), alteration (vikāra), inversion (viparīta), and substitution (ādesa) also occur. In those initial, medial, and final positions, without contradicting the Blessed One's Pali text, strengthening occurs in some places, elision occurs in some, augmentation occurs in some, alteration occurs in some, inversion occurs in some, and substitution occurs in some. In doing so, initial strengthening (ādi-vuddhi) is found in 'ābhidhammiko' (one who studies Abhidhamma), and so on. Medial strengthening (majjhe-vuddhi) is found in 'sukhaseyyaṃ' (sleeping peacefully), and so on. Final strengthening (uttara-vuddhi) is found in 'kāliṅgo' (the king who rules the Kalinga kingdom), and so on. Initial elision (ādi-lopa) is found in 'tālīsaṃ' (forty), and so on. Medial elision (majjhe-lopa) is found in 'kattukāmo' (one who wishes to do), and so on. Final elision (uttara-lopa) is found in 'bhikkhu' (monk), and so on. Initial augmentation (ādi-āgama) is found in 'dubhato vanavikāse' (in the two forest groves), and so on. Medial augmentation (majjhe-āgama) is found in 'samaṇamacalo' (the unshakable Arahant), 'etadatthā kathā' (this purposeful speech), and so on. Here, 'samaṇamacalo' means that the Arahant is both tranquil (samaṇa) and unshakable (acala); thus, he is 'samaṇamacalo.' It has the meaning of 'samaṇācalo' (the unshakable Arahant).

Venerable Sir, since the word 'macala' occurs in the sense of a thief, does this term 'samaṇamacalo' not seem to have an unseemly meaning? Do not say so. In this context, the letter 'ma' has no meaning and is merely placed near the word 'acala'; furthermore, the term 'samaṇamacalo' is traditionally established only for the unshakable Arahant (and thus it is not unseemly). This is indeed true. It is said, 'Conventional language is true; it is based on worldly consensus.' This term is also a conventional designation made by the Blessed One, who is skilled in worldly usage. By the mere fact that the Blessed One preached 'samaṇamacalo,' deities and humans understood it to have a very clear and beautiful meaning.
