For example, in the verse beginning with 'Assaddho akataññū ca' (Dhammapada 97), the terms 'assaddha' (not believing the words of others due to personal realization of the supramundane), 'akataññū' (knowing Nibbāna, which is not created by causes), 'sandhiccheda' (one who has cut the connection of the cycle of rebirth), 'hatavakāsa' (one who has destroyed the opportunity for rebirth by exhausting the seeds of kamma), and 'vantāsa' (one who has vomited out all desires) appear as if they have beautiful meanings. Similarly, this term 'samaṇamacalo' also has only a beautiful meaning and not an unseemly one. Just as a golden-hued young swan would converse and consult with another golden-hued young swan, or a radiant golden swan with another radiant golden swan regarding the Dhamma. In this place...
265:
The terms sandhiccheda (cutting the connection of Saṃsāra), hatavakāsa (destroying the place of rebirth), and vantāsa (having vomited out craving) possess beautiful and appropriate meanings. Similarly, the term 'samaṇamacala' (the immovable recluse) also has a beautiful meaning, not an unbeautiful one.

"When a golden-hued swan youth speaks and consults with another golden-hued swan youth, and a golden-shining swan youth with another golden-shining swan youth,
What business has a jackal there, who is lowly in the four aspects (body, birth, voice, and virtue)? O jackal, enter your hole!"

In this Jātaka, the consonant (sound) of 'catumaṭṭhassa' is beautiful, but the literal meaning is unbeautiful because it is a word of reproach. Also, in the Upasālaka Jātaka, in the passage "There is no place in the world that is not a cemetery (anāmata)," the word 'anāmata' refers to the cemetery, which is the place of the dead. Because the word 'amata' usually refers to the noble Great Nibbāna or divine food, here the beautiful consonant 'amata' has come to have an unbeautiful meaning (cemetery). It should be understood that in the world, people often use words or meanings that are inauspicious by associating them with auspicious terms, just as the designation 'amata' (deathless) is used for a cemetery, or as Tuesday (aṅgāravāra - charcoal day) is conventionally called 'maṅgalavāra' (auspicious day).

Among those grammatical terms, uttara-āgamo (the arrival of a subsequent letter) includes examples like vedallaṃ. Ādi-vikāro (alteration at the beginning) includes ārisyaṃ, āsabhaṃ, etc. Majjhe-vikāro (alteration in the middle) includes varārisyaṃ, etc. Uttara-vikāro (alteration at the end) includes yāni tāni, etc. Ādi-viparitō (reversal at the beginning) includes uññātaṃ, 'daharo ti na uññātabbo', 'ūhato rajo', etc. Here, in the word 'uññātaṃ', it should be understood that first the word 'ava' is changed to 'o', and then 'o' is changed to 'u'. Similarly, in the word 'ūhato', it should be understood that 'o' is changed to 'ū'. Majjhe-viparitō (reversal in the middle) includes samūhato, etc. Uttara-viparitō (reversal at the end) includes digu, etc. Ādi-ādesō (substitution at the beginning) includes yūnaṃ, etc. Majjhe-ādesō (substitution in the middle) includes nyāyogo, etc. Uttara-ādesō (substitution at the end) includes sabbaseyyo, sabbaseṭṭho, cittaṃ, etc. Here, the teachers say, "The procedure indicated by the nominative case (paṭhamā vibhatti) is called ādesa," while vikāra (alteration) is...
266:
They say, "The procedure indicated by the accusative case (dutiyā vibhatti) is called vikāra," and "Viparita is the ancient name for 'o' which is made from 'ava'." Other teachers, however, say:

"The change of one letter into another, the unification of conjuncts, and a single letter becoming a conjunct are called vikāra."

Yet other teachers say:
"The shortening of a long vowel, the lengthening of a short vowel, a single letter becoming a conjunct, the unification of conjuncts, consonants becoming vowels, the change into another consonant, and the change of a vowel into another vowel are called viparita (reversal)."

These three views of the three teachers are contradictory to one another; therefore, this matter should be noted separately.

860. For the letters a, i, and u, there are instances of vuddhi (strengthening) into ā, e, and o, as well as instances where vuddhi does not occur. (For example:) ābhidhammiko, venateyyo, oḷumpiko, abhidhammiko, vinateyyo, uḷumpiko, etc.

861. In words such as vasiṭṭha, vuddhi always occurs because of the suffix 'ṇa'. (For example:) vāseṭṭho, bāladevo, etc.

862. In words such as vinata, vuddhi is not constant. In words such as vinata, even when the suffix 'ṇakāra' follows, vuddhi is not constant. (For example:) venateyyo, vinateyyo, kāruññako, etc.

863. Vuddhi does not occur in words such as nīla. In words such as nīla, even when the suffix 'ṇakāra' follows, vuddhi does not occur. A blue cloth is his property, thus he is called nīlavatthiko. Similarly, pītavatthiko (one who has yellow cloth). Why is it said "in words such as nīla"? It is to show that vuddhi does not occur in the word peṭakopadesa (the Peṭakopadesa treatise).
268:
867. The Third Person (paṭhamapurisa), Second Person (majjhimapurisa), and First Person (uttamapurisa) each have two forms (in parassapada and attanopada). 'Ti' and 'anti' are the Third Persons. 'Si' and 'tha' are the Second Persons. 'Mi' and 'ma' are the First Persons. Similarly, 'te' and 'ante' are the Third Persons. 'Se' and 'vhe' are the Second Persons. 'E' and 'mhe' are the First Persons. This description is stated according to the present tense (vattamānā vibhatti). In the remaining tenses/moods, this same method should be applied.

868. When expressed together (when different persons are mixed), the person that comes later in the hierarchy must be used to coordinate. (Example:) He cooks, and you cook; (then) you (plural) cook. Or, you cook, and he cooks; (then) you (plural) cook. He cooks, you cook, and I cook; (then) we cook. Or, I cook, you cook, and he cook; (then) we cook. In this manner, the later person should be applied in the remaining tenses. Why is it said "when expressed together"? To show that in a case like "He cooks, you will cook, I cooked," because the times (tenses) are different, they cannot be combined as "We cooked."

869. Whether a noun is explicitly used or not, if there is a common grammatical relation (in the agentive sense), the Third Person (paṭhamapurisa) is used. (Example:) He goes. Even if the noun is not used with the word 'pi', (it is still Third Person, example:) He speaks or he does. Why is it said "if there is a common grammatical relation"? (To show that in) "You are struck by that Devadatta," (Devadatta is not in the nominative case, thus the Third Person verb does not agree with it).

870. Whether the word 'tumha' (you) is used or not, if there is a common grammatical relation, the Second Person (majjhimapurisa) is used. (Example:) You go, you (plural) go, (you) go, (you plural) go. Why is it said "if there is a common grammatical relation"? (To show that in) "The rice is cooked by you," (the word 'you' is not the direct agent in the nominative, thus the Second Person verb is not used).

871. Whether the word 'amha' (I/we) is used or not, if there is a common grammatical relation, the First Person (uttamapurisa) is used. (Example:) I worship, we worship, (I) worship, (we) worship. Why is it said "if there is a common grammatical relation"? (To show that in) "The Buddha is worshipped by me," (the word 'me' is not the direct agent in the nominative, thus the First Person verb is not used).
269:
872. The Vattamānā (present tense) suffix occurs in the present time. In this rule, 'time' refers to the action. (Example:) The Blessed One dwells in the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī.

873. The Vattamānā suffix also occurs in the past time that is near to the present. Because of its proximity to the present time, the Vattamānā suffix is used figuratively for the past time. In the statement, "Monk, from where do you come?", it should be understood that the monk has already arrived and is sitting there.

874. The Vattamānā suffix occurs in the future time when associated with the particles yāva, pure, and purā.
As long as the knowledge of a fool is only for his own harm.
Before the unrighteousness shines.
Cut these tusks before I die.
Before it rains.

875. The Vattamānā suffix occurs in the future time in the senses of certainty (ekaṃsa), inevitability (avassambhāvī), and indefinite time (aniyama).
In the sense of certainty: "I shall surely go to hell; there is no doubt for me in this."
In the sense of inevitability: "I shall certainly become a Buddha."
In the sense of indefinite time: "If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind."
In this context, since the Vattamānā expression is desired to denote general time without specifying a particular time, it also implies the meanings: "has spoken or has acted, will speak or will act."

876. In the opinion of other teachers, the Vattamānā suffix optionally occurs in the future time when associated with the particles kadā and karahi. "When does he go?", "When does he go?". Why is it said "optionally"? Because the future tense is also used: "Venerable sir, when will he go?", "When will he go?"
270:
877. The Vattamānā suffix also occurs in the past time in a question-response context where the particle nanu is used as an adjacent word. In one opinion of the teachers, the Vattamānā suffix occurs in the past time when the particle nanu is used in a question-response preceded by an inquiry. Example: When asked, "O Devadatta, did you make the mat?", the response "Sir, I am making it (nanu karomi bho)" uses the Vattamānā suffix. Why is it said "in a question-response"? It is to prevent the Vattamānā suffix from being used in ordinary sentences such as "Devadatta made the mat (akāsi kaṭaṃ devadatto)."

878. The Vattamānā suffix optionally occurs in the past time in a question-response context where the particles na and nu are used as adjacent words. In one opinion of the teachers, the Vattamānā suffix optionally occurs in the past time when na and nu are used in a question-response. Example: When asked, "O Devadatta, did you make the mat?", one may respond, "Sir, I do not (na karomi bho)" or "I did not (nākāsiṃ)." Also: "Do I make it? (ahaṃ nu karomi)" or "Did I make it? (ahaṃ nwakāsiṃ)."

881. The Vattamānā suffix also occurs in the past time when it is capable of expressing the past meaning. Example: "Then fear does not arise (bhayaṃ tadā na bhavati)" means "Then fear did not arise (bhayaṃ tadā nāhosi)." Grammatical scholars, however, desire the Vattamānā expression in the sense of benediction (wishing), which is the domain of the Pañcamī suffix, saying "The virtuous are victorious (jayanti santo)" instead of "May the virtuous be victorious (jayantu santo)." That opinion should not be accepted because it is not in accordance with the Teaching (Sāsana). For in the Teaching, the word 'jayati' (is victorious) is not found where 'jayatu' (may he be victorious) should be said. Only "May the Great King Vessantara be victorious (jayatu bhavaṃ vessantaramahārājā)" is found. Just as the first person is used in place of the second person when associated with the particle mā (Example: "Great King, do not fear (mā bhāyi mahārājā)"), the Vattamānā expression is not seen in the sense of the Pañcamī for benediction. Therefore, that statement should not be accepted.

880. The Pañcamī suffix occurs in the unspecified time (anuttakāla) in these senses: commanding (āṇatti), wishing (āsiṭṭha), reviling (akkosa), swearing (sapatha), requesting (yācana), prescribing (vidhi), inviting (nimantana), calling (āmantana), entreating (ajjhiṭṭha), questioning (samppucchana), and praying (patthanā). Among these, āṇatti means commanding. It is also called 'niyoga' in the science of grammar.
271:
Ordering (āṇatti) is called niyoga in grammatical treatises. In grammatical treatises, niyoga is intended to be preceded by disrespect (anādara). In this Dispensation, however, whether preceded by disrespect or respect (ādara), niyoga characterized by ordering is intended in both cases. In that sense of ordering (āṇatti)— "Go to the village," "Let those who wish to expel, expel; let those who wish to kill, kill," "Let him dwell on Mount Vaṅka," "Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma; listen to that Dhamma," and so forth.

Aspiration (āsīsana) means the longing (āsiṭṭha) for a desired benefit. In that sense of aspiration— "May you be happy," "May they be free from disease and happy," "May this prince be long-lived," and so forth. Cursing (akkosana) is the same as abuse (akkosa). In that sense of cursing— "Let a fierce buffalo pursue him," "Let thieves cut him into pieces," and so forth.

In the sense of an oath (sapatha)— "Whoever stole your mangoes, O hermit, let him sleep alone on his bed," "O Vepacitti Asura, may your fear never end," and so forth. In the sense of request (yācana)— "Please grant the noble white elephant," and so forth. Injunction (vidhi) is the instruction of what should be done. In that sense of injunction— "Perform merit," "Plough the field," "Cook rice," and so forth.

An order preceded by respect is called an invitation (nimantana). In that sense of invitation— "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal," "May the gentleman sit here," and so forth. Allowing one to act as one pleases is called āmantana. In that sense of āmantana— "May the gentleman come," "Let King Vessantara rule in the kingdom of Sivi as he pleases," and so forth. Entreaty (ajjhesana) is an order preceded by reverence (ajjhiṭṭha). In that sense of entreaty— "May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma," "May both King Vessantara and Queen Maddī act as our rulers," and so forth. Inquiry is called sampucchana. In that sense of inquiry— "Sir, shall I listen to the Abhidhamma or the Vinaya?" and so forth. A wish (patthanā) is the longing for a benefit to be obtained in the future, whether it be good or bad. In that sense of wishing—
272:
"Venerable Sir, even if I am reborn in many lives in Saṃsāra, may I not have a life of longing; may I be beloved wherever I am born, like this jasmine garland," or "May I be one capable of depriving this person of life," and so forth.

881. The Sattamī (Optative) case occurs in the senses of consent (anumati), conjecture (parikappa), injunction (vidhi), invitation (nimantana), permission (āmantana), entreaty (ajjhiṭṭha), inquiry (sampucchana), and wish (patthanā). Among these, in the sense of consent— "O King, you should come at that time," "You should go," and so forth. In the sense of conjecture— "What should I do?", "Even if the wind should carry away Mount Meru," and so forth. In the sense of injunction— "One should go to the village," "One should cook rice," and so forth. In the sense of invitation— "May the gentleman eat here," and so forth. In the sense of permission— "May the gentleman sit here," and so forth. In the sense of entreaty— "One should teach the young man," and so forth. In the sense of inquiry— "Sir, should I learn the Dhamma or the Vinaya?" and so forth. In the sense of wish— "I would give, I would not waver," "I would not go to another's wife, I would be devoted to my own wife, I would not come under the power of women," "May I be an Omniscient One who does not return from there (to a new birth)," and so forth.

882. Both the Pañcamī (Imperative) and Sattamī (Optative) cases occur in the senses of command (pesa), permission (atisagga), and proper time (pattakāla). Sending or ordering (pesana) is called pesa. In that sense of pesa— "Sir, please make a mat" (karotu - Pañcamī), "Sir, you should make a mat" (kareyya - Sattamī). Granting permission to act as one pleases is called atisagga. In that sense of atisagga— "Sir, please perform merit," "One should perform merits that bring happiness," and so forth. In the sense of proper time— "This is the proper time for you to speak the truth," "One should speak the truth."

883. The Sattamī case occurs in the sense of time (kāla), occasion (samaya), and period (velā) when in proximity to the word 'yaṃ'.
273:
It is the time when the master should eat. It is the opportunity when the master should wait. It is the time when the master should speak. Here, the word 'yaṃ' is a particle.

## 884. Arahasattīsu ca.
The Sattamī suffix occurs in the senses of worthiness (araha) and capability (satti). Between these two, in the sense of worthiness: The master indeed should take the maiden; the master is worthy of this (maiden). In the sense of capability: The master indeed should be able to carry the load; in this matter, the master should be able to speak; who can disentangle this tangle of craving? Here, 'vijataye' means 'who is capable of disentangling?'. Other examples should be applied in the same way.

## 885. Appaccakkhetīte parokkhā.
The Parokkhā suffix occurs in the past time that was not witnessed (indirect). It is said [he] said in a dream; thus the ancients said.

## 886. Paccakkhe vā hiyyopabhutihiyyattanī.
The Hiyyattanī suffix occurs in the past time from yesterday onwards, whether witnessed or not witnessed. He went to the path; they went to the path.

## 887. Ajjatanī samīpamhi.
The Ajjatanī suffix occurs in the recent past time from today onwards, whether witnessed or not witnessed. He went to the path; they went to the path.

## 888. Māyogatthāne tā pāyena.
Those Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī suffixes mostly occur when associated with the particle 'mā'. Among them, the Hiyyattanī first: "May [the Blessed One] not step on him in the mud"—this should be connected with 'Bhagavā'. "May the moment of a Buddha's arising not pass by." "May the benefit for the Great King not pass by." If the plural is desired, it should be said "atthā mā upajjagū," as in the Aṅguttara Pali: "They have transcended all suffering." These examples are of Hiyyattanī and Ajjatanī: "O King, do not neglect the Dhamma"—this should be connected with 'tvaṃ'. "Do not perform evil deeds"—this should be connected with 'tumhe'. "May I not be like the foolish crow..."
274:
May I, King Arindama, not follow the desires of the senses with sensual lust, like a foolish crow. In this context, the word 'anvagaṃ' can be either the first person singular of the Parassapada in the Hiyattanī tense, or the first person singular of the Attanopada in the Ajjatanī tense. This is the Ajjatanī tense: 'O sixty thousand Ceta kings, may you not delight in going to request from the father.' To say 'May that which is subject to aging not age' is an impossible thing. 'May [it] not be ill, may [it] not die, may [it] not be exhausted, may [it] not be destroyed, may they not age, may they not be ruined.' 'I went, we went.' 'Indeed, may the country not be destroyed.' Other words should also be investigated. In the Pāḷi Canon, these Hiyattanī and Ajjatanī inflections occur in thousands of ways in connection with the word 'mā'.

## 889. The Pañcamī inflection is rare in the Pāḷi Canon.
The Pañcamī inflection is rare in the Pāḷi Canon in places associated with the word 'mā'; it is not very frequent. However, in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) and other texts, it is more frequent. If it is asked why that Pañcamī inflection is rare in the Pāḷi Canon—it is because in some places where the Pañcamī should be used, the Hiyattanī and Ajjatanī inflections are used instead, such as 'mā majjhe bhaṅgo ahosi' (may there be no break in the middle). If it is asked why that Pañcamī inflection is more frequent in the Commentaries and other texts—it is because it appears in forms such as 'mā vada' (do not speak), 'mā gaccha' (do not go), 'mā vadāhi', 'mā gacchāhi', 'mā bhuñjassu', 'mā hotu', etc., and also because it appears as an explanation of the meaning of Pāḷi passages like 'mā jīrī' (may it not age) as 'mā jīratu'. Among those uses of the Pañcamī, the Pañcamī applications from the Pāḷi Canon such as 'mā te bhavantvantarāyā' (may there be no dangers for you) and 'dāṭhinī mātimanyavho' (do not despise the tusked creature) are very few.

## 890. Parokkhā and Vattamānā are even rarer.
The Parokkhā and Vattamānā inflections are very rare in places associated with the word 'mā'. 'Mā kisittho mayā vinā' (may you not be weary without me); here, it should be connected with 'you' (tvaṃ). This is an application of the Parokkhā. 'Mā deva paridevesi' (O King, do not lament); here, it should be connected with 'you' (tvaṃ). This is an application of the Vattamānā. Other words should also be applied in this manner.
275:
891. In the alternative view of other teachers, when associated with the word 'mā', the Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, and Pañcamī suffixes occur in all tenses. In the alternative view of the teachers, it is stated (in the scriptures) that whenever there is an association with the word 'mā', then the Hiyattanī, Ajjatanī, and Pañcamī suffixes occur in all tenses. Examples of these are: mā gamā, mā vacā, mā gamī, mā vacီ, mā gacchāhi, so mā bhavā, mā bhavi, mā te bhavantvantarāyā.

In the view of those teachers, the word 'mā gamā' has a present meaning as 'mā gacchati', a past meaning as 'mā gacchā', a future meaning as 'mā gacchissati', and a conditional (kālātipatti) meaning as 'mā gacchissā'. The word 'mā gacchāhi' also has the present, past, future, and conditional meanings as 'mā gacchati, mā gacchi, mā gacchissati, mā gacchissā'. Similarly, the word 'mā bhavatu' also has the present, past, future, and conditional meanings as 'mā bhavati, mā bhavā, mā bhavissati, mā bhavissā'. Although all these explanations of meaning are not found in the Commentaries and other texts, they should be accepted if they are found suitable after careful investigation.

Some grammarians say the Pañcamī suffix is 'āṇatti' (command), while the Sattamī suffix is 'parikappanā' (hypothesis). Having said this, they claim that just as suffixes that do not specify a particular time occur in all three tenses, so too āṇatti and parikappanā occur in all three tenses. That statement should not be accepted because a word ending in the āṇatti suffix like 'karotu' cannot express meanings like 'karoti' (present), 'akāsi' (past), or 'karissati' (future). Likewise, a word ending in the parikappanā suffix like 'kareyya' cannot express meanings like 'karoti', 'akāsi', or 'karissati'. Therefore, that statement should not be accepted. The statement that 'suffixes that do not specify a particular time occur in all three tenses' is only appropriate for Kit (derivative) words; it should be understood as the conclusion here that it is not appropriate in this kind of context.

892. In the future tense, the Bhavissantī suffix is applied. So gacchissati (He will go).
276:
893. How is it that, due to the association with the word "kathañhināma," there is a usage of the future tense in the sense of the past? How indeed, by the association of the word "kathañhināma," does the usage of the future tense occur in the past sense?

In this context, "kathañhināma" is a collection of particles (nipāta) used in the sense of indicating reproach. "How indeed, you foolish man, could you go forth for the sake of your stomach in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya?"—this is from the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi. Why is it said "due to the association with kathañhināma"? It is to show that in passages such as "How indeed, dear sir, did you cross the flood?" where "kathañhināma" is absent, the usage of the future tense in the past sense does not occur.

However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) of that Pāḷi, without taking the word "kathañhi," only the word "nāma" is taken, and it is stated: "Due to the association with the word nāma, there is a usage of the future tense in the past sense." But we have stated "due to the association with the word kathañhināma" for the sake of confirmation. This is because there is no certainty in the association with the word "nāma" alone. Why is there no certainty? Because in the passage, "Do you also think that I should be spoken to in this way?" the usage of the future tense does not occur. However, in the Commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, in the passage, "For six years, he will subsist (yāpessati) on just a handful of mung bean soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup," the usage of the future tense occurs. Therefore, it is stated in that Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā): "In the phrase 'yāpessati nāma,' the word 'nāma' should be brought in and connected; for due to the association with the word 'nāma,' there is a usage of the future tense, meaning 'he subsisted' (yāpesi)."

In this matter, if it were actually a future tense word used in a past sense, the Sub-commentator would not have said "usage like the future." Indeed, a horse should not be called "like a horse"; only something that is not a horse but resembles a horse should be called "like a horse."

894. In the opinion of other teachers, because of the intention to express that time, the future tense (bhavissantī) is used even in the past. In the opinion of other teachers, when there is an intention to express the future time...
277:
The future tense (bhavissantī) occurs even in the past sense. For example: "Through the wandering of many births in saṃsāra, I have run through (sandhāvissaṃ) without finding [the builder]."

In this context, if it is said that the future tense occurs in the past sense when there is an intention to express the future time, this statement is inappropriate because that future tense should only occur in the future sense.

Some teachers might respond to this as follows: This statement is not inappropriate; it is indeed appropriate. Is it not stated by the teachers in the Commentary on the Vimānavatthu, while explaining the meaning of this Pāḷi from the Uttarāvimāna:

"On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
And during the extraordinary fortnight (pāṭihāriyapakkhā),
Well-undertaken with the eight factors,
I have observed (upavassissaṃ) the Uposatha, always restrained in virtue."

Is it not stated by the teachers who commented on this: "'Upavassissaṃ' means 'upavasi' (I observed). For this is a future word (anāgatavacana) in the past sense"? It is true that it was stated so; nevertheless, the meaning should be taken as "like a future word" because it is used in the past sense. Because it resembles a future word, it is appropriate to call it a "future word," just as a city that is complete like the city of the gods is called "the city of the gods" (devanagara). The meaning here is: This city of Amaravatī is complete with garments, ornaments, etc., and because it is like the city of the gods, it is called "the city of the gods."

Alternatively, in the term "anāgatavacana," it should be understood that the word "viya" (like) is elided, meaning "like a future word," just as in the phrase "samiddhaṃ devanagaraṃ." Here, the meaning is possible through the elision of the word "viya," as in "complete like the city of the gods." Therefore, without having doubt in words like "sandhāvissaṃ" and "upavassissaṃ," it should be understood that this is a past tense word in the past sense itself, not a future word in the past sense. For in worldly usage, the Blessed One, who is supremely skilled, omniscient (sabbaññū), and all-seeing, would not speak a future word to indicate the past sense when the past sense is to be spoken. This method should also be carefully borne in mind here.
278:
How so? When the teachers speak of the future word in the past sense, they only say so in the context of the word "-ssaṃ," such as in "sandhāvissaṃ" and "upavassissaṃ." However, they do not say so in the case of words such as "sandhāvissati, sandhāvissanti, upavassissati, upavassissanti, sandhāvissaṃ, sandhāvissaṃsu." Should it not be stated in such places as well? Since it is not stated that there is a future word in the past sense in Pāḷi passages devoid of the word "-ssaṃ," it is known that in verses such as "anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ," the words like "sandhāvissaṃ" are past tense words in the past sense, not future words in the past sense. This method should also be carefully borne in mind here.

How so? Words having the sound "sandhāvissaṃ, upavassissaṃ, apaccissaṃ" become past tense words in the past sense in some places according to the usage, and in other places, they become future words in the future sense; however, they do not become future words in the past sense. This meaning should be understood by way of commonality of sound (sutisamanya). How so? The word "gacchaṃ" is a primary derivative (kitanta) in some places and a finite verb (ākhyāta) in others. The word "abhi" is a prefix (upasagga) in some places and a finite verb in others. The word "pati" is a prefix in some places, a noun (nāmika) in others, and a finite verb in others. Their usages have been shown below. In the same way, words like "sandhāvissaṃ, upavassissaṃ, apaccissaṃ" become past tense words in the past sense in some places according to the usage, and in other places, they become future words in the future sense. Among such words that have the same sound but different classifications, in the passage "anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ," the word "sandhāvissaṃ" is a past tense word in the past sense only, not a future word in the past sense. This is the rule in other similar places as well.

Furthermore, if words like "sandhāvissaṃ, upavassissaṃ" were only future words in the past sense, then in the passage "ahaṃ pure saññamissaṃ"...
279:
The meaning of the word 'pure' (formerly), which denotes the past, and the meaning of the word 'saññamissaṃ', which denotes the future, cannot be connected. If it were so, the meaning 'In the past, I will restrain from giving, I will shrink back, I will not give' would be inappropriate. Therefore, instead of taking it this way, one should take the past tense in the sense of the past: 'In the past, I restrained from giving, I shrank back, I did not give.' Just as in the word 'ahaṃ pure saññamissaṃ' there is a past tense in the sense of the past, similarly in words like 'anekajātisaṃsāraṃ sandhāvissaṃ annibbisaṃ', 'sandhāvissaṃ' etc. are only past tense in the sense of the past. It should be understood as a conclusion here that it is not a future tense in the sense of the past. In this sense, the substitution (ādesa) of the 'iṃ' suffix with 'issaṃ' should be noted. The past tense in the past is for a person who has completed their task, as in 'anekajātisaṃsāraṃ sandhāvissaṃ'. However, teachers say that because there are no characteristics for word-formation in the Dispensation (Sāsana), in words like 'uposathaṃ upavasissaṃ', 'upavasissaṃ' etc. are future tenses in the sense of the past because they resemble future words. We, however, shall state the rule for substituting the 'iṃ' suffix with 'issaṃ' in accordance with the Dispensation.

895. The Kālātipatti (conditional) suffix occurs in the past and future tenses when an action has failed to take place. Here, the failure of an action to occur is called 'kriyātipanna'. This 'kriyātipanna' is the absolute non-occurrence of the action due to the lack of power to accomplish it. Although here the action should not be referred to by the words 'past' or 'future', it should be understood that the terms 'past' and 'future' are obtained through the specific time of the agent's behavior related to the occurrence of that action. 'If he had obtained a vehicle, he would have gone.' Thus it is in the past. 'Even for a long time, it would have been food, if we had not disputed.' 'If I had not gone...'
280:
...it would have been a great loss.' Thus Kālātipatti occurs in the future.

896. The twelve words 'ti anti, si tha, mi ma; te ante, se vhe, e mhe' are called Vattamānā (Present). The name of the twelve words beginning with 'ti anti' is Vattamāna.

897. The twelve words 'tu antu, hi tha, mi ma; taṃ antaṃ, su vho, e āmase' are called Pañcamī (Imperative).

898. The twelve words 'eyya eyyuṃ, eyyāsi eyyātha, eyyāmi eyyāma; etha eraṃ, etho eyyāvho, eyyaṃ eyyāmhe' are called Sattamī (Potential).

899. The twelve words 'a u, e ttha, aṃ mha; ttha re, tho vho, iṃ mhe' are called Parokkhā (Perfect).

900. The twelve words 'ā ū, o ttha, aṃ mhā; ttha tthuṃ, se vhaṃ, iṃ mhasse' are called Hiyattanī (Imperfect).

901. The twelve words 'ī uṃ, o ttha, iṃ mhā; ā ū, se vhaṃ, aṃ mhe' are called Ajjattanī (Aorist).

902. The twelve words 'ssati ssanti, ssasi ssatha, ssāmi ssāma; ssate ssante, ssase ssavhe, ssaṃ ssāmhe' are called Bhavissantī (Future).

903. The twelve words 'ssā ssāṃsu, sse ssatha, ssaṃ ssāmhā; ssatha ssiṃsu, ssase ssavhe, ssiṃ ssāmhase' are called Kālātipatti (Conditional).

904. Hiyattanī, Sattamī, Pañcamī, and Vattamānā are called Sabbadhātuka. These four types of suffixes beginning with Hiyattanī receive the name Sabbadhātuka. They are called Sabbadhātuka because they generally occur with all roots. What is that Sabbadhātuka? It consists of forty-eight words beginning with 'ā ū' etc., grouped under four names. Since these words are essentially only four types of suffixes, it should be understood that the four types of suffixes beginning with Hiyattanī are called Sabbadhātuka.
281:
905. Suffixes (paccaya) are attached after roots (dhātu), nouns (liṅga), and onomatopoeic words (anukaraṇa). (Example:) He does, he goes, he causes to do, he acts like a mountain, Vāseṭṭha (son of Vasiṭṭha), he acts firmly (or acts harshly), he makes the sound 'cicciṭ'. Other words should also be combined in this manner.

906. In the sense of patience (khanti), the suffix 'kha' is attached after the root 'tija'. (Example:) He endures. Why is it said 'in the sense of patience'? (Answer:) To prevent it from being attached in the word 'tejati' (he is sharp or he shines).

907. In the sense of censure (nindā), the suffix 'cha' is attached after the root 'gupa'. (Example:) He censures as disgusting. Why is it said 'in the sense of censure'? (Answer:) To prevent it from being attached in the word 'gopati' (he protects).

908. In the sense of removing disease (rogāpanayana), the suffix 'cha' is attached after the root 'kita'. The suffix 'cha' occurs after the root 'kita' which has the meaning of removing disease. (Example:) He treats (medically). Why is it said 'in the sense of removing disease'? (Answer:) To prevent it from being attached in the word 'ketati' (he dwells).

909. In the sense of investigation (vīmaṃsā), the suffix 'sa' is attached after the root 'māna'. (Example:) He investigates. Why is it said 'in the sense of investigation'? (Answer:) To prevent it from being attached in the word 'māneti' (he honors).

910. After roots such as 'bhuja', 'ghasa', 'hara', 'supa', etc., the suffixes 'kha', 'cha', 'sa' optionally occur in the sense of 'desiring to', which is the meaning of the 'tum' suffix. (Example:) He desires to eat, he wants to eat. He desires to eat, he wants to eat. He desires to take, he wants to take. He desires to hear, he wants to hear. He desires to drink, he wants to drink. He desires to conquer, he wants to conquer. Why is 'vā' (optionally) said? (Answer:) Because it can also exist without the suffix, as in 'bhottumicchatī' (he wants to eat). Why is it said 'in the sense of desiring to, which is the meaning of the tum suffix'? (Answer:) To prevent it from being attached in the simple sense of 'bhuñjati' (he eats).

911. In the sense of 'ācāra' (behavior), the suffix 'āya' is attached after a noun that is a comparison (upamāna) for the agent (kattar). The suffix 'āya' occurs in the sense of behavior after a noun that is a comparison for the agent. The Saṅgha behaves so as to remain firm like a mountain.
282:
He acts like a mountain (pabbatăyati); similarly, he acts like an ocean (samuddāyati); the sound behaves like itself making a 'cicciṭa' sound, thus it is called cicciṭāyati. He acts like craving (taṇhāyati). The cloth behaves like smoke (it becomes smoke-colored), thus it is called dhūmāyati.

912. Īyo cupamānā. The suffix -īya is added after a noun used in comparison in the sense of behavior (ācāra). One behaves towards what is not a parasol as if it were a parasol (shading/covering); thus it is called chattīyati. A teacher behaves towards a pupil who is not his son as if he were a son (teaching him); thus it is called puttīyati. Why is it said "in comparison (upamanā)"? To prevent its application in cases like "he practices the Dhamma (dhammaṃ ācarati)". Why is it said "in the sense of behavior (ācāratthe)"? To prevent its application in cases like "he protects what is not a parasol as if it were a parasol (achattaṃ chattami-va rakkhati)".

913. Atticchatthe nāmato. The suffix -īya is added after a noun in the sense of desiring one's own property. He desires his own bowl; thus it is called pattīyati. Similarly, vatthīyati (he desires his own cloth), parikkhārīyati (he desires his own requisite), cīvarīyati (he desires his own robe), and paṭīyati (he desires his own garment). Why is it said "in the sense of desiring one's own property"? To prevent its application in cases like "he desires another's bowl (aññassa pattam-icchati)".

914. Ṇeṇayaṇāpeṇāpayahetvatthe dhātuto, kāritā ca te. When the sense of causing a simple agent (suddhakattā) to act, which is called the cause (hetu), is to be expressed, the suffixes ṇe, ṇaya, ṇāpe, and ṇāpaya are added after the roots. These suffixes also receive the name kārita. In this rule, "kāritā" means "that which causes to do," hence it is called "kāretā". Who is that? It is the causal agent (hetukattā). The one who causes to do (kāretā) is indeed called kārita. Because they indicate that causing to do, the suffixes starting with ṇe are called kārita. For example, just as a text that explains the Khuddasikkhā is called Khuddasikkhā, and the commentary that explains the Visuddhimagga is called Visuddhimagga.

915. Ṇeṇayā uvaṇṇantehi. The suffixes ṇe and ṇaya are added after roots ending in u or ū. Someone hears; another person says to that person who hears, "Hear! Hear!" Or, he induces the one who hears to hear; therefore, it is sāveti, sāvayati (he causes to hear). Someone exists; another person says to that person who exists, "Exist! Exist!" Or, he induces the one who exists to exist; therefore, it is bhāveti, bhāvayati (he causes to be or he develops).
283:
916. Ṇāpeṇāpaya dādantehi. The suffixes ṇāpe and ṇāpaya occur after roots ending in dā. Dāpeti, dāpayati (he causes to give).

917. Anekassarato caturo dve vā. After roots with many vowels (polysyllabic), all four causative suffixes or the two suffixes ṇe and ṇaya occur in some instances. Kāreti, kārayati, kārāpeti, kārāpayati (he causes to do). Obhāseti, obhāsayati (he causes to shine).

918. Curādīhi ṇāpeṇāpaya. After roots of the Curādi class, the suffixes ṇāpe and ṇāpaya occur in the causative sense (hetvatthe); these suffixes also receive the name kārita. Corāpeti, corāpayati (he causes to steal). Cintāpeti, cintāpayati (he causes to think). Why is it said "in the causative sense"? To distinguish from coreti, corayati (he steals) and cinteti, cintayati (he thinks).

919. Dhāturūpe nāmato ṇayo ca. When the nature of a root is to be produced, or when meanings like "he does" or "he surpasses" are to be employed, the suffix ṇaya occurs after a noun, and it also receives the name kārita. He surpasses with an elephant: atihatthayati (he causes to surpass with an elephant). He sings accompanying with a lute: upavīṇayati (he causes to sing accompanying with a lute). He makes firm: he causes effort to be firm (daḷhayati). Likewise, samānayati (he causes to be complete), amissayati (he causes to be unmixed). The night is pure: visuddhayati (he makes the night pure). He asks about well-being: kusalayati (he asks about well-being).

920. Kamme yo bhāve ca. The suffix ya occurs in the sense of the object (kamma) and the state (bhāva). Karīyate (it is done), bhūyyate (it is being / it should be).

921. Yassa cavaggayavattanti sadhātvantassa. The suffix ya, together with the end of the root, is changed to the palatal group (cavagga), ya, or va. Vuccate (it is said), majjate (it is polished/cleansed), bujjhate (it is known), haññate (it is killed), kayyate (it is done), dibbate (it is played).

922. Ivaṇṇāgamo tamhi vā. When that suffix ya follows, the augment i or ī occurs after all roots in some instances. Kariyyate, karīyate (it is done). Gacciyyate, gaccīyate (it is gone to). Why is it said "optionally (vā)"? Because of forms like kayyate (it is done).
284:
923. Pubbarūpaṃ yo. After all roots, the suffix ya is assimilated to the preceding consonant (the end of the root) in some instances. Vuḍḍhate (it should be increased/plucked), phallate (it should be produced/split), dammate (it should be tamed), labbhate (it is obtained), dissate (it is given). Why is it said "optionally (vā)"? Because of forms like damyate (it is tamed).

924. Tathā kattaripi. Just as the substitution of the suffix ya occurs in the sense of state (bhāva) and object (kamma), so also the substitution of the suffix ya should be made in the sense of the agent (kattari). Bujjhati (he knows), vijjhati (he discerns/pierces).

925. Bhūvādito a. After the group of roots starting with bhū, the suffix a occurs in the sense of the agent. Bhavati (he is), pacati (he cooks), etc.

926. Rudhādito ca majjhe niggahītaṃ. After the group of roots starting with rudhi, the suffix a occurs in the sense of the agent, and the augment niggahīta (anusvāra) occurs in the middle of the roots. Rundhati (he obstructs), chindati (he cuts), sumbhati (he strikes).

927. Yathārahaṃ ivaṇṇekārokārā ca. After the group of roots starting with rudhi, the suffixes i, ī, e, and o occur appropriately in the sense of the agent, and the augment niggahīta occurs in the middle of the roots. Rundhiti, rundhīti, rundheti, sumbhoti, etc.

928. Divādito yo. After the roots starting with divu, the suffix ya occurs. Dibbati (he plays), sibbati (he sews), tāyati (he protects), etc.

929. Svādīhi ṇuṇāuṇā. After the roots starting with su, the suffixes ṇu, ṇā, and uṇā occur. Suṇoti, suṇāti (he hears). Saṃvuṇoti, saṃvuṇāti (he restrains). Āvuṇoti, āvuṇāti (he restrains). Sakkuṇoti, sakkuṇāti (he is able). Pāpuṇāti (he reaches), cinoti, cināti (he collects/increases), etc.

930. Kīyādito na. After the roots starting with kī, the suffix nā occurs. Kiṇāti (he buys), jināti (he conquers), munāti (he knows), lunāti (he reaps), punāti (he purifies), vicināti (he investigates), etc.
285:
## 931. Gahādito yathārahaṃ ākhyātattenāmattē ca ppaṇhā.
When expressing the state of a verb or a noun, suffixes such as ppaṇhā are applied to the group of roots beginning with gah in the active voice (kattari) as appropriate. Examples: gheppati, gaṇhāti (takes). That which one learns, and which arises and progresses for one's benefit, welfare, and happiness, is called sippaṃ (art/craft). Having heated the blade of a billhook, it heats water or milk; it is capable of burning, therefore it is called uṇha (heat). It craves, therefore it is called taṇhā (craving). It causes the world's delight and joy to arise, therefore it is called juṇha (the bright fortnight). Although it has no light of its own, it shines and is beautiful due to the light of the moon and stars, and thus possesses light; therefore it is called juṇhā (night). By its own subtle nature, it brings even a subtle meaning to its conclusion or completion; therefore it is called saṇha (subtle wisdom). Other words should also be investigated in this manner.

## 932. Tanādito oyirā.
The suffixes o and yirā are applied to the roots beginning with tan. Examples: tanoti, karoti, kayirati, kubbati, jāgaroti, sakkoti, and so forth.

## 933. Curādito ṇeṇayā.
The suffixes ṇe and ṇaya are applied to the roots beginning with cur. Examples: coreti, corayati, cinteti, cintayati, and so forth.

## 934. Bhāvakammesvattanopadaṃ.
The attanopada inflections are applied in the impersonal (bhāva) and passive (kamma) voices. Examples: vuccate, labbhate, and so forth.

## 935. Kattari ca.
The attanopada inflections are also applied in the active voice (kattari). Examples: maññate, rocate, and so forth.

## 936. Dhātupaccayēhi vibhattiyo.
Inflections are applied after suffixes ending with the causative, starting from kha, etc., which are indicated after the roots. Examples: titikkhati (endures), jigucchati (disdains), vīmaṃsati (investigates). Just as the ocean acts upon itself so as not to exceed its shore, a reservoir acts upon itself so as not to exceed its bank; therefore it is called samuddāyati. Pattīyati (desires one's own bowl), pācayati (causes to cook), and so forth.

## 937. Kattari parassapadaṃ.
The parassapada inflections are applied in the sense of the active voice (kattari). Examples: pacati, paṭhati, and so forth.
286:
## 938. Bhūvādayo dhātavo.
Groups of words beginning with bhū are called roots (dhātu). Examples: bhavati, bhoti, ajjhayati, rundhīyati, dibbati, and so forth.

## 939. Kvacādivaṇṇassekassarassa dvittaṃ.
The reduplication (dvitta) of an initial letter having a single vowel occurs in some instances. Examples: titikkhati, jigucchati, tikicchati, vīmaṃsati, bubhukkhati, pivāsati, daddaḷhati, dadāti, jahāti, caṅkamati, cañcalati. Why is "kvaci" (in some instances) said? Because reduplication does not occur in kampati and calati.

## 940. Pubbobbhāso.
The first part of a reduplicated root is called abbhāsa. Examples: dadhāti, dadāti, babhuva.

## 941. Rasso.
A vowel existing in the abbhāsa becomes short (rassa). Examples: dadāti, dadhāti, jahāti.

## 942. Dutiyacatutthānaṃ paṭhamatatiyā.
The second and fourth letters existing in the abbhāsa become the first and third letters. Examples: ciccheda, bubhukkhati, babhuva, dadhāti.

## 943. Kavaggo cavaggattaṃ.
Velar consonants (kavagga) existing in the abbhāsa change into palatal consonants (cavagga). Examples: cikicchati, jigucchati, jighacchati, caṅkamati, jaṅgamati, cañcalati, jagamakira, bhujaṅgo.

## 944. Mānakitānaṃ vatattaṃ vā.
The letters of the roots māna and kita existing in the abbhāsa optionally change to va and ta respectively. Examples: vīmaṃsati, tikicchati. Why is "vā" (optionally) said? Because cikicchati also exists.

## 945. Hassa jo.
The letter ha existing in the abbhāsa is changed to ja. Examples: jahāti, juhoti, jahāra.
287:
946. The final vowel of the abbhāsa optionally becomes ivaṇṇa (i, ī) or akāra (a). Examples: jigucchati (disdains), pivāsati (desires to drink), vīmaṃsati (investigates), jighacchati (desires to eat), babhuva (became), dadhāti (bears). Why is "vā" said? Because it does not occur in bubhukkhati (desires to eat).

947. The niggahīta (ṃ) is also optionally added to the end of the abbhāsa. Examples: caṅkamati (walks), cañcalati (trembles), jaṅgamati (goes). Why is "vā" said? Because it does not appear in pivāsati and daddaḷhati (shines).

948. Following that abbhāsa, the roots pā and māna change to vā and maṃ respectively when the suffix sa follows. Examples: pivāsati (desires to drink), vīmaṃsati (investigates).

949. The roots ṭhā and pā optionally change to tiṭṭha and piva respectively. Examples: tiṭṭhati (stands), pivati (drinks). Why is "vā" said? Because ṭhāti (stands) and pāti (drinks) also exist.

950. The root ñā optionally changes to jā, jaṃ, or nā. Examples: jānāti (knows), jāneyya (should know), jāniyā (should know), jaññā (should know), nāyati (knows). There is also the usage: "animittā na nāyare" (they cannot be known as they are signless). Why is "vā" said? Because viññāyati (is known) also exists.

951. In the sense of seeing, the root dis optionally changes to passa or dakkha. Examples: rūpaṃ passati (sees a form), dakkhati (sees). If it is not in the sense of seeing, there is: "dhammadessī parābhavo" (one who hates the Dhamma is in decline). Why is "vā" said? Because addasa (saw) exists. Teachers also desire the change of the root dis to dissa in this rule; thus "dissati" exists. We have mentioned that form in the divādigaṇa. The reason is that some transitive roots, upon reaching the divādigaṇa, become intransitive, such as "suttaṃ chijjati" (the thread breaks) and "taḷākaṃ bhijjati" (the tank bursts). This transitive root dis, upon reaching the divādigaṇa...
288:
It is without karma (kamma). For example, "te kumārā na dissare" (those boys are not seen). Here, "na dissare" means "na paññāyanti" (they are not seen/known).

952. Due to the suffix 'cha', the final consonant of a root ending in a consonant is changed to 'ca'. Examples: jigucchati (he despises), tikicchati (he heals), jighacchati (he wishes to eat).

953. Due to the suffix 'kha', the final consonant of a root ending in a consonant is changed to 'ka'. Examples: titikkhati (he endures), bubhukkhati (he wishes to eat).

954. Due to the suffix 'se', the root 'hara' is changed to 'gī'. Example: jigīsati (he wishes to carry).

955. The root 'ji' is also changed to 'jigī' due to the suffix 'se'. Example: vijigīsati (he wishes to conquer).

956. Due to the Parokkhā tense suffix, the roots 'brū' and 'bhū' are changed to 'āha' and 'babhuva' respectively. Examples: āha (he said), āhu (they said), babhuva (it became), babhuvu (they became). If it is not the Parokkhā tense, it is 'abravuṃ' (they said).

957. The final 'ma' of the root 'gamu' optionally becomes 'ccha' before all tense suffixes. Examples: gacchati, gameti (he goes, he causes to go), gacchatu, gametu (let him go), gaccheyya, gameyya (he should go), agacchā, agamā (he went), agacchi, agami (he went), gacchissati, gamissati (he will go), agacchissā, agamissā (he would have gone), gacchamāno, gacchanto (one who goes). Why is it said "gamissā"? Because it does not occur in 'icchati' (he wishes).

958. Due to the Ajjatanī tense suffix, the 'a' in the root 'vaca' is changed to 'o'. Examples: avoca (he said), avocuṃ (they said). If it is not the Ajjatanī tense, it is 'avacā', 'avacū' (he said).

959. Due to the suffixes 'hi', 'mi', 'ma', and 'mahe', the 'a' vowel must be lengthened (dīgha) to 'ā'. Examples: gacchāhi (go!), gacchāmi (I go), gacchāma (we go), gacchāmahe (we go).

960. The 'hi' suffix is also optionally elided. Examples: gaccha (go!), gacchāhi (go!).
289:
961. Due to the Bhavissanti tense suffix, the 'ū' vowel of the root 'hū' becomes 'eha', 'oha', or 'e'; the 'ssa' suffix is also elided in some views. Examples: hehiti, hehinti; hohiti, hohinti; heti, henti; hehissati, hehissanti; hohissati, hohissanti; hessati, hessanti. Why is it specified as the root 'hū'? Because of 'bhavissati'. Why is it specified as being in the Bhavissanti tense? Because of 'honti'.

962. Due to the Bhavissanti tense suffix, the root 'kara' is changed to 'kāha'; the 'ssa' suffix is also elided in some views. Examples: kāhati, kāhiti; kāhasi, kāhisi; kāhāmi, kāhāma. Why is 'vā' (optionally) used? Because of 'karissati'.

963. The suffixes 'ssāmi' and 'ssāma' following the roots 'vaca' and 'hana' are changed to 'khāmi' and 'khāma'. Examples: vakkhāmi, vakkhāma; paṭihaṅkhāmi, paṭihaṅkhāma.

964. The suffixes 'ssāmi' and 'ssāma' following the roots 'vasa' and 'labha' are changed to 'chāmi' and 'chāma'. Examples: vacchāmi, vacchāma; lacchāmi, lacchāma. Why is 'vā' used? Because of 'vasissāmi' and 'labhissāmi'.

965. When changing 'ssāmi' and 'ssāma' to 'khāmi' and 'khāma', the 'ca' which is part of the root 'vaca' becomes 'ka'. Examples: vakkhāmi, vakkhāma.

966. When changing 'ssāmi' and 'ssāma' to 'chāmi' and 'chāma', the 'sa' of the root 'vasa' and the 'bha' of the root 'labha' optionally become 'ca'. Examples: vacchāmi, lacchāmi, vacchāma, lacchāma. Why is 'vā' used? Because of 'vasissāmi' and 'labhissāmi'.

967. Due to the changes to 'khāmi' and 'khāma', the 'na' which is part of the root 'hana' becomes a Niggahīta. Examples: paṭihaṅkhāmi, paṭihaṅkhāma. Since the term 'vā' (optionally) follows from the previous context, why is it specified? Because of 'paṭihanissāmi'.
290:
968. The 'ssa' of the Bhavissanti tense following the roots 'vasa' and 'labha' is changed to 'cha'; due to that 'cha' change, the final consonant of the root becomes 'ca'. Examples: vacchati, vacchanti, vacchasi, vacchatha, vacchate; lacchati, lacchanti, lacchasi, lacchatha, lacchate. Since the term 'vā' follows from the previous context, why is it specified? Because of 'vasissati' and 'labhissatti'.

969. The 'ssa' of the Bhavissanti tense following the root 'hana' is changed to 'kha'; due to that 'kha' change, the 'na' becomes a Niggahīta. Examples: haṅkhati, haṅkhanti, paṭihaṅkhati, paṭihaṅkhanti, paṭihaṅkhasi, paṭihaṅkhatha, etc. Why is 'vā' used? Because of 'hanissati' and 'paṭihanissati'. In this case, by seeing the Pali text "paṭihaṅkhāmi", forms such as "haṅkhati, paṭihaṅkhati" etc., should be accepted even if they do not appear directly in the Pali scriptures; for what is not seen should be understood by the method of what is seen. These forms like 'haṅkhati' are similar to "vakkhati, vakkhanti" etc.

970. The 'ssa' of the Bhavissanti tense following the root 'vaca' is always changed to 'kha'; due to that 'kha' change, the final consonant of the root becomes 'ka'. Examples: vakkhati, vakkhanti, vakkhasi, vakkhate, vakkhante.

971. Alternatively, according to the Pali method, the root 'vaca' is optionally changed to 'vakkha' in the Bhavissanti tense. Examples: vakkhissati, etc. In this regard, this is the scripture (pāṭha) spoken by the Buddha himself: "I shall preach my conduct, listen to my words" (as found in the Cariyāpiṭaka). This, however, is the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) text: "The King, having exchanged greetings with you, will say, 'Knowing the place, sit down'" (as found in the Mahosadha Jātaka Commentary). In this context, the great and noble commentators, who knew the intention of the Buddha, composed the words in the commentaries in accordance with the Pāvacana (Scripture). Therefore, by meaning, by word, and by intention...
291:
The Buddha taught the Dhamma and the Vinaya,
Which were known by his sons (the Great Elders) exactly as taught.
Without abandoning their (the Elders') intention,
Therefore, the ancient teachers of old composed the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).

972. Due to the suffixes 'mi' and 'ma', the final vowel of the root 'dā' must be changed to 'aṃ'. (Examples:) dammi, damma.

973. The vowel of a root that does not end in a conjunct consonant (asaññoga) must undergo Vuddhi (strengthening) due to a causative (kārita) suffix. (Examples:) kāreti, kārayati. Why is it said "not ending in a conjunct consonant"? (Example:) cintayati.

974. The vowel of roots beginning with 'ghaṭa' etc., which do not end in a conjunct consonant, optionally undergoes Vuddhi due to a causative suffix. (Examples:) ghāṭeti, ghaṭeti, ghāṭayati, ghaṭayati, ghāṭāpeti, ghaṭāpeti, ghāṭāpayati, ghaṭāpayati, gāmeti, gameti, gāmayati, gamayati. Why is it said "beginning with ghaṭa etc."? (Example:) kāreti.

975. The vowel of all roots that do not end in a conjunct consonant must undergo Vuddhi due to other suffixes besides causative ones. (Examples:) jayati, hoti, bhavati, bhoti.

976. The vowel of the 'ṇu' suffix, which is a sign (vikaraṇa), must also undergo Vuddhi. (Examples:) abhisuṇoti, saṃvuṇoti.

977. The vowel of the roots 'guha' and 'dusa' reaches the state of being long (dīgha) in some places due to a causative suffix. (Examples:) gūhayati, dūsayati.

978. The 'va' of roots such as 'vaca', 'vasa', and 'vaha' must be changed to 'u' when followed by the suffix 'ya'. (Examples:) "Wisdom is called 'mona'". "He who is not dependent (on craving and views), who is unshaken (by worldly conditions) and endowed with the quality of 'tādi', is called a Brahmin". "He is called a wise man (paṇḍita)". Examples: vussati, vuyhati.
292:
979. In the Pāvacana (scripture), when the substitute u follows, the augments va and ra always occur. When the u-vowel, which has become a substitute, follows, the augments va and ra always occur; the u-vowel does not stand alone. Examples: vuccati, vuccate, nirutti, niruttaṃ. Vuttehutaṃ. Why is it said "in the Pāvacana"? It is to indicate that in non-scriptural forms such as kimatthamidamuccate, uttase, and uttate, the augment va/ra does not occur.

980. The ha-vowel of the root vah and the suffix ya undergo metathesis. Or, the substitute la occurs for the suffix ya. Examples: vuḷhati, vuyhati.

981. When the suffix ppa follows, the root gah becomes ghe. Example: gheppati.

982. When the suffix ṇhā follows, the ha-vowel of the root gah is elided. Example: gaṇhāti.

983. When an ajjatanī (aorist) termination follows, the root kar optionally becomes kāsa. Examples: akāsi, akāsuṃ, akari, akaruṃ.

984. After the roots hū, dā, and brū, the augment sa occurs as appropriate in the ajjatanī termination. Examples: So bhikkhu arahā ahosi (That monk became an Arahant). Ahaṃ rājā ahosiṃ (I became a king). So dānaṃ adāsi (He gave a gift). Bhikkhūnaṃ payirudāhāsi (He spoke to the monks). Ahaṃ payirudāhāsiṃ. Jāto kaṇho pabyāhāsi (The black-born one spoke). Ahaṃ pabyāhaṃsiṃ.

985. The root brū following the combination of prefixes and particles pa-vi, pari, and uda becomes āhā when the augment sa follows in the ajjatanī termination as appropriate. Examples: pabyāhāsi, payirudāhāsi.
293:
986. The termination uṃ following the substitute āhā becomes aṃsu. Examples: te pabyāhaṃsu, te payirudāhaṃsu.

987. The terminations mi and ma following the root as become mhi and mha. Optionally, the end of the root is elided. Examples: amhi, amha, asmi, asma. "Bho, mayaṃ tevijjā asma" (O Venerable Gotama, we are masters of the three Vedas).

988. The termination tha following the root as becomes ttha. The end of the root is also elided. Example: tumhe attha.

989. The termination ti following the root as becomes tthi. The end of the root is also elided. Example: atthi. In the phrase "puttā matthi dhanā matthī," the word atthi is an indeclinable (nipāta). Therefore, it can be both singular and plural. In the phrase "atthi khīrā brāhmaṇī," it is also an indeclinable. For this reason, it can form a compound (samāsa) with the following word.

990. When intended as a name (designation), a verbal form (ākhyāta) becomes a nominal form (nāmika). In that case, its designation as a verb disappears. Just as when one attains the status of a monk, the status of a novice disappears, so it is with the designation of a name. For example: "Aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño" (Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood). Based on this inspired utterance (udāna) of the Teacher, the Venerable Koṇḍañña became known by the name "Aññāsikoṇḍañña." Here, the verbal nature disappears. Similarly, based on the words "mā khali, mā khali" (do not stumble), the ascetic Gosāla became known by the name "Makkhali." Here too, the verbal nature disappears. Therefore, they are used as "Makkhaliṃ, Makkhalinā," etc. Similarly, from the words "iha āsa" (it happened here)...
297:
1013. The root gamu becomes ghamma and gaggha. Examples: ghammati, ghammatu, gagghati. "Therefore, monk... to whatever place you go (gagghasi), you shall go (gagghasi) only in comfort." Why is "vā" (optionally) said by the authority of the rule? Because the form gacchati also exists.

1014. Because of the suffix ya, the final vowel of roots such as dā, dhā, mā, ṭhā, hā, pā, maha, and matha becomes ī. Examples: dīyati, dhīyati, mīyati, ṭhīyati, hīyati, pīyati, mahīyati, mathīyati.

1015. When the suffix ya follows, the initial letter of the root yaj becomes i. Example: Ijjate mayā buddho (The Buddha is honored by me).

1016. After all roots, the termination uṃ becomes iṃsu. Examples: upasaṅkamiṃsu (they approached), nisīdiṃsu (they sat down). In the phrase "te taṃ asse ayācisuṃ" (they asked for those horses), it should be understood that the niggahīta has moved to another position; this characteristic has been explained below.

1017. After the root dis, the termination uṃ becomes āsuṃ. Example: addasāsuṃ (they saw).

1018. The roots jara and mara become jīra, jiyya, and miyya. Examples: jīrati, jiyyati, miyyati, marati.

1019. In all terminations and suffixes, the initial letter of the root as is elided. Examples: santi, santu, ahi, siyā, siyuṃ, santo, samāno. Why is "vā" (optionally) said by the authority of the rule? Because the form asi also exists.

1020. In non-conjugational (asabbadhātuka) terminations, the root as becomes bhū. Example: bhavissati,
298:
bhavissanti, abhavissa, abhavissā, abhavissaṃsu. Why is "vā" said? Because the form āsuṃ also exists.

1021. The termination eyya following the root ñā optionally becomes iyā or ñā. Examples: jāniyā, vijāniyā, jaññā. Because of the word "vā," the form jāneyya also exists.

1022. The suffix nā following the root ñā is optionally elided or becomes ya. Examples: jaññā, nāyati. Because of the word "vā," the form jānāti also exists.

1023. The suffix a becomes e, or it is elided. Examples: vajjeti, vadeti, vajjemi, vadāmi.

1024. The suffix o becomes u. Examples: kurute, karoti, tanute, tanoti. Why is "o" specified? To prevent the change to u in the form hoti.

1025. The a-vowel of the root kar also becomes u. Examples: kurute, karoti, kubbati, karīyati. Why is "of the root kar" specified? To prevent the change to u in forms like sarati and marati.

1026. According to the scriptural method (pāvacananaya), the root kar becomes ku and kru, and the suffix o becomes va in all terminations and suffixes. Examples: Sīlavanto na kubbanti (The virtuous do not do [evil]), Bālo sīlāni kubbati (The fool practices [bad] habits). Tapo idha krubbasi brahmapattiyā (Do you practice austerity in this religion for the sake of attaining the supreme?). Pharusāhi vācāhi pakrubbamāno (Overwhelming with harsh words).
299:
1027. When a vowel follows, the letter 'o' at the end of a root is substituted by 'ava'. (e.g.) cavati (departs/passes away), bhavati (becomes). Why say "when a vowel follows"? hoti (here, because the suffix 'a' is elided, no vowel follows, so the substitution to 'ava' does not occur). Why say "the letter 'o'"? jayati (here, because it is not the letter 'o', the substitution to 'ava' does not occur).

1028. When a vowel follows, the letter 'e' at the end of a root is substituted by 'aya'. (e.g.) nayati (leads), jayati (conquers). Why say "when a vowel follows"? neti (here, because no vowel follows, the substitution to 'aya' does not occur).

1029. When a causative suffix (kārita) follows, those letters 'o' and 'e' undergo substitution to 'āva' and 'āya'. (e.g.) lāveti (causes to reap), nāyeti (causes to lead).

1030. When non-general (asabbadhātuka) terminations follow, the augment 'i' is inserted. (e.g.) gamissati (will go), karissati (will do). Why say "when non-general terminations follow"? agamā, gaccheyya, gacchatu, gacchati (because these terminations are general (sabbadhātuka) terminations, the augment 'i' is not inserted).

1031. Middle voice (attanopada) terminations in some cases become active voice (parassapada). (e.g.) karīyati, labbhati, karīyate, labbhate.

1032. When the imperfect (hiyyattanī), aorist (ajjattanī), and conditional (kālātipatti) terminations follow, the augment 'a' is inserted in some cases. (e.g.) agamā, agamī, agamissā. Why say "in some cases"? gamā, gamī, gamissā (here, the augment 'a' is not inserted).

1033. When the termination 'ti' follows, the augment 'ī' is inserted after the root brū in some cases. (e.g.) bravīti (speaks), brūti (speaks).

1034. The final vowel of a root having more than one vowel is elided in some cases. (e.g.) gacchati, gacchanti. Why say "a root having more than one vowel"? pāti (drinks, protects, uses), yāti (goes, reaches). Why say "in some cases"? mahīyati (is honored), mathīyati (is churned). In these cases, the final vowel of the root is not elided.
300:
1035. The final letter of roots such as isu, yamu, etc., is substituted by 'ccha' in some cases. (e.g.) icchati (desires, likes), niyacchati (restrains, observes), vacchati (dwells, approaches). Why say "in some cases (vā)"? esati (desires), niyamati (restrains), upāsati (approaches, dwells, stays).

1036. After roots such as tara, kara, etc., the termination 'u' is substituted by 'aṃsu' in some cases. (e.g.) "By this path, they crossed over in the past (ataṃsu)". "They followed and performed the words of the Teacher (akaṃsu)". "They dwelt (vihaṃsu), and they dwell now (viharanti)". Why say "in some cases (vā)"? atariṃsu, akariṃsu, vihariṃsu.

1037. When the termination 'ssaṃ' follows, the root kara is substituted by 'ka' in some cases. (e.g.) "I too shall perform (kassaṃ) worship". Why say "in some cases (vā)"? karissaṃ.

1038. When the termination 'ssati' follows, the root hara preceded by the prefix vi (vihara) is substituted by 'ha' in some cases. (e.g.) "He will dwell (vihassati) diligently". Why say "in some cases (vā)"? viharissati.

1039. The letter 'ssa' of terminations such as 'ssati' is elided in some cases. (e.g.) dakkhati (will see), dakkhanti. "When he shall see (dakkhasi) the great elephant". dakkhissati, vibhajiṃ, vibhajissiṃ, vikāsati, vikāsissati.

1040. When the suffix 'ṇe' follows, the vowel 'ī' of the substituted word 'sīda' is changed to 'ā' in some cases. (e.g.) nisādeti (causes to sit/stay), or nisīdāpeti. In this regard, the Pāḷi is: "The father, having seated me (nisādetvā) on his lap, admonishes me on what is beneficial." There, 'nisādetvā' means 'nisīdāpetvā'. In some places, it also appears as 'nisīdetvā'; the meaning is the same. The word 'nisīdetvā' from the root of the bhū-group, together with the letter 'e', is a causal agentive form (hetukattu) because it expresses that causal agent. However, the word 'nisīditvā' together with the augment 'i' is a simple agentive form (suddhakattu) because it expresses that simple agent.
301:
Furthermore, the form together with the augment 'i' is a simple agentive form (suddhakattu) because it expresses that simple agent.

1041. A vowel standing in the position of an inflectional ending is optionally (vā) shortened. (e.g.) avoca, agacchi, etc. Why say "optionally"? To prevent shortening in instances such as "agamā rājagahaṃ buddho" (The Buddha-to-be went to the city of Rājagaha).

1042. When a conjunct consonant follows, the vowel of the root is shortened. (e.g.) acchati. Why say "when a conjunct consonant follows"? To prevent shortening in instances such as "upāsati".

1043. When the imperfect (hiyyattanī) and aorist (ajjattanī) terminations follow, the vowel 'a' in the letter 'va' of the root vaca must be substituted by 'o'. (e.g.) "etadavoca satthā" (The Teacher said this). He said (avaca, avaci), they said (avocuṃ). I said (avocaṃ, avacaṃ).

1044. When the terminations 'ttha' and 'mha' follow, the augment 'u' occurs in the root vaca. (e.g.) You all said (avocuttha), we said (avocumha).

1045. When the future (bhavissantī) termination follows, the 'da' of the root ruda is substituted by 'ca', and 'ssa' is substituted by 'cha'. (e.g.) "cirarattāya rucchati" (He will weep for a long time). rucchanti, rucchasi. Alternatively, it also appears as rodissati.

1046. After the prefixes ā and nī, roots such as kusa must undergo doubling (reduplication), and those prefixes must be shortened. (e.g.) akkosati, akkosasi, niyyāti, niyyāsi.

1047. When the aorist (ajjattanī) termination follows, the root visa preceded by pa must be substituted by 'pāvekkha'. (e.g.) "pāvekkhi antepuraṃ surammaṃ" (He entered the very delightful inner palace). Alternatively, it also appears as pāvisi.

1048. When the suffix 'ya' follows, the letter 'ha' must be transposed (metathesis). (e.g.) vuyhati (is carried away).
302:
1049. The suffix 'ya' preceding the letter 'ha' is optionally (vā) substituted by 'ḷa'. (e.g.) vuḷhati. Why say "optionally"? So that 'vuyhati' may also exist.

1050. When the substituted letter 'la' follows, or when the suffix 'ya' preceding the letter 'ha' follows, the vowel 'a' in the letter 'va' of the root vaha must be substituted by 'u'. (e.g.) vuḷhati, vuyhati.

1051. When the imperfect (hiyyattanī) termination follows, the vowel 'ū' of the root hū is substituted by 'uva'. (e.g.) ahuvā (it was/became).

1052. The aorist termination 'ī' following the root hū must be elided. (e.g.) "ahu rājā" (There was a king).

1053. The aorist termination 'o' following the root hū must be substituted by 'i'. (e.g.) "tvaṃ ahosi" (You were/became).

1054. The aorist termination 'iṃ' following the root hū is substituted by 'uṃ' in some cases. (e.g.) "ahaṃ kevaṭṭagāmasmiṃ, ahuṃ kevaṭṭadārako" (In Kevaṭṭa village, I was a fisherman's son). Why say "in some cases (kvaci)"? To prevent the substitution to 'uṃ' in instances such as "ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ" (Was I indeed?).

1055. After the root ṭhā preceded by saṃ, the augment 'ha' occurs; when that augment 'ha' follows, the final vowel of the root is shortened in some cases. (e.g.) saṇṭhahati, or saṇṭhāti.
303:
1056. After the root ṭhā preceded by the prefix pati-, the letter ha is also augmented. When that ha augment occurs, the final vowel of the root is shortened in some instances. Patiṭṭhahati (he stands), or patiṭṭhāti (he stands).

1057. The letter pa of the word pipa is sometimes changed to va. Pivati (he drinks), or pipati (he drinks).

1058. In all inflectional suffixes, the root han is sometimes changed to vadha. Vadhati (he strikes, beats, or kills), vadhanti. All forms such as vadhasi, etc., should be applied accordingly. In this regard, many instances are found in the Pāḷi Canon, such as: "Attānaṃ vadhitvā vadhitvā rodati" (striking himself repeatedly, he weeps), "Vadhatī na rodati" (he strikes, he does not weep), "Akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ" (he abused me, he struck me), and "Ahaṃ taṃ avadhiṃ sāmaṃ" (I myself killed that Suvaṇṇasāma).

1059. In the context of reduplication (abbhāsa), the vowel a of the prefix api- situated before the root is always elided, and the letter dha is changed to ha. Dvāraṃ pidahati (he closes the door). Why is it said "in the context of reduplication"? Consider apidhānaṃ (a lid/covering) and apidheti (he closes/covers). In the phrase "apidhetuṃ mahāsindhuṃ" (to block the great ocean), the aforementioned rule does not apply because it is not in the context of reduplication. If it is asked, "What about the phrase 'dvāraṃ apidahitvā' (having closed the door)?" In this instance, the letter a is a particle (nipāta) meaning prohibition/negation, and is not a part of the prefix (upasagga). Therefore, it should be understood that one letter a was elided previously and disappeared. This method should be well-borne in mind.

1060. The inflectional suffix ssa following the root bhuj is sometimes changed to kha; because of that change to kha, the letter ja is sometimes changed to ka. Bhokkhati (he will eat), bhokkhanti. Why is the word "vā" (optionally) included? Because of bhukkhiissati and bhokkhiissanti (he will eat).
304:
1061. Some roots, because they end in a conjunct (saṃyogan-tatta), undergo strengthening (vuddhi) as a natural state. Bhokkhati (he eats).

1062. Roots that have a niggahīta augment do not undergo strengthening. Even if they naturally end in a non-conjunct, roots that occur with a niggahīta augment do not reach strengthening (vuddhi). Muñcati (he releases), parisaṅkati (he doubts).

1063. When the suffix ya follows, the final vowel of the root dā preceded by the prefix ā- is changed to i. Dhanaṃ ādiyati (he takes wealth). Sīlaṃ samādiyati (he perfectly undertakes the precepts).

1064. When the suffix ya follows, the final consonant of the root jan is changed to ā. Jāyati (he is born/arises).

1065. In the aorist (ajjatanī) and other tenses, the final consonant of the root sak is changed to kha along with the augment of the letter ka. Asakkhi (he was able), sakkhi, asakkhiṃsu. Sakkhiissati, sakkhiissanti. Asakkhiissā, asakkhiissaṃsu.

1066. Because of the suffix nā, the vowel of the root kī is shortened, and the letter na is changed to ṇa. Kiṇāti (he buys), vikkiṇāti (he sells).

1067. As appropriate, the augment sa sometimes follows a root. Ajesi yakkho naravīraseṭṭhaṃ (The yakkha conquered the king of the Kurus, the best of heroic men).

1068. In the passive voice (kammakaraka), when the suffix ya follows, the letter ra of the root kar is sometimes changed to ya. Kayyate (it is done), kariyyati (it is done).
305:
1069. When the passive suffix (ya-paccaya) follows, the final vowel of the root ñā sometimes becomes e by the word "vā". Dhammo purisena ñeyyati (The Dhamma is to be known by the man), dhammā ñeyyanti (The Dhammas are to be known). Why is the word "vā" used? Because ñāyati and viññāyati (is known) also exist. Although a rule pulled by the word "ca" in a sutta does not follow into the next sutta, when there is no pulling by "ca", it may still follow by the "frog's leap" (maṇḍūka-gati) method.

1070. In some instances, the optative suffix eyyāma is changed to emu. Tayajja guttā viharemu divasaṃ (Protected by you today, may we dwell the whole day). Kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ (How shall we know you?). Na no dakkhemu sambuddhaṃ (We might not see the Buddha), etc.

1071. After the tanādi class of roots, the suffix eyyāma is changed to omu. Pappomu (may we reach).

1072. In the context of the root ñā, the inflectional suffix ssa following the augment i preceded by the suffix ya is sometimes changed to hi. Paññāyihiti (it will be manifest), paññāyihinti (they will be manifest).

1073. Because of the suffix nā, the final vowel of the root mā is always changed to i. Mināti (he measures/compares), minanti. Why is it said "nā-mhi"? Consider māneti (he honors). Mā naṃ rūpena pāmesi (Do not compare him by his appearance). Chāyā metabbā (The shadow should be measured).

1074. When the suffix nā follows, the final vowel of roots having long vowels is always shortened. Lunāti (he reaps/cuts), munāti (he knows), punāti (he purifies), dhunāti (he shakes off).

1075. As appropriate, the augment sa occurs after a root. Akāsi (he did). Why is "yathārahaṃ" (as appropriate) said? Because akā (he did) also exists.

1076. The augment i that follows a root is changed to e as appropriate. Aggahesi (he took), aggahesuṃ (they took). Why is "yathārahaṃ" said? Because karissati (he will do) exists.
306:
1077. The final vowel of the letter ka in the root kar is changed to u as appropriate. Kurute (he does). Why is "yathārahaṃ" said? Because karoti (he does) exists.

1078. When following the vowel u, the letter ra of the root kar is elided, and the vowel u following that u is changed to the letter ba (resulting in the conjunct bb). Kubbati (he does), kubbanti, kubbasi, etc.

1079. When the suffix yira follows, the letter ra of the root kar is elided. Kayirati (he does), kayiranti, etc.

1080. According to various opinions of teachers, in the passive voice, the suffix ya and the root-final ra are transposed. Kayirati (it is done), kayirate; tena kayiranti (they are done by him), etc.

1081. After the suffix yira, the optative suffix eyya is changed to ā. Kayirā (he should do).

1082. After the suffix yira, the optative suffix etha is changed to ātha. Kayirātha dhīro puññāni (The wise man should perform meritorious deeds). Why is it said "after yira"? Consider sabbhireva samāsetha (one should associate only with the virtuous).

1083. After the suffix yira, the optative suffix eyyuṃ is changed to uṃ. Te puññaṃ kayiruṃ (They should perform merit).

1084. After the suffix yira, the optative suffix eyyāsi is changed to āsi. Tvaṃ kayirāsi (You should do).

1085. After the suffix yira, the optative suffix eyyātha is changed to ātha. Tumhe kayirātha (You all should do).

1086. After the suffix yira, the optative suffix eyyāmi is changed to āmi. Ahaṃ kayirāmi (I should do).
307:
1087. Eyyāmassāma. The substitution of 'āma' for the 'eyyāma' suffix occurs after the 'yira' suffix. Mayaṃ kayirāma—We should do.

1088. Sabbāheyyāseyyāmeyyāname. The substitution of 'e' for the suffixes 'eyyāsi', 'eyyāmi', and 'eyya' occurs after all roots. Tvaṃ puññaṃ kare—You should do merit. Ahaṃ kare—I should do. So puriso kare—That man should do. In this way, bhuñje, gacche, care, etc., should be understood.

1089. Hiyattaniyaṃ karassattaṃ vā. In the Hiyattanī suffix, the substitution of 'a' for [the 'ra' of] the root 'kara' occurs in some places. Akā loke sudukkaraṃ—He did that which is very difficult to do in the world. Sabbārivijayaṃ akā—He achieved victory over all enemies. Because of the word 'vā' (optionally), there is also 'akara' (he did).

1090. Abhisaṅkharassa kharo tyādīsu. The substitution of 'khara' for the root 'kara' preceded by 'abhi-saṃ' occurs when followed by suffixes such as 'ti'. Abhisaṅkharoti—he constructs/prepares, abhisaṅkharonti—they construct/prepare, etc.

1091. Gamissanto kvaci añcho ajjataniyaṃ. In the Ajjatanī suffix, the substitution of 'añcha' for the final part of the root 'gamu' occurs in some places. So agañchi—He went. Te agañchiṃsu—They went. Because of the word 'kvaci' (in some places), there is also 'agacchī' (he went).

1092. Gamimhā sāgamo ca. The augment 'sa' occurs after the root 'gamu'. Agamāsi—He went.

1093. Umaṃsu. The substitution of 'aṃsu' for the 'uṃ' suffix after the root 'gamu' occurs in some places. Agamaṃsu—They went.

1094. U-āgamo tthambhesu. The augment 'u' occurs before the suffixes 'ttha' and 'mha'. Tumhe gamuttha—You went, mayaṃ gamumha—We went.

1095. Gamissa gattaṃ yathātanti. The substitution of 'ga' for the root 'gamu' occurs according to the sequence of the Pāḷi text. So dhanaṃ ajjhagā—He obtained wealth. Te ajjhagu—They obtained. Sopāgā samitiṃ vanaṃ—He also arrived at the assembly in the forest. Kambalassatarāāguṃ—The Kambala and Assatara nāgas came.

1096. Bhavissantīyaṃ chidassa vā checcho ssena. In the Bhavissantī suffix, the substitution of 'checca' for the root 'chid' together with the suffixal part 'ssa' occurs in some places. In the Bhavissantī suffix, the substitution of 'checca' for the root 'chid'...
308: Or it occurs together with the letter 'ssa', which is a part of the inflection. Checchati, checchanti, checcbasi. Why is 'vā' (optionally) said? Because chindissanti (may also exist). ## 1097. Bhidassa bheccho. After the root bhida, when the bhavissanti inflection occurs, the substitution of bheccha occurs optionally (vā) together with the letter 'ssa', which is a part of the inflection. Bhecchati, bhecchanti, avijjaṃ bhecchati (he will break through ignorance). ## 1098. Chidabhidānamajjatanīyañca. Again, the mention of the roots chida and bhida is to prevent the meaning that it must occur together with the inflection. In the ajjatanī inflection, the roots chida and bhida are respectively substituted with checcha and bheccha optionally. Acchecchi kaṅkhaṃ (he cut off doubt). Acchecchuṃ vata bho rukkhaṃ (O friends, they have indeed cut down the tree). Everything should be applied as in abhecchī, abhecchuṃ, abheccho, abhecchittha, etc., and accheccho, acchecchittha, etc. Why is 'vā' said? Because acchindi and abhindi (may also exist). ## 1099. Kvaci purisavipallāso. In some Pāli passages, there is a confusion of person (purisa), just as there is confusion of inflections, etc. Puttaṃ labhetha varadaṃ (May she obtain a son who grants noble boons). ## 1100. Lūnīto kāritesu ṇeva. After the roots lū and nī, among the causative (kārita) suffixes, only the suffix ṇe occurs. Lāveti (he causes to reap/cut), nāyeti (he causes to lead). In this rule, the mention of 'lūnīto' is merely a primary example; other roots of such nature should also be sought. ## 1101. Pariavasoto ṇe ca ṇāpe ca. After the root so (in the sense of finishing) preceded by pari or ava, the suffixes ṇe and ṇāpe occur simultaneously. In this regard, there is this Pāli: 'He himself completes the work begun by himself; there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa. He causes others to complete the work begun by himself; there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa.'
309: In this place, the analysis (Nīti) has been placed by us below; let the venerable ones contemplate that analysis. ## 1102. The letter 'se' comes after verbal and nominal terms. The letter 'se' is added after a verb (ākhyāta) or a noun (nāma) for the sake of the smoothness of the speech. 'We have never before made a marriage with the Nāgas.
