How shall we make that unsuitable marriage with the Nāgas?' Thus, the letter 'se' comes after a verb. 'Whoever have gone to the Buddha for refuge...' Thus, it comes after a noun. In the passage 'We have done your work' (akaramhasa te kiccaṃ), the vowel 'e' in the letter 'se' is changed to 'a' for the sake of protecting the meter. In the passage 'May the spirits of the mountains and forests be respectful' (ukkantāmasi bhūtāni...), it should be noted that the vowel 'e' is changed to 'i' for the sake of protecting the meter. The characteristics of that rule have been explained below. ## 1103. In verses (gāthā), the substitution of issaṃ for the inflection iṃ occurs in the past sense. When the past sense is to be expressed, the substitution of issaṃ for the inflection iṃ occurs optionally in verses. 'Formerly, I refrained from giving.' 'I wandered without finding the [Omniscient] Knowledge.' 'I observed the Uposatha.' In the passage 'I was cooked in hell' (nirayamhi apaccisaṃ), one letter 'sa' is dropped for the sake of protecting the meter. Why is 'in verses' said? Because the substitution of issaṃ does not occur in prose, such as 'He was born in that existence' or 'Having such a name, I lived in this existence.' Why is 'in the past sense' said? To prevent the substitution of issaṃ in the future sense, such as 'I shall go to that unconditioned Nibbāna.' Why is 'vā' (optionally) said? Because there are instances where the substitution of issaṃ does not occur, such as 'I did not follow the word of the Teacher.' In that example, some people, not desiring an excess of syllables in the verse feet, read it as 'uposathaṃ upavasiṃ'. Such reading is not appropriate. This is because there are instances of excess syllables and deficient syllables in the verse feet of the Buddha's teachings.
310:
Similarly, verses are seen with deficient or excessive syllables and feet, such as: "Sa kattā taramānova, sivirājenapesito," and "Ime nu maccā kimakaṃsu pāpaṃ, yemejanā adhimattā dukkhā tibbā, kharā kaṭukā vedanāvedayantī," and "Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittampaññañca bhāvayaṃ."

Even though such verses are seen, there is not even an atom's weight of fault, because this is a Dispensation that leads out of suffering (niyyānika-sāsana), and because it is a Dhamma teaching delivered by the Fully Enlightened One in accordance with the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those capable of being enlightened.

For it is said in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: "The Blessed One, however, does not take into account the lightness or heaviness of words; rather, he determines the teaching in such and such a way without contradicting the nature of Dhamma, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be enlightened. Therefore, no criticism should be made regarding the abundance or deficiency of syllables."

If this is so, why did the former teachers say in various places, "elision of syllables for the sake of not breaking the meter in verses," "reversal for the sake of protecting the prosody," and "for the sake of protecting the meter and for ease of pronunciation"?

What is said is true. In a case where the meter and prosody should be protected, why would the Blessed One not protect the meter and prosody? (He certainly protects them). However, in a case where it is not necessary to protect those two, the Blessed One does not protect the meter and prosody. It is with reference to such instances that it was said, "The Blessed One, however, does not take into account the lightness or heaviness of words," and so on.

Even when protecting the meter and prosody, the Blessed One does not protect them through the exertion of effort like poets and others. Rather, because of the familiarity with syllables and language acquired during his time as a Bodhisatta throughout countless hundreds of thousands of births over an immeasurable period, the words emerge from his glorious lotus-like mouth as already perfected. Among those words, some proceed in a manner similar to the protection of meter and prosody, while others do not proceed in that way. With reference to those words that proceed in a manner similar to protection...
312:
## 7-Kitakappa

Following this section on verbs (ākhyāta), I shall speak of the excellent Kitaka treatise, which is beneficial for the proficiency of the wise in the Pariyatti Pali.

1106. The suffix ṇa is added after a root when it is in proximity to an object (kamma). When in proximity to an object, the suffix ṇa occurs after a root. One who performs an action; therefore, he is called kammakāra. Likewise, mālakāra (florist), kumbhakāra (potter), and so on.

1107. When a name is to be expressed, the suffix a is added after a root in proximity to an object, and the augment nu comes after the noun. When a name or designation is to be expressed, the suffix a occurs after a root in proximity to an object, and there is also the arrival of the syllable nu after the noun. One who subdues enemies; therefore, he is called arindama. Likewise, vessantara and so on.

1108. The suffix a is added after this root da when in proximity to the word pura, and the 'a' of the word pura is changed to iṃ. When in proximity to the word pura, the suffix a occurs after this root da, and there is also the changing of the 'a' of the word pura to iṃ. One who gives gifts in the past; therefore, he is called purindada.

1109. The suffixes ṇvu, tu, and āvī occur optionally after all roots, whether an object is in proximity or not. The suffixes a, ṇvu, tu, and āvī occur after all roots, whether an object is in proximity or not. One who does that action; therefore, he is called takkara. One who does what is beneficial; therefore, he is called hitakkara. One leads away (transgressions of body and speech) respectively by that rule, or one leads in that rule; therefore, it is called vinaya. One lives depending on that teacher; therefore, he is called nissaya.

Regarding the suffix ṇvu: One who makes a chariot; therefore, he is called rathakāraka. One who gives food and snacks; therefore, he is called annadāyaka. One who leads beings (to Nibbāna); therefore, he is called vināyaka. One who does; therefore, he is called kāraka. One who gives; therefore, he is called dāyaka. One who leads; therefore, he is called nāyaka.

Regarding the suffix tu: One who does that action is called takkaṭṭā. One who gives food is called bhojanadātā. One who does; therefore, he is called kattā. That which flows; therefore, it is called saritā.

Regarding the suffix āvī: One who sees danger; therefore, he is called bhayapassāvī. Thus and so on.
313:
1110. The suffix ṇa is added after roots such as visa, ruja, and pada. Because it enters into an object, it is called pavesa. Because it causes pain, it is called roga. Because it arises, it is called uppāda. Because it touches, it is called phassa. Because they live together, it is called oka. Because it becomes, it is called bhāva. Because it arises, it is called āya. Because one knows well, it is called sambodha.

1111. The suffix ṇa is also added in the sense of bhāva (state/action). When the sense of bhāva is to be expressed, the suffix ṇa occurs after roots. The act of cooking is pāka; the act of relinquishing is cāga; the act of becoming is bhāva. Thus and so on.

1112. The suffix kvi is added after all roots. Because it comes into being well, it is called sambhū. In the same way, vibhū and abhibhū also occur. Because it goes in a curved manner, it is called bhujaga. Because it digs well, it is called saṅkha.

1113. The suffix (mma) is added after the root dhara and others. Because it upholds beings who practice according to the instruction so that they do not fall into the four woeful states, it is called dhamma. Or, because it exists by that nature, it is called dhamma. Because that action is performed, it is called kamma.

1114. The suffixes ṇī, tu, and āvī occur after all roots in these senses: having that habit (tassīla), having that nature (taddhamma), or being one who performs that well (tassādhukārī). A king who has the habit of praising one who is dear is called piyappasaṃsī. Or, because he has the habit of praising one who is dear, he is piyappasaṃsī; because he has the nature of praising one who is dear, he is piyappasaṃsī; because he performs well in praising one who is dear, he is called piyappasaṃsī. A person who has the habit of practicing the sublime life is called brahmacārī. Or, because he has the habit of practicing the sublime life, he is brahmacārī; because he has the nature of practicing the sublime life, he is brahmacārī; because he performs well in practicing the sublime life, he is called brahmacārī. In other instances as well, understand in this manner as appropriate. A king who has the habit of proceeding by means of oppression is that king...
314:
One who has the habit of prevailing by force or speaking by force is called 'pasayhappavattā'. A monk who is habituated to seeing danger is called 'bhayadassāvī'. One who is habituated to wrestling is called 'mallakārī'. Similarly, one who is habituated to doing evil is 'pāpakārī', and one who is habituated to going fast is 'sīghayāyī'. Among these terms, if one wishes to speak in the feminine gender, one should say 'piyappasaṃsinī', 'brahmacārinī', etc. If one wishes to speak in the neuter gender, one should use the short vowel (rassa), such as 'piyappasaṃsi', 'brahmacārī', etc.; for example, 'piyappasaṃsi kulaṃ' (a family that habitually praises loved ones), 'brahmacārī cittaṃ' (a mind that habitually practices what is noble). This method applies to other examples as well.

1115. After the root gamu, the suffix 'ro' ending in 'o' is applied. Because it goes, it is called 'go' (ox/cow).

1116. After the root su, the suffix 'ā' is applied. Because it listens to sound, it is called 'sā' (dog).

1117. After roots meaning making sound, being angry, trembling, and decorating, and after the root ruca etc., the suffix 'yu' is applied in the sense of habit (tassīla) etc. Because of the habit of shouting, the nature of shouting, or being good at shouting, it is called 'ghosano'. Similarly, 'bhāsano' (one who habitually speaks), 'kodhano' (one who habitually gets angry), 'rosano' (one who habitually shows irritation), 'calano' (one who habitually shakes), 'kampano' (one who habitually trembles), 'phandano' (one who habitually quivers), 'maṇḍano' (one who habitually decorates), 'vibhūsano' (one who habitually adorns), 'rocano' (one who habitually shines), 'tejano' (one who habitually brightens), 'vaḍḍhano' (one who habitually increases), and so forth.

1118. After the root gamu preceded by prefixes such as pāra etc., the suffix 'rū' is applied in the sense of habit etc. A person who habitually goes to Nibbāna, which is the further shore of existence, is called 'bhavapāragū'. One who habitually reaches the end is 'antagū'. One who habitually knows the Four Noble Truths through the four path-knowledges is 'vedagū'. Why is it said 'in the sense of habit etc.'? In the case of 'pāraṅgato' (one who has gone to the shore), the suffix 'rū' is not applied because habit is not intended. Why is it said 'the root gamu preceded by prefixes such as pāra etc.'? In the case of 'anugāmī' (follower), the suffix 'rū' is not applied because prefixes like pāra are not present.

1119. After roots such as bhikkha etc., the suffix 'rū' is also applied in the sense of habit etc. One who habitually begs is called 'bhikkhu'. One who habitually knows is called 'viññū'.
315:
1120. Ṇuko hanatyādīnaṃ. At the end of roots such as hana etc., the suffix ṇuka is applied in the sense of habit etc. One who has the nature of habitually harming is called āghātuko. One who has the nature of habitually doing is called kāruko.

1121. Aññatthesu ca ṇī. The suffix ṇī is applied in the aforementioned senses as well as in other senses. One who thinks of oneself as wise is paṇḍitamānī. Similarly, bahussutamānī (one who thinks of oneself as very learned). One who kills living beings is sattughātī. One who lives for a long time is dīghajīvī. One who speaks the Dhamma is dhammavādī. One who roars fearlessly like a lion is sīhanādī. One who sleeps on the ground is bhūmisāyī, and so forth.

1122. Padante nvāgamo niggahītaṃ. The letter 'n' that comes at the end of a word changes to a niggahīta. One who subdues enemies is arindamo. One who goes to the path of the merchants is vessantaro, referring to the King. One who makes the light of his own radiance and wisdom is pabhaṅkaro, referring to the Buddha.

1123. Samādihanatvaññāya vā ro hanassa gho. After the root hana preceded by prefixes like saṃ etc., or after other roots, the suffix ra is applied, and the root hana is changed to gha. One who approaches a common task with unity, or one who well destroys the distress of defilements, is called saṅgho. One who harms in return is paṭigho. One who intensely kills various beings is byaggho. That which is dug around the outside of a city is parikhā. One who makes an end is antako. Why is it said 'samādi'? This is to prevent such changes in upaghāto (assault/killing).

1124. Ramhi ranto rādi lopaṃ. When the suffix ra follows, the entire end portion of the root, starting from the letter r, undergoes elision. Examples include antako (Death), pāragū, satthā, diṭṭho, and so forth.

1125. Bhāve kamme ca tabbāniyā. After all roots, the suffixes tabba and anīya are applied in the sense of state (bhāva) and object (kamma). It is become (bhūyate).
316:
It was, it will be, it should be, the state of being, it is to be become. It should be, the state of being, it is to be become. It should be eaten, the act of eating, it is to be eaten. It should be eaten, the act of eating, it is to be eaten. It should be gone to, the act of going, it is to be gone to. It should be gone to, the act of going, it is to be gone to. It should be done, the act of doing, it is to be done. It should be done, the act of doing, it is to be done. It should be gone to, the act of going, it is to be gone to. It should be gone to, the act of going, it is to be gone to. It should be delighted in, the act of delighting, it is to be delighted in. It should be delighted in, the act of delighting, it is to be delighted in.

1126. After roots, the suffixes ṇya and teyya are applied as appropriate in the sense of state and object. That which is to be done is called kattabbaṃ or kāriyaṃ. That which is to be developed is called cetabbaṃ or ceyyaṃ. That which is to be led is called netabbaṃ or neyyaṃ. That which is to be known is called ñātabbaṃ or ñāteyyaṃ. That which is to be seen is called passitabbaṃ or diṭṭheyyaṃ.

1127. After the root kara, the suffix ricca is applied in the sense of state and object. That which is to be done is called kattabbaṃ or kiccaṃ.

1128. After the root bhū, the suffix ṇya together with the vowel ū is changed to abba. That which is to be become is called bhavitabbo or babbo, and bhavitabbaṃ or babbaṃ.

1129. After the roots vada, mada, gama, yuza, garaha, and roots ending in the vowel ā etc., the suffix ṇya together with the end of the root is changed respectively to jja, mma, gga, yha, and eyya. Also, the root garaha is changed to gāra in the sense of state and object. That which is to be spoken is called vattabbāṃ or vajjaṃ. That which is to be intoxicated by is called madanīyaṃ or majjaṃ. That which is to be reached is called gamanīyaṃ or gammaṃ. That which is to be joined is called yojanīyaṃ or yoggaṃ. That which is to be blamed is called garahitabbaṃ or gārayhaṃ. That which is to be given is called dātabbaṃ or deyyaṃ. That which is to be drunk is called pātabbaṃ or peyyaṃ. That which is to be abandoned is called hātabbaṃ or heyyaṃ. That which is to be measured is called mātabbaṃ or meyyaṃ. That which is to be known is called ñātabbaṃ or ñeyyaṃ, and so forth.

1130. In accordance with the Pali scriptures, the suffix tabya is applied not only in the sense of state and object but also in the sense of the agent (kattar). "They reached the state of consuming the objects of desire." Here, "pātabyatā" means either the state of being consumed or the act of consuming having been done. The word 'pā' has the meaning of consumption (paribhoga).
317:
1131. These five suffixes, starting from 'tabba' and ending with 'ricca', should be known as Kicca suffixes. The purpose of naming them Kicca is for use in rules such as 'bhāvakammesu kiccaktakkhatthā' and to complete the application of Kicca suffixes in the sense of state (bhāva) and object (kamma).

1132. Suffixes other than Kicca suffixes are named Kit. The purpose of naming them Kit is for use in rules such as 'kattari kit' and to complete the application of Kit suffixes in the sense of the agent (kattar).

1133. The suffix yu occurs after the root nanda and others in the sense of state (bhāva) and object (kamma). (Examples:) Rejoicing is 'nandanaṃ'. Alternatively, that which is rejoiced in is 'nandanaṃ'. That which is taken is 'gahanaṃ'. That which is practiced is 'caraṇaṃ'.

1134. The suffix yu also occurs in the sense of the agent (kattar), instrument (karaṇa), and location (adhikaraṇa). In the sense of the agent—it is called 'rajoharaṇaṃ' because it removes dust. In the sense of the instrument—it is called 'karaṇaṃ' because one acts by means of it. In the sense of the location—it is called 'ṭhānaṃ' because one stands in this place.

1135. After roots ending in the letters 'ra' or 'ha', the substitution of 'ana' should be changed to 'ṇa'. It is called 'karaṇaṃ' because one acts by means of it. It is called 'pūraṇaṃ' because one fills by means of it. The act of seizing is 'gahanaṃ'. Other words should also be formed in this manner.

1136. In words such as vanagahana, the substitution of 'ana' to 'ṇa' does not occur. (Examples:) 'vanagahanaṃ', 'udakagahanaṃ', 'kalalagahanaṃ', etc. Why is it said 'in words such as vanagahana'? It is to allow the 'ṇa' substitution in words like 'paṭisandhiggahaṇaṃ'.

1137. Suffixes from ṇa to yu should be known as applying to all three periods of time. For example—one is called 'kumbhakāro' (pot-maker) because he is making, has made, or will make a pot. It is called 'karaṇaṃ' because one is acting, has acted, or will act by means of it. Other words should also be formed in this manner.
318:
1138. In the sense of an appellation (name), the suffix i occurs after the roots dā and dhā. 'Ādi' (beginning) is so called because it is taken; likewise 'upādi'. 'Udadhi' (ocean) is so called because it bears water. 'Mahodadhi' is so called because it bears much water; likewise 'jaladhi'. It is called 'vāladhi' (tail) because hair is borne on that tail. 'Sandhi' (connection) is so called because it is joined or it joins. 'Nidhi' (treasure) is so called because it is deposited. Likewise, 'vidhi' is so called because it is performed, it performs, or it is the performance itself. 'Samādhi' (concentration) is so called because it bears the mind well or evenly.

1139. In the sense of aspiration (āsiṭṭha), the suffixes ti and Kit occur after all roots. 'Jinabuddhi'—May the Victorious Buddha know the beings. 'Dhanabhūti'—May wealth arise for that person. Regarding the Kit suffix—'bhūto' (may it be). 'Dhammadinno'—May the Dhamma give to this person. 'Vaḍḍhamāno'—May it increase. Other words should also be formed in this manner.

1140. In the sense of the feminine gender, the suffixes a, ti, and yu occur after all roots according to the usage in the Pāḷi texts. Firstly, regarding the suffix a—'jarā' (old age) is the act of aging or that which ages. 'Paṭisambhidā' (analytical insight) is so called because it knows by distinguishing each part. 'Paṭipadā' (practice) is so called because one practices in this manner. Likewise, 'sampadā' and 'āpadā' are formed. 'Upādā' (clinging) is so called because it clings intensely. 'Cintā' (thought) is the act of thinking. 'Patiṭṭhā' (establishment) is the act of standing. 'Sikkhā' (training) is the act of learning or that which is learned; likewise 'bhikkhā' (alms). 'Abhijjhā' (covetousness) is so called because it looks towards wealth and prosperity. 'Upajjhā' (preceptor) is the act of looking closely at major and minor faults. Because it is the state of being a preceptor, it is said with reference to: "The preceptor should be made to take (the robe)." It is connected as "one who is looking for higher ordination (upasampadā)." Regarding the suffix ti—'mati' (wisdom/thought) is so called because one knows, or it is the act of knowing. 'Sati' (mindfulness) is the act of remembering. Regarding the suffix yu—'cetanā' (volition) is so called because it instigates. 'Vedanā' (feeling) is so called because it feels. Other words should also be formed in this manner.
319:
1141. The suffix ririya occurs after the root kar. When expressing either the feminine or non-feminine (masculine/neuter) sense from the root kar, the suffix ririya is applied. 'Kiriyā' (action) is that which is to be done. 'Kiriyaṃ' is the act of doing.

1142. In the past tense, the suffixes ta, tavantu, and tāvī are applied. One who has practiced the holy life is called 'vusito', 'vusitavā', or 'vusitāvī'. One who has made an offering to the fire is called 'huto', 'hutavā', or 'hutāvī'. One who has eaten rice is called 'bhutto', 'bhuttavā', or 'bhuttāvī'. In those examples, 'vusito' is so called because he has lived in that holy life. 'Huto' is so called because he has offered. 'Bhutto' is so called because he has eaten. This method applies to the remaining suffixes tavantu and tāvī as well. Among those words, words like 'vusitavā' are similar to 'guṇavantu' in terms of declension (padamālā). However, words like 'vusitāvī' are similar to 'daṇḍī'. When the suffix inī is applied, they become 'vusitāvinī', etc. In the neuter gender, due to the shortening of the vowel, they become 'vusitāvi', etc.

1143. The suffix ta occurs in the sense of state (bhāva) and object (kamma). In the past tense, the suffix ta occurs after all roots in the sense of state and object. Firstly, in the sense of state—it is called 'gītaṃ' because it is the act of singing or because one has sung. It is called 'naccaṃ' or 'naṭṭaṃ' because it is the act of dancing or because one has danced. Likewise, 'hasitaṃ' is the act of laughing. In the sense of the object—it is called 'bhāsitaṃ' because it was spoken by the man. Likewise, 'desitaṃ' (preached), 'kataṃ' (done), and 'sayitaṃ' (slept) are formed. It is formed as 'roditaṃ' or 'ruṇṇaṃ' because it was cried, and so forth.

1144. After roots such as budh and gamu, the suffix ta occurs in the sense of the agent (kattar) in all periods of time. After roots such as budh and gamu, the suffix ta occurs in the sense of the agent in all periods of time. He is called 'Buddho' because he knows, has known, or will know all phenomena categorized as conditioned (saṅkhata), unconditioned (asaṅkhata), and conventional (sammuti). Likewise, 'saraṇaṅgato' (one who has gone for refuge), 'samathaṅgato' (one who has attained tranquility), and so forth are formed.

1145. The suffix ina occurs after the root ji. After the root ji, the suffix ina occurs in the sense of the agent (kattar) in all periods of time. He is called 'Jino' (The Conqueror) because he conquers, has conquered, or will conquer evil unwholesome states.
320:
1146. Supasmā bhāve ca. After the root 'sup', the suffix 'ina' is applied in the sense of the agent (kattar) and the state (bhāva). Because he sleeps, it is called 'supino'; or, the act of sleeping is called 'supino'.

1147. Īsadusuto kho bhāvakammesu. After roots preceded by the prefixes 'īsa', 'du', and 'su', the suffix 'kha' is applied in the sense of the state (bhāva) and the object (kamma). The venerable one should sleep a little; therefore, it is called 'īsassayo' (sleeping a little). The venerable one should sleep with difficulty; therefore, 'dussayo' (sleeping with difficulty). The venerable one should sleep easily; therefore, 'sussayo' (sleeping easily). The venerable one should perform the task a little; therefore, it is called 'īsakkaraṃ'. The venerable one should perform the benefit with difficulty; therefore, 'dukkaraṃ'. A fool performs evil easily; therefore, 'sukaraṃ'. One with great desires is difficult to support; therefore, 'dubbharo'. One with few desires is easy to support; therefore, 'subharo'. The mind is difficult to guard; therefore, 'durakkhaṃ'. The Dhamma is difficult to see; therefore, 'duddaso'. The faults of others are easy to see; therefore, 'sudassaṃ'. The Dhamma is difficult to understand; therefore, 'duranubodho'. It is easy to understand; therefore, 'subodhaṃ'. And so on.

1148. Icchatthesu tavetuṃ vā samānakattukesu. When there are roots expressing desire (icchā) having the same agent, the suffixes 'tave' and 'tuṃ' are optionally applied after all roots in all tenses in the sense of the agent. He desires to perform meritorious deeds; he desires to hear the True Dhamma.

1149. Tumarahasakkādīsu. The suffix 'tuṃ' is applied after all roots in the sense of 'deserving' (araha), 'being able' (sakkā), etc. Who is worthy of blaming him? One is not able to conquer [death] even with wealth. He is capable of entering the path (niyāma/magga). The venerable one is worthy of receiving the gift. It is suitable to do this work. It is proper to give. He gets to give and to speak. Thus it is proper to speak. It is not proper to bind. It is time to eat. And so on.
321:
1150. Pubbakālekakattukānaṃ tunatvānatvāpāyena. Among roots having the same agent, the suffixes 'tuna', 'tvāna', and 'tvā' generally occur for the preceding action. Having done the work, he goes. Beings suffer without having done merit. Having heard the Dhamma, he rejoices. Having heard, we shall know. And so on.

1151. Kadāci samāne ca. Sometimes, the suffixes 'tuna', 'tvāna', and 'tvā' occur among roots having the same agent in the same time. This sun emerges, having dispelled the darkness. Here, by showing the use of the suffix 'tvāna', the uses of 'tuna' and 'tvā' are also shown.

1152. Apare ca. Sometimes, the suffixes 'tuna', 'tvāna', and 'tvā' occur among roots having the same agent for the subsequent action. Having closed the door, he enters.

1153. Asamānakattaripi. Sometimes, the suffixes 'tuna', 'tvāna', and 'tvā' occur even when the agents are not the same. Upon seeing the lion, fear arises. Having seen that [Dhamma] with wisdom, the taints (āsavas) are exhausted.

1154. Parapadayoge ca. Sometimes, the suffixes 'tvā', etc., occur when associated with other words. The mountain exists before reaching the river. The river exists after passing the mountain.

1155. Lakkhaṇahetuādippayoge ca. Sometimes, the suffixes 'tvā', etc., occur in the sense of a characteristic (lakkhaṇa), a cause (hetu), etc. Upon seeing the lion, fear arises. Strength arises because of drinking ghee. Having made the sound 'dha', the stick fell.
322:
1156. In cases of clear meaning and established grammatical usage, suffixes such as tvā and others sometimes arise from roots. Examples: Matter depending on matter (upādāya-rūpaṃ). Going after bathing (nhatvā), sleeping after eating (bhutvā), and so forth.

1157. In the present tense, when expressing an incomplete action, the suffixes māna and anta arise from all roots. He cries while remembering (saramāno). He takes while going (gacchanto). That Bhāradvāja, while going, saw the hermit Accuta.

1158. When not expressing an incomplete action and in an indefinite time, the suffix anta arises from the root. He is great, he was great, he will be great. He is great, he was great, he will be great.

1159. The suffix ratthu arises from roots such as sāsa. Because He disciplines the world together with the devas, the Blessed One is called the Teacher (Satthā).

1160. The suffix ritu arises from roots such as pā. Because he protects the son, he is called father (pitā). Or, because he loves the son, he is called father (pitā). Or, because he satisfies or gratifies the son, he is called father (pitā). Because she is supported by the parents, she is called daughter (dhītā).

1161. The suffix rātu arises from roots such as māna. Because she naturally cherishes the son, she is called mother (mātā). Because he speaks first, he is called brother (bhātā). Generally, the eldest brother is called bhātā because he speaks first; therefore, another person is also called bhātā because he speaks afterwards.

1162. The suffix tuka arises from the root gamu preceded by ā. Because he comes, he is called a guest (āgantuka).
323:
1163. In the sense of capability (bhabba), the suffix -ika is added after the root Gamu. A monk who will go or is fit to go is called Gamika.

1164. In the views of other teachers, suffixes that cannot be precisely established by individual rules are established by the rule of nipātana (irregularity). It is said that in the views of other teachers, those words in numerals, nouns, compounds, derivatives (taddhita), verbs (ākhyāta), and primary derivatives (kita) which, along with their suffixes, do not reach completion through standard rules, are established only through nipātana. This point should also be borne in mind: those good words which are in common usage in the world, if they are not produced by the aforementioned suffixes, are established by nipātana.

1165. The root Ge is changed to Gī because of the suffixes -ta and -ti. Gītaṃ (singing), Gīti (singing), Saṅgīti (rehearsal or communal chanting of the Vinaya Piṭaka, etc.).

1166. After the root Nati, the suffix -ta together with the end of the root is changed to cca and ṭṭa. Naccaṃ (dancing), Naṭṭaṃ (dancing).

1167. After the words Ima, Samāna, and Apara, the suffixes -jja and -jju are added. At this time: Ajja (today). At a time similar to the present day: Sajju (at that moment). To illustrate this, it is said: "An evil deed committed does not bear fruit at that very moment, just as freshly milked milk does not change [curdle] immediately." Here, Sajju-khīraṃ means the warm, fresh milk coming out from the cow's udders at the very moment of milking. At another time: Aparajju (yesterday or tomorrow). The day immediately passed is meant by Hiyyo (yesterday). Or it means Suve (tomorrow). To illustrate this, it is said: "Having entered the monastery after returning from the alms-round, he departs either in the evening or at the proper time on the following day (aparajju)." Here, they say the meaning is specifically the morning of the following day.

1168. The word Ima is changed to A because of the suffix -jja. Ajja (today).
324:
1169. Samānassa jja-mhi so. When the suffix -jja follows, the word Samāna is changed to Sa. Sajja. (In the Nissaya, the usage Sajju is explained as "at that moment only," "on the following day," etc.)

1170. Sāsadisehi riṭṭho tassa. After the roots Sā and Disa, the suffix -ta is changed to riṭṭha. "That person has been instructed by me." "A form has been seen by me."

1171. Disato kiccatassa raṭṭho. After the root Disa, the suffix -ta having the sense of kicca (potential/necessity) is changed to raṭṭha. "Worthy of being seen," "that which should be seen."

1172. Tuṃtvānaṃ raṭṭုံ. After the root Disa, the suffixes -tuṃ and -tvāna are changed to raṭṭhuṃ. "He goes to the monastery to see the Saṅgha of monks." "Because of seeing renunciation as safety." Here, daṭṭhu means "having seen" (disvā) or "due to the cause of seeing" (dassana-hetu).

1173. Tvāssa raṭṭhā ca. After the root Disa, the suffix -tvā is also changed to raṭṭhā. "Because of my seeing Ummādantī who was wearing a string of pearls." One who has reached the end because of seeing the Four Noble Truths is called Diṭṭhappatta. It means one who has reached or attained Nibbāna, the end of Saṃsāra, having seen it with the eye of wisdom.

1174. Disassa vā salopādesenissattañca. The elision of the letter s of the root Disa, and the change of the vowel i to a along with the letter r which is part of the substitute, occur optionally (vā). Daṭṭhabbaṃ, Daṭṭhuṃ. Why is "optionally" (vā) said? Ahaṃ diṭṭhā (I have been seen), Rūpaṃ diṭṭhaṃ (The form has been seen).

1175. Diṭṭhassittaṃ patte. When the word patta follows, the vowel ā of the word diṭṭhā which expresses the meaning "having seen" is changed to i. Diṭṭhippatto. Why is "of diṭṭha" (diṭṭhassa) said? Diṭṭhippatto. Because of having reached through wisdom (diṭṭhi), it is called Diṭṭhippatto.
325:
1176. After roots ending in the letter s, the root pucch, the root bhañj, the root han, and so forth, the suffix -ta should be changed to ṭṭha along with the preceding consonant in the appropriate place. For example: Tuṭṭho (pleased), Ahinā daṭṭho (bitten by a snake), Mayā puṭṭho (asked by me), Bhaṭṭho (trampled), Haṭṭho (joyful), Pahaṭṭho (greatly joyful), Yiṭṭho (sacrificed/offered), Juṭṭho (pleased or associated with), Saṃsaṭṭho (mixed/associated), Paviṭṭho (entered). Other words should also be understood by comparison in this manner.

1177. After the root Vas, the suffix -ta should be changed to uttha along with the preceding consonant in the appropriate place. For example: Vassaṃ vuttho (having spent the rainy season).

1178. When the suffix -ta follows, the letter v of the root Vas should be changed to the letter u in some places. For example: Vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ (the holy life has been lived), Uṭṭho or Vuṭṭho (dwelt).

1179. After roots ending in dh, ḍh, bh, and h, the suffix -ta should be changed to dha and ḍha respectively. For example: Buddho Bhagavā (the Blessed One who is the Enlightened One), Vuḍḍho bhikkhu (an elder monk), Laddhaṃ me pattacīvaraṃ (the bowl and robe have been obtained by me), Agginā daḍḍhaṃ vanaṃ (the forest was burnt by fire).

1180. After the root Bhañj, the suffix -ta should be changed to gga along with the preceding consonant. For example: Bhaggo (broken).

1181. The final consonant of roots such as Bhuj should be elided, and the suffix -ta should be doubled (dvebhāva). For example: Bhutto, Bhuttavā, Bhuttāvī (eaten/having eaten), Catto (relinquished), Satto (attached), Ratto (lustful), Yutto (joined/yoked), Vivitto (secluded).

1182. The letter v of the root Vac should be changed to u, the final letter c should be elided, and the suffix -ta should be doubled (dvebhāva). For example: "Thus was it said by the Blessed One," "It was said by the Arahant."
326:
1183. The final consonant of roots such as *gup* is elided, and the suffix *-ta* is doubled. (Examples are:) well-guarded (*sugutto*), known (*citto*), smeared (*litto*), greatly tormented (*santatto*), burning (*āditto*), secluded (*vivitto*), and so forth.

1184. After roots such as *tar*, the suffix *-ta* is substituted with *iṇṇa*, and the final consonant of the root is elided. *Tiṇṇohaṃ tāreyyaṃ*: "Having crossed over, I shall help others cross." Crossed over (*uttiṇṇo*), full (*sampuṇṇo*), completely full (*paripuṇṇo*), pierced (*tuṇṇo*), decayed/old (*parijiṇṇo*), strewn (*ākiṇṇo*).

1185. After roots such as *bhid*, the suffix *-ta* is optionally substituted with *inna*, *anna*, or *īṇa*, and the final consonant of the root is elided. Broken (*bhinno*), shattered (*sambhinno*), cut (*chinno*), well-cut (*sañchinno*), given (*dinno*), seated (*nisinno*), covered (*channo*), completely covered (*acchanno*), exhausted (*khinno*), forbidden or weeping (*ruṇṇo*), *khīṇā jāti*: "Birth is exhausted." Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated? To prevent the substitution in forms such as a wall (*bhitti*).

1186. After these roots—*sus*, *pac*, and *sak*—the suffix *-ta* is substituted with *kkha* or *kka*, and the final consonant of the root is elided. Dry wood (*sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ*), ripe fruit (*pakkaṃ phalaṃ*), *sakkohaṃ*: "I am Sakka."

1187. After roots such as *kamu*, the suffix *-ta* is substituted with *nta*, and the final consonant of the root is elided. Gone (*pakkanto*), wandering (*vibbhamanto*), moved/transferred (*saṅkanto*), calm or exhausted (*santo*), patient (*khanto*), tamed (*danto*), vomited (*vanto*).

1188. After roots such as *khamu*, the suffix *-ta* is substituted with *nti*, and the final consonant of the root is elided. Patience (*khanti*), going/moving (*kanti*), peace (*santi*).
327:
1189. Because of the suffixes *-ta* and *-ti*, the final consonant of roots such as *jan* is substituted with *ā*. Because it has arisen, it is called *jāto*. Arising is called *jāti*.

1190. Because of the suffixes *-ta* and *-ti*, the final consonant of roots such as *gam*, *khan*, *han*, and *ram* is elided. One who has gone well is *sugato*; a good destination is *sugati*; that which is dug is *khataṃ*; that which is oppressed is *upahataṃ*; one who delights in those who are in harmony is *samaggarato*; delighting in those who are in harmony is *samaggarati*; one who is greatly delighted is *abhirato*; great delight is *abhirati*; one who is known or dead is *mato*; knowledge or desire is called *mati*.

1191. Because of the suffixes *-ta* and *-ti*, the final *r* of roots is also elided. One who is oppressed is *pakatော*; nature or state is *pakati*; one who is mindful is *sato*; mindfulness is called *sati*.

1192. Because of the suffixes *-ta* and *-ti*, the final of these roots such as *ṭhā* and *pā* becomes *ivaṇṇa* (*i*). One who stands is *ṭhito*; standing is *ṭhiti*; one who has drunk gruel is *yāguṃ pīto*; *yāguṃpītassa bhikkhuno*: "to the monk who has drunk gruel"; *dhammapīti*: "drinking the Dhamma (delighting in it), one sleeps happily."

1193. After roots ending in the letter *h*, the suffix *-ta* is substituted with *ha*; the final *h* of roots other than *dah* and *nah* is optionally substituted with *ḷ*. One who has ascended is *ārūḷho*; one who has entered/plunged is *gāḷho*; *ajjhogāဠှော mahannave*: "plunged into the great ocean"; one who is intense is *bāḷho*; one who is deluded is *mūဠှော*. Why are the roots *dah* and *nah* excluded? Because they result in *daḍḍho* (burnt) and *sannaddho* (firmly bound/armored).

1194. Before the suffix *-ṇa* in the senses of *bhāva* (state), *kattu* (agent), and *karaṇa* (instrument), the *j* of the root *rañj* is optionally substituted with *jo* (resulting in *rāga*). *Rāgo* is so called because beings are attached by that greed, or it attaches itself, or it is merely the state of attaching. Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated? Because there are forms like *raṅgo* (dye or stage/theater).
328:
1195. **Ghāto hanatissa.** When the suffix *-ṇa* follows, the entire root *han* is substituted with *ghāta*. The destruction of wealth is called *upaghāto*. One who kills cattle is called *goghātako*.

1196. **Sabbattha vā vadho.** In all instances, the entire root *han* is optionally substituted with *vadha*. One who kills is called *vadho*, or the act of killing is called *vadho*. *Esa vadho khaṇḍahālassa*: "This is the killing of the Brahmin Khaṇḍahāla." One who kills is called *vadhako*. *Avadhi* or *ahani* (killed).

1197. **Ākārantānamāyo.** When the suffix *-ṇa* follows, roots ending in *ā* are substituted with *āya*. One who gives a gift is called *dānadāyako*. *Dānadāyī* (one who gives gifts), *majjadāyī* (one who gives intoxicants), *nagarayāyī* (one who goes to the city).

1198. **Purasamupaparīhi karဿ khakharā vā tapaccayesu ca.** After *pura*, *saṃ*, *upa*, and *pari*, the root *kar* is optionally substituted with *kha* or *khara* when the suffixes *-ta* and *-ṇa* follow. *Purakkhato* (placed in front/honored), *saṅkhato* (conditioned/prepared), *upakkhaṭo* (prepared/arranged), *parikkhāro* (requisite), *saṅkhāro* (formation/conditioning). Why is "optionally" (*vā*) stated? Because this substitution does not occur in *upakāro* (benefit/help).

1199. **Tavetunādīsu kā.** When suffixes such as *-tave* and *-tuna* follow, the root *kar* is optionally substituted with *kā*. *Kātave* (to do), *kātuṃ* or *kattuṃ* (to do), *kātuna* or *kattuna* (having done).

1200. **Gamakhanahanādīnaṃ tuṃtabbādīsu na.** When suffixes such as *-tuṃ* and *-tabba* follow, the final letter of roots such as *gam*, *khan*, and *han* is optionally substituted with *n*. *Gantuṃ* or *gamituṃ* (to go), *gantabbaṃ* or *gamitabbaṃ* (should go). *Khantuṃ* or *khanituṃ* (to dig), *khantabbaṃ* or *khanituṃ* (should dig). *Hantuṃ* or *hanituṃ* (to kill), *hantabbaṃ* or *hanitabbaṃ* (should kill). *Mantuṃ* or *manituṃ* (to know), *mantabbaṃ* or *manitabbaṃ* (should know). *Gantuna*, *khantuna*, *hantuna*, *mantuna*, *gantvāna*, *khantvāna* (having dug the pit), *rantvā*, *ramitvā*.
329:
1201. After all roots, suffixes such as tuna and others are changed to the letter ya in some instances. (Examples:) abhivandiya, abhivanditvā (having worshipped); ohāya, ohitvā (having abandoned); upanīya, upanetvā (having brought); passiya, passitvā (having seen); uddissa, uddisitvā (having pointed out); ādāya, ādiyitvā (having taken).

1202. After all roots, suffixes such as tuna and others are also changed to yāna in some instances. (Examples:) anubhaviyāna (having experienced), khādiyāna (having chewed), and so forth. Why is "optionally" (vā) said? Because there are also forms like anubhavituna, anubhavitvā, anubhavitvāna, anubhaviya, and anubhuyya.

1203. After roots ending in the letters ca, na, and ra, suffixes such as tuna and others are changed to racca in some instances. (Examples:) Being secluded from sensual pleasures, being secluded from unwholesome states. āhacca (having struck/impinged); upahacca (having harmed/offended); having performed a circumambulation (kacca); having bowed down at the feet (nipacca). Why is "optionally" (vā) said? Because there are also forms like akātuna (without having done merit), hantvā (having killed), katvā (having done), and nipatitvā (having bowed down).

1204. After the root disa, suffixes such as tuna and others are changed to svāna and svā, and the final letter of the root is elided. (Examples:) disvāna, disvā (having seen). Why is "optionally" (vā) said? It occurs in the context: "I have seen madness." Here, "diṭṭhā" has the same meaning as "disvā" (having seen).

1205. After roots ending in ma, ha, da, and bha, suffixes such as tuna and others are changed to mma, yha, jja, bbha, and ddhā in some instances, and the final letter of the root is elided. (Examples:) āgamma, āgantvā (having come); okkamma, okkamitvā (having descended); nikkhamma, nikkhamitvā (having gone out); abhiramma, abhiramitvā (having delighted in); paggayှa, paggaṇhitvā, paggahetvā (having raised up); sannayha, sannahitvā (having bound); ārūyha, ārūhitvā (having climbed); ogāyha, ogāhetvā (having plunged into); uppajja, uppajjitvā (having arisen); upasampajja, upasampajjitvā (having attained/completed); acchijja, acchinditvā (having cut off); chijja, chindiya (having cut); ārabbha, āraddha, ārabhitvā (having exerted/begun/harmed); upaladdhā, upalabhitvā (having obtained), and so forth.
330:
1206. After roots ending in the letter dha, the suffixes tvā and tvāna are respectively changed to ddhā and ddhāna, and the end of the root is elided. In the sentence "Who shot me (with an arrow) and is hiding?", the form viddhā occurs. viddhāna, buddhā, and buddhāna are also formed in the same way. Here, because the usage laddhāna in "having obtained the distinction of what precedes and follows" and the usage viddhā in "Who shot me and is hiding?" are found, forms such as viddhāna and others should exist.

1207. After the root labha, the suffix tvāna is changed to ddhāna, and the end of the root is elided. In the sentence "The foolish person, having obtained wealth," the form laddhāna occurs.

1208. The suffix kāra arises after a letter. akāra, ākāra, and so forth, as well as kakāra, khakāra, and so forth.

1209. Sometimes, the suffix kāra does not arise after a letter due to the specific intention (different meaning) of the speaker. Doing is called kāra. The kāra called "ra" is rakāra. It means the recitation of "ra" or the sound "ra". This same method applies in cases like akāra and others.

1210. According to tradition, the augment i (ikāra) occurs in all suffixes after all roots. Because of this, forms such as kāriya, bhavitabba, janitabba, vidita, karitvā, icchita, gamitabba, veditabba, haritvā, and pacitvā arise.

1211. After roots ending in the letters da and dha, the augment ya sometimes occurs in suffixes such as tuna and others, according to tradition. In the sentences "The Buddha, having arisen in the world" and "Having known the Dhamma," the forms uppajjitvā and bujjitvā occur. Why is "after roots ending in da, dha" (dadhantato) said? To prevent it from occurring in the form labhitvā. Why is "sometimes" (kvaci) said? To prevent it from occurring in the form uppādetvā.
331: 1212. The letter 'na' (n), which is the beginning of a conjunct (saṃyoga), becomes Niggahīta. These are forms such as raṅga, bhaṅga, saṅga. 1213. In the place of the root 'sad', there is the substitution of 'sīda'. These are forms such as nisinna, nisīdati. 1214. In the place of the root 'sad' preceded by 'sanni', there is the substitution of 'siva'. In the sentences 'Now the birds have perched' and 'While the birds were perching', these are the forms sannisivā and sannisivesu. 1215. The vowel of the root 'yaj' becomes 'i' when followed by the suffix 'ṭṭha' (the substitution of 'ṭṭha' for the suffix 'ta'). In the sentence 'That sacrifice of mine was well-sacrificed', these are the forms yiṭṭha and suyitṭhaṃ. Why say 'ṭṭhe'? It is to prevent it in the form 'yajana'. 1216. For roots ending in 'ha' and the fourth consonants (gha, jha, ḍha, dha, bha), the final consonant of the root becomes 'da' when followed by the suffix 'dha' (the substitution of 'dha' for the suffix 'ta'). These are forms such as sannaddha, kuddha, yuddha, siddha, laddha, āraddha. 1217. For roots ending in 'ha' and the fourth consonants, the final consonant of the root becomes 'ḍa' when followed by 'ḍha' (the substitution of 'ḍha' for the suffix 'ta'). These are forms such as daḍḍha, vuḍḍha. Why say 'ḍhakāre'? It is to prevent it in the form 'dāha'. 1218. According to other teachers, in the place of the root 'gah', the substitution of 'ghara' sometimes occurs when followed by the suffix 'ṇa'; the rule along with its commentary (vutti) is thus cited. The examples of those teachers are ghara and gharāṇi. Why say 'vā' (sometimes)? It is to prevent it in the form 'gāha'. Here, the word 'ghara' is accomplished by the power of the root 'ghara secane' (to sprinkle). ...
332:
1219. Changing the letter 'd' of the root *daha* to 'ḷ'. When the suffix *ṇa* follows, the letter 'd' of the root *daha* becomes 'ḷ'. Example: *pariḷāha* or *paridāha* (burning/fever).

1220. Deletion of the end of the root when the suffix *kvi* follows. Examples: *bhujaga* (snake), *saṅkha* (conch), etc.

1221. Deletion of the end of the root *bhuja* in certain instances when the suffixes *tvā* and *tvāna* follow. Examples: *bhutvā*, *bhuñjitvā*, *bhutvāna*, *bhuñjitvāna* (having eaten).

1222. The suffix *ū* occurs at the end of the root *vida*. Example: *lokavidū* (the Buddha who knows the world).

1223. The end of roots ending in *n, m, k, r* is not deleted when the suffix *ta* conjoined with the augment *i* follows. Examples: *hanituṃ* (to kill), *gamituṃ* (to go), *aṅkito* (marked), *saṅkito* (doubted), *ramito* (delighted), *sarito* (remembered), *karitvā* (having done). If not conjoined with the augment *i*: *kato* (done), *sato* (remembered), *hato* (killed).

1224. The letters *c* and *j* do not become *k* and *g* when the suffix *ṇvu* follows. Examples: *pācako* (a cook), *yājako* (a sacrificer).

1225. Changing the final consonant of the root *kara* and others to the letter 't' when the suffix *tu* follows. Examples: *kattā* (doer), *vattā* (speaker), etc.

1226. Optional changing of the final 'r' of the root *kara* to 't' when the suffixes *tuṃ, tuna, tabba* follow. Examples: *kattuṃ*, *kātuṃ* (to do); *kattuna*, *kātuna* (having done); *kattabbaṃ*, *kātabbaṃ* (that which should be done).

1227. A suffix containing the *ṇ* anubandha (indicatory letter) should be regarded as a causative (*kārita*) suffix. Examples: *dāho* (burning), *deho* (body).
333:
*dāyako* (giver), *nāyako* (leader), *kārī* (one who does habitually), *ghāyī* (one who kills habitually), *dāyī* (one who gives habitually), etc. Why is the word 'viva' (optionally) used? In *upakkharo* (chariot accessory), the suffix *ṇa* does not act as a causative.

1228. Substitution of the suffixes *yu* and *ṇvu* with *ana* and *aka*. The substitutions *ana* and *aka* occur in place of the suffixes *yu* and *ṇvu*. Examples: *nandanaṃ* (rejoicing), *bhavanaṃ* (mansion), *gahanaṃ* (taking), *naḷakārako* (basket-maker).

1229. Substitution of *c* and *j* at the end of roots with *k* and *g* when a suffix containing the *ṇ* anubandha follows. Examples: *pāko* (cooking), *yāgo* (sacrifice).

1230. Deletion of the final letter of roots as appropriate when the suffixes *tu* and *ta* follow. Example: *ratho* (chariot).

1231. The *kit* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattu-kāraka*). Examples: *karoatīti kāru* (he who acts is called *kāru*), *kāruko*, *kārako* (doer), *pācako* (cook), *kattā* (doer), *janitā* (producer), *pacitā* (cook), *netā* (leader).

1232. The suffixes *kicca, kta,* and *khattha* occur in the senses of state (*bhāva*) and object (*kamma*). Examples: *upasampādetabbaṃ* (should be ordained), *sayitabbaṃ bhavatā* (it should be slept by you), *kattabbaṃ kammaṃ* (the work that should be done), *bhottabbo odano* (the rice that should be eaten), *asitabbaṃ bhojanaṃ bhavatā* (the food should be eaten by you), *asitaṃ sayitaṃ pacitaṃ bhavatā* (it was eaten, slept, cooked by you), *asitaṃ bhojanaṃ bhavatā* (the food was eaten by you), *sayitaṃ sayanaṃ bhavatā* (the sleep was slept by you), *pacitaṃ odanaṃ bhavatā* (the rice was cooked by you), *kiñcissayo, īsassayo, dussayo, sussayo bhavatā* (it was slept a little, slept well, etc., by you), *kiñcissayo mañco* (a couch on which one has slept a little), *īsassayo, dussayo, sussayo*.

1233. The suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent when the second case (accusative) is present in the sense of the object. Examples: *dānaṃ dinno devadatto* (Devadatta is the giver of the gift), *sīlaṃ rakkhito devadatto* (Devadatta is the observer of virtue), *bhattaṃ bhutto devadatto* (Devadatta is the eater of the meal), *garuṃ upāsito devadatto* (Devadatta is the attendant of the teacher).
334:
1234. The suffix *man* follows the roots *khī, bhī, su, ru, hu, vā, dhū, hi, lū, pī, ada*, etc. From the root *ada*, the suffix *man* also follows, and in some instances, 'm' is changed to 't'. Dangers and obstacles are exhausted in this Nibbāna, therefore it is called *khema* (safety). People are afraid of this person, therefore he is called *bhīma* (fearful). Radiance flows or arises, therefore it is called *soma*. It arises or moves, therefore it is called *roma* (hair). It is worshipped, therefore it is called *homa*. It moves or wafts, therefore it is called *vāma*. It shakes, therefore it is called *dhūma* (smoke). It arises, therefore it is called *hema* (gold). It cuts, therefore it is called *loma* (hair). Delight is called *pema* (love). It consumes (experiences) pleasure and pain, therefore it is called *atta* (self).

1235. When the suffix *man* follows, the initial vowel of the root *ada* is lengthened, 'd' is changed to 't', and the letter 'u' is inserted in the middle. It consumes (experiences) pleasure and pain, therefore it is called *ātumā* (self).

1236. The suffixes *tha* and *ma* follow the roots *sama, dama, mada, ra*, etc. It calms the defilements, therefore it is called *samatha* (tranquility). Disciplining is *damatha*. Burning (distress) is *daratha*. It is approached and taken (ridden), therefore it is called *ratha* (chariot). Cursing is *sapatha*. They dwell in that place, therefore it is called *āvasatha* (dwelling). It arises in a mixed manner, therefore it is called *yūtha* (herd/group). It reaches growth, therefore it is called *duma* (tree). It arises, therefore it is called *hima* (snow). It is bound or demarcated, therefore it is called *sīma* or *sīmā* (boundary). People are afraid of this person, therefore he is called *bhīma*. It performs cutting, therefore it is called *dāma* (garland/rope). It moves or reaches, therefore it is called *yāma* (a watch of the night). They stand by this power, therefore it is called *thāma* (strength). It shows ash here and there, therefore it is called *bhasmā* (ash). It is capable, therefore it is called *sāma*. It grows through various qualities, therefore it is called *brahmā*. Burning is *usmā* (heat/power). Other terms should also be combined in this manner.

1237. The letter preceding the final letter is called *upadhā*. The letter before the last letter is the *upadhā*.
335:
Because they are afraid of that ogre, he is called 'Bhīmo'. Because he performs the act of cutting, he is called 'Dāmo'. Because he moves by dividing [the time] into six or eight watches without overflowing, he is called 'Yāmo'. Because he stands by that power, he is called 'Thāmo'. Because he shows ashes here and there, he is called 'Bhasmā'. Because he is capable, he is called 'Sāmo'. Because he increases through various virtues, he is called 'Brahmā'. Heat is called 'Usmā'. Other words should also be applied in this manner.

1237. The letter preceding the final letter of a root is called 'Upadhā' (penultimate).

1238. In a non-compound, the 'a' which is the upadhā of the root gah must always be changed to 'e'. Because it takes various buildings, it is called 'Gehaṃ' (house). 'Geho' is also desired as a masculine form. Why is it said 'in a non-compound'? Because in compounds such as 'Gahakāraṃ gavesanto' (seeking a house-builder), 'Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi' (House-builder, you are seen), 'Gahaṭṭho' (householder), 'Gahakūṭaṃ' (pinnacle of a house), and 'Rājagahaṃ' (Rājagaha), the upadhā is not changed to 'e'.

1239. The 'su' of the noun stem 'masu' should be changed to 'cchara' and 'cchera'. Here, 'masu' can be an underived stem (anipphanna-pāṭipadika) or a derived stem (nipphanna-pāṭipadika). Indeed, stems are of two types: derived (nipphanna) and underived (anipphanna). Among them, 'kārako', 'pācako', etc., are derived, while 'ghaṭo', 'paṭo', etc., are underived. Since the root 'masu' is seen in the sense of stinginess (macchara), it is also desired as 'maccharo' in the sense of 'massati' (he is stingy).

1240. The root 'car' preceded by 'ā' should be changed to 'cchara', 'cchera', and 'cchariya'. The letter 'ā' should also be shortened (to 'a'). Because it is practiced excessively, it is called 'accharaṃ', 'accheraṃ', or 'acchariyaṃ'. Alternatively, 'acchariyaṃ' is so called because it is worthy of a finger-snap (accharā). It is a derivative (taddhita) word meaning 'that which is worthy of a finger-snap by those with amazed hearts'.

1241. The suffixes 'la' and 'ya' follow the roots 'al' (to be able), 'kal' (to count), and 'sal' (to go). They become 'allaṃ', 'kallaṃ', 'sallaṃ', 'alyaṃ', 'kalyaṃ', and 'salyaṃ'.

1242. The suffixes 'yāṇa' and 'lāṇa' follow the roots 'kal' and 'sal'. They become 'kalyāṇaṃ', 'paṭisalyāṇaṃ', 'kallāṇော', and 'paṭisallāṇော'. If the root is 'lī' (to cling), then 'paṭisalliyanaṃ' and 'paṭisallānaṃ' are formed with the 'yu' suffix.
336:
1243. The 'tha' of the root math is changed to 'lla' and 'llaka'. The root math is in the sense of kneading or churning. 'Mallo' or 'Mallako' (a wrestler who kneads/wrestles). Or 'malla' itself is called 'mallaka'.

1244. The 'kicca' suffixes occur in the senses of commanding (pesana), authorizing or giving permission (atissagga), and announcing the arrived time (pattakāla). Here, 'pesana' is the urging of a person who is commanded, 'This work should be done by you.' 'Atissagga' is the permission given to one who asks, 'How should I do this work?' or the authorization by showing the practice, such as when a monk who has reached the noble state of a bhikkhu is made to abstain from intentionally depriving a living being of life with the thought of it being a 'being'. 'Pattakāla' is the time that has arrived; 'kicca' suffixes also occur in announcing that time. Examples: 'The work should be done by you.' 'The task should be performed by you.' 'The food should be eaten by you.' 'The food should be consumed by you.' 'The lesson should be learned by you.' 'The subject should be studied by you.'

1245. The suffix 'ṇī' and 'kicca' suffixes occur in the senses of necessity (avassaka) and debt (adhamiṇa). 'You should certainly do my work.' 'You should certainly carry my burden.' Here, the word 'avassaṃ' (certainly) need not be spoken; saying 'kārīsi me kammaṃ, hārīsi me bhāraṃ' is sufficient. Nevertheless, 'avassaṃ' is used to make the sense of necessity clear. There, 'kārīsi' means 'you are fit to do [it] certainly.' 'Hārīsi' means 'you are fit to carry [it] certainly.' In the sense of debt: 'You should give the hundred [units of] debt to me.' 'You should bear the thousand [units of] debt to me.' Here, 'dāyīsi' means 'you are fit to give.' 'The work should certainly be done by you for me.' 'The hundred [units of] debt should be given by you to me.' 'The thousand [units of] debt should be borne by you for me.' 'The task should be performed by you.' 'It should certainly be done.' 'The duty should be performed by you.'
337:
1246. When associated with words such as araha, sakka, and bhabba, the suffix tuṃ occurs after all roots. (For example:) The venerable one is fit to speak. The venerable one is able to conquer (subdue). The venerable one is worthy to realize the fruit of Arahatship. The venerable one is suitable to go on a mission.

1247. The suffix ṇya occurs after words such as vaja, ija, and añja. It is called pabbajjā (going forth) because it is reached first before taking the refuges and so on. Trembling is called ejā. An assembly (prominence in a festival) is called samajjā. Sitting is called nisajjā. Knowing, or because of knowing, it is called vijjā. Solving a doubt is called visajjā. Lying down is called nipajjā. Killing is called vajjhā. One who is to be killed is called vajjho. Because one sleeps in this place, it is called seyyā. Conduct is called cariyā. Dwelling (arranging) is called sajjā.

1248. The suffix a occurs after the root dhā preceded by saṃ. Because one places the mind well by this quality, or because one believes in it oneself without wavering, it is called saddhā (faith).

1249. The suffix a also occurs after the root ñā and others. (For example:) saññā, paññā, pabhā, nibhā, pucchā, and so on.

1250. The suffix cha occurs after the root ruja and others. Ailing is called rucchā. Depletion (non-association) is called ricchā. Medical treatment is called tikicchā. Contraction is called saṅkucchā. Constant negligence is called macchā. Obtaining is called lacchā. Because it is scratched by travelers, or because it is suitable for a chariot, it is called racchā (a highway). Going downwards is called tiracchā. Going together is called sāgacchā (this is said by the power of the root gamu preceded by saṃ). Eating badly is called dobhacchā. Being badly angry (irritation) is called dorucchā. Delusion is called mucchā. Splendor is called kacchā. Conversing together is called sākacchā. Pricking is called tucchā. Entering is called vicchā. That which is true and unfailing is called tacchā. That which is perverted in speech is called vigacchā.
338:
1251. The suffixes ccha and cchāna occur after the root tira. Tiraccho, tiracchā, tiracchāno, tiracchānā (animal). Suffering among animals; an animal.

1252. The suffix chilla occurs after the root pisa. Becoming powder is called picchillā.

1253. The suffixes tyu and ṭṭu occur after the root musa. Because it gives up life, it is called maccu (the King of Death); likewise, it is called maṭṭu.

1254. Alternatively, according to the method of other commentators, the suffix ratya occurs after the root mara. Because of the nature of being subject to death, it is called macco (a mortal being). A mortal being thus born should perform much merit. A point to be noted here: in the place where maccā should be said, the word mātiyā is found as in "Kammabandhū hi mātiyā."

1255. The suffix tya occurs after the root dhū preceded by u. Successive shaking is called uddhaccaṃ (restlessness).

1256. Alternatively, the suffix ṇya occurs after the word uddhata in the sense of state (bhāva). The state of a restless mind is called uddhaccaṃ. This word is a Taddhita derivative.

1257. The suffix tya also occurs after the root kara preceded by ku. A loathsome deed that has been done is called kukkuccaṃ (remorse).

1258. Alternatively, the suffix ṇya occurs after the word kukata in the sense of state (bhāva). The state of a loathsome deed that has been done is called kukkuccaṃ.

1259. The suffix ja occurs after the roots aja and sada. The root aja is used in the sense of going or throwing; discarding the path is called ajjā. The root sada is used in the senses of spreading, going, and finishing; giving, sitting, or going is called sajjā.

1260. The suffix tya occurs after sata, nata, and niti. Saccaṃ (truth), naccaṃ (dancing), and niccaṃ (permanence) are formed.
339:
1261. When the suffix ṇya follows, the letter ka of the word kukata undergoes doubling, and the letter a becomes u. Example: kukkuccaṃ (the state of performing a loathsome deed).

1262. When the suffix cha and others follow, the final consonant of the root becomes ca. Examples: madanaṃ macchā (intoxication), labhanaṃ lacchā (obtaining), radanaṃ racchā (scratching), and so on.

1263. The combination of the letters da and ya (dya) becomes double ja (jja). Example: sadanaṃ sajjā (dwelling).

1264. When the suffixes tyu and ṭṭu follow, the letter u of the root musa becomes a. Examples: maccu (death), maṭṭu.

1265. When the suffix tya follows, the letter ū of the root dhū also becomes a. Upward shaking is called uddhaccaṃ (restlessness).

1266. The suffix kvi, which occurs after roots such as bhū, dhū, and bhā, is elided. Examples: vibhū (one who has become special), sayambhū (the self-become one), abhibhū (the conqueror), sandhu (shaking out well), uddhu (shaking upwards), vibhā (special radiance), nibhā (complete radiance), pabhā (various radiance), ābhā (great radiance), bhujago (a snake, going by the breast), turaṅgo (a horse, going swiftly). The root yamu is used in the sense of restraint: viyo (special restraint). The root mana is used in the sense of knowing: sumo (one who knows well). The root tanu is used in the sense of spreading: parito (spreading all around), and so on.

1267. When a suffix with the indicatory letter ṇ (ṇānu-bandha) follows, the final consonants of roots ending in sa, ca, and ja are replaced by ka and ga respectively. The root uca is used in the sense of speech belonging to a wise person: ucanaṃ oko (speaking), pāko (cooking), seko (sprinkling), soko (sorrow), viveko (seclusion), cāgo (relinquishment), yogo (yoking), bhogo (enjoyment), rogo (ailment), rāgo (lust), bhāgo (portion, donation), bhaṅgo (destruction), saṅgo (attachment).
340:
1268. From the roots such as nud, sud, and jan, as well as from roots accompanied by causative suffixes such as phanda, citi, and āṇa, the substitutions of the suffixes yu and ṇvu—namely ana, āna, aka, and ānaka—occur respectively in the senses of the agent (kattar), the state (bhāva), and the instrument (karaṇa).

Panudatīti panūdano (one who dispels); likewise sūdano, janano, savano, lavano, havano, pavano, bhavano, ñāṇo, asano, and samaṇo occur in the sense of the agent.

In the sense of the state (bhāva): panujjate (dispelling) is panūdanaṃ; sujjate (flowing) is sūdanaṃ; jāyate (arising) is jananaṃ; suyyate (hearing) is savanaṃ; luyate (cutting) is lavanaṃ; huyate (offering) is havanaṃ; puyate (purifying) is pavanaṃ; bhūyate (becoming) is bhavanaṃ; ñāyate (knowing) is ñāṇaṃ; asate (eating) is asanaṃ; samate (calming) is samaṇo; sañjāniyate (knowing) is sañjānanaṃ; and kuyate (sounding) is kāyanaṃ. Also in the causative: phandāpayate (causing to tremble) is phandāpanaṃ; cetāpayate (causing to incite) is cetāpanaṃ; and āṇāpayate (causing to command) is āṇāpanaṃ—these occur in the sense of the state.

In the sense of the instrument (karaṇa): because of the sense 'one dispels by means of this [dhamma],' there are nūdanaṃ, sūdanaṃ, jananaṃ, savanaṃ, lavano, havano, pavano, bhavano, jānanaṃ, asano, and samaṇo.

Again, in the sense of the agent: nudatīti nudako; sūdatīti sūdako; janetīti janako; suṇotīti sāvako; lunātīti lāvako; juhotīti hāvako; punātīti pāvako; bhavatīti bhāvako; jānātīti jānako; asatīti āsako; upāsatīti upāsako; and samatīti samaṇo. Again, in the causative: āṇāpayatīti āṇāpako; likewise phandāpako, cetāpako, sañjānanako, and so forth.

1269. The final vowel of these pronouns—ima, ya, ta, amha, kiṃ, and eta—becomes long (dīgha). In some instances, the vowel u of the root dus undergoes guṇa substitution, the letter d becomes r, and at the end of the root, the substitutions sa, kkha, and ī occur as appropriate. In this rule, because 'vuddhi of ākāra, etc.' is taken, the term guṇa includes ikāra and so forth. Among those pronouns, the letter 'i' represents the word ima.
341:
The letter 'ma' represents the word amha as a part of the substitution (ādesa); the letter 'e' represents the word eta; and the letter 'sa' represents the word samāna. One who sees another as he sees this person is called 'īdiso'. One who sees as he sees which person is called 'yādiso'. Likewise, there are tādiso, mādiso, kīdiso, ediso, sādiso, īriso, yāriso, tāriso, māriso, kīriso, eriso, sāriso, īdikkho, yādikkho, tādikkho, mādikkho, kīdikkho, edikkho, sādikkho, īdī, yādī, tādī, mādī, kīdī, edī, and sādī. By the inclusion of the word 'ca', it is said that the final vowel of those words such as iya should be made long (dīgha) in some instances. For example: īdikkho, yādikkho, tādikkho, mādikkho, kīdikkho, edikkho, sādikkho, idiso, sadiso, sariso, and sarikkho.

1270. The suffix kta is applied after roots such as bhī, as well as after roots having the meanings of desiring (mati), knowing (buddhi), and worshipping (pūjā). The suffix kta occurs after roots such as bhī, supu, and midi; after roots such as mati; after roots such as buddhi; and after roots such as pūjā. Examples are: bhīto (frightened), sutto (asleep), mitto (loved), sammato (desired/agreed upon), saṅkappito (intended), sampādito (accomplished), avadhārito (borne), buddho (known), ito (known), vidito (known), takkito (thought), pūjito (honored), apacāyito (honored), mānito (honored), apacito (honored), vandito (venerated), sakkato (honored), and garukato (revered).

1271. The suffix thu is applied after the roots vepu, si, dava, and vama in the sense of 'produced by' (nibbatta). Trembling is called 'vepana' or 'vepa'; because it is produced by that trembling, it is called 'vepathu'. Sleeping or increasing is called 'sayana' or 'saya'; because it is produced by that sleeping or increasing, it is called 'sayathu'. Burning or distress is called 'davana' or 'dava'; because it is produced by that burning, it is called 'davathu'. Vomiting is called 'vamana' or 'vama'; because it is produced by that vomiting, it is called 'vamathu'.

1272. The suffix ttima is applied after the roots bhū, ku, and dā. Becoming or increasing is called 'bhūti' or 'bhavana'; because it is produced by that becoming, it is called 'bhottimaṃ'. Making is called 'kutti' or 'karaṇa'; because it is produced by that making, it is called 'kuttimaṃ'. Giving is called 'dāti' or 'dāna'; because it is produced by that giving, it is called 'dattimaṃ'.

1273. The suffix ṇima is applied after the root hu. Worshipping is called 'avahuti' or 'avahanaṃ'; because it is produced by that worshipping, it is called 'ohāvimaṃ'.
342:
1274. Anyato'pi te. These suffixes—thu, ttima, and ṇima—also occur after roots other than vepu, si, dava, vama, ku, dā, bhū, and hu; such examples should be sought. For this reason, the Kaccāyana grammar includes the word 'ādi' (etcetera), stating: "The suffixes thu, ttima, and ṇima are produced from the roots vepu, si, dava, vama, ku, dā, bhū, hu, etc." (For example, by applying the suffix thu after the root asa, words like asathu, āmayathu, and rogathu are formed. One should also seek and note how pūrattimaṃ is formed from the root pūra, kittimaṃ from the root ki, and pūjimaṃ and mānimaṃ from the roots pūja and māna respectively.)

1275. Ku karassa ttime. When followed by the suffix ttima, the root kara must be changed to ku. That which is produced by the act of doing (karaṇa) is called kuttima (artificial or made).

1276. Kuttito vā imo. Alternatively, the suffix ima is added to the word kutti. The act of doing is called kutti; that which is produced by kutti is kuttima. In this context, the Pali passage: "One should not act like a king in gesture or in the modulation of voice (sarakutti)" serves as evidence. This method should be carefully borne in mind.

1277. Tabbhāvakriyāyamimo. When the state or action (bhāva) of that is to be expressed, the suffix ima is added after either completed (nipphanna) or uncompleted (anipphanna) stems. These are aṇimā, mahimā, and lahimā. In the Sanskrit language, it is pronounced as "laghimā." Among these, aṇimā refers to the act of making one's body extremely subtle like an atom (paramāṇu), performed by those with psychic powers. The derivation is: the act of becoming like an atom is aṇimā. The act of becoming great is mahimā. The act of becoming light or swift is lahimā, which is the same as laghimā. These words are of the feminine gender.

1278. Ahaṃ pubbanti kriyāyaṃ iko. When an action is expressed in the manner of "I shall go first, I shall go first" or "I shall attend, I shall attend," the suffix ika is added to the word ahaṃ-ahaṃ. It becomes ahamahamikā (the competition or scramble of "I first, I first"). This word is of the feminine gender.

1279. Ahopurisato. After the word ahopurisa, the suffix ṇika is added in the sense of pride (dappana). In the sense of the arrogance of self-conceit (ahaṅkāra), saying "Indeed, I am a great man," the suffix ṇika is added to the word purisa preceded by the word aho.
343:
1279. In the sense of pride (dappana) as in "Indeed, I [am a great man]," the suffix ṇika is added after the word ahopurisa. In the sense of the arrogance of self-conceit (ahaṅkāra), the suffix ṇika occurs after the word purisa preceded by the word aho. The form is ahopurisikā (the pride of thinking "Indeed, I am an amazing man"). This word is of the feminine gender.

1280. Tamiva parikappitakīḷābhaṇḍe puttādito liko. In the sense of a toy (kīḷābhaṇḍa) that is conceived as if it were that child, the suffix lika is added after the word putta and so on. When a toy is spoken of as being conceived like the actual object such as a son, the suffix lika occurs after the word putta etc. The forms are puttalikā (a boy-doll) and dhītalikā (a girl-doll). These words are of the feminine gender.

1281. Namhi akkose āni. When the particle na is the preceding word (upapada) in the sense of abuse or scolding (akkosa), the suffix āni is added after all roots. When abuse is understood and the particle na is the preceding word, the suffix āni occurs after all roots. "Agamāni te jamma deso" means "O wretch, you should not go to this place." "Akarāni te jamma kammaṃ" means "O wretch, you should not do this deed." In these instances, "na gamāni" becomes "agamāni" and "na karāni" becomes "akarāni" as a Kammadhāraya compound.

In this context, if it is asked: among the three genders, which gender do these words with the suffix āni take? Among the seven cases, with which case are they associated? Among the two numbers, which number do they have?

Since they have an indeterminate gender (aniyataliṅga) among the three genders, they can take all genders (sabbaliṅga). Among the seven cases, they are associated only with the Nominative case (paṭhamā). Among the two numbers, they may end in either the singular or the plural.

For example: "Agamāni te jamma deso" (masc. sing.), "Agamāni te jamma nānādesā" (masc. plur.), "Agamāni te jamma rājādhānī" (fem. sing.), "Agamāni te jamma rājadhāniyo" (fem. plur.), "Agamāni te jamma nagaraṃ" (neut. sing.), "Agamāni te jamma nagarāni" (neut. plur.). Also, "Akarāni te jamma kammaṃ," "Akarāni te jamma kammāni," "Akarāni te jamma ghaṭo," "Akarāni te jamma ghaṭā," "Akarāni te jamma kumbhī," "Akarāni te jamma kumbhiyo."

Furthermore, it should be stated here that words with the suffix āni are like the word seyyo in: "Seyyo amitto," "Esāva pūjanā seyyo," "Ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ..."
344:
...seyyo. Just as this word seyyo is compatible with all three genders, these words [with the suffix āni] should be described as words similar to indeclinables (avyaya) that are compatible with all three genders. This is because they have no declension paradigm (vibhattimālā) and no variation in form according to number (vacana). This method should be carefully borne in mind. Why is it said "when na is present" (namhi)? To exclude cases like "Vipatti te" (Your ruin), where na is absent. Why is it said "in the sense of abuse" (akkose)? To exclude cases like "Agati te" (You have no recourse), where it is not a matter of scolding.

1282. Ekādito vāratthe kkhattuṃ. In the sense of times or turns (vāra), the suffix kkhattuṃ is added after numerals such as eka, dvi, ti, and catu. After the count of eka, dvi, ti, catu, etc., the suffix kkhattuṃ occurs in the sense of 'times'. One time is ekakkhattuṃ. Two times is dvikkhattuṃ. Three times is tikkhattuṃ. Four times is catukkhattuṃ, and so on. In sentences such as "Tikkhattuṃ purise pesesi," the meaning should be understood through the sense of the Accusative plural (upayoga-bahuvacana), as in "he sent men for three times."

1283. Dhātthe vā kvaci kkhattuṃ. Alternatively, in some instances, the suffix kkhattuṃ is added after numerals like eka in the sense of the suffix dhā. Here, the sense of dhā refers to division (vibhāga), because the suffix dhā functions in the sense of division. In the passage "Sahassakkhattuṃ attānaṃ, nimminitvāna panthako" (Panthaka, having created himself a thousandfold), we find examples like ekakkhattuṃ, dvikkhattuṃ, etc. There, "sahassakkhattuṃ" should be connected as "having created himself into a thousand parts (sahassadhā)." This is because the use of the suffix dhā is seen in "Ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti" (Being one, he becomes manyfold). In terms of meaning, it means "having created a thousand bodies of himself." This is because the use of the Accusative case is seen in "Each one created a hundred bodies in the form of a young maiden, etc."

1284. Matantare ekādito sakiassa kkhattuṃ. According to the opinion of other teachers (matantara), the substitution (ādesa) of kkhattuṃ occurs in place of the word sakiṃ after numerals such as eka, dvi, ti, catu, pañca, cha, satta, aṭṭha, nava, and dasa. For example...
345:
The words "once, twice," and so on, appear. "Once for one" is stated as "ekakkhattuṃ," which is a tappurisa compound. By this method, the viggaha (grammatical analysis) is also stated as "dvikkhattuṃ" for "once for two," up to "dasakkhattuṃ" for "once for ten."

In this context, in passages such as "Sutasoma, association with the virtuous occurs only once (sakiṃ)" and "The young men tremble just by drinking liquor once (sakiṃ), as if shaken by the wind," the word "sakiṃ" expresses the meaning of "a little" or "a small measure." The meaning of that word "sakiṃ" is "once." Because it means "once," when one says "ekassa sakiṃ," it would mean "once for one." Even when one says "dasassa sakiṃ," it would mean "once for ten." Therefore, "sakiṃ" means once, and "asakiṃ" means many times. This point should be well-considered.

1285. Sunassunassoṇavānuvānūṇuṇakhuṇānā. For the pāṭipadika (stem) "suna," the "una" part is replaced by the substitutions oṇa, vāna, uvāna, ūṇa, unakha, uṇa, ā, and ānā. Thus: soṇo, svāno, suvāno, sūṇo, sunakho, suṇo, sā, sāno. Here also, by the power of the derived stem, it is called "soṇo" because it means "one who goes." Similarly, "svāno" and so on are formed.

1286. Suṇotismā vā oṇādayo. Alternatively, the suffixes oṇa and so on occur after the root "su." Or, the suffixes oṇa, vāna, uvāna, and so on occur after the root "su" in the sense of hearing (savana). It is called "soṇo" because it means "one who listens to the master's words." Similarly, "svāno," "suvāno," and so on are formed.

The substitution of "susu" for the word "taruṇa" is not prescribed here.
If it were prescribed, words like "paṇḍita" would obtain treatments like "dhīrayoga."
The words "susu," "taruṇa," and so on exist with distinct natures;
For words with such endings, such a rule is not desired.
346:
1287. Uvānu nauṇā vā yuvassuvassa. For the pāṭipadika (stem) "yuva," the "uva" part is optionally (vā) replaced by the substitutions uvāna, una, and ūna. Thus, it stands as: yuvāno, yuno, yūno. Why is "vā" (optionally) said? It is to prevent the substitution in instances such as "daharo yuvā nātibrahā" (a young man is not too large).

1288. Vattamānātītesu ṇuyutā. The suffixes ṇu and yu occur in the present and past tenses. Examples: kāru, vāyu, bhūtaṃ.

1289. Bhavissatikāle ṇīghiṇ gamādito. The suffixes ṇī and ghiṇ occur after roots such as "gam" in the future tense. One who has the habit or nature of going is called "gāmī." Similarly: bhājī, dassāvī, paṭṭhāyī.

1290. Ṇvutu kriyāyaṃ karādito. When wishing to indicate an action, the suffixes ṇvu and tu occur after roots such as "kar" in the future tense. Thinking "he will do," the doer (kārako) goes; thinking "he will eat," the eater (bhottā) goes.

1291. Bhāvavacane catutthī. When wishing to express the action called bhāva (state/being), the dative case (catutthī) occurs after the word expressing the state in the future tense. Cooking is called "pāka"; he goes for the purpose of cooking (pākāya). Eating is called "bhoga"; he goes for the purpose of eating (bhogāya). Dancing is called "nacca"; he goes for the purpose of dancing (naccāya).

1292. Kammūpapade ṇo. When an object (kamma) is nearby, the suffix ṇa occurs in the future tense. Because he will build a city, the city-builder (nagarakāro) goes. Because he will reap rice, the rice-reaper (sālilāvo) goes. Because he will sow grain, the grain-sower (dhanyavāpo) goes. Because he will give wealth, the wealth-giver (bhogadāyo) goes. Because he will drink river water, the water-drinker (sindhupāyo) goes.
347:
1293. Sesatthe ssaṃntumānanā. In the sense of an incomplete action (vattamāna), the suffixes ssaṃ, antu, māna, and āna occur in the future tense when an object is nearby. Because of the meaning "he will do the work," the one who will do the work (kammaṃ karissaṃ), the one who is doing the work (kammaṃ karonto), the one who is doing the work (kammaṃ kurumāno), and the one who is doing the work (kammaṃ karāno) goes. Because of the meaning "he will eat food," the one who will eat food (bhojanaṃ bhuñjissaṃ), the one who is eating food (bhojanaṃ bhuñjanto), the one who is eating food (bhojanaṃ bhuñjamāno), and the one who is eating food (bhojanaṃ bhuñjāno) goes. Because of the meaning "he will eat snacks," the one who will eat snacks (khādanaṃ khādissaṃ), the one who is eating snacks (khādanaṃ khādanto), the one who is eating snacks (khādanaṃ khādamāno), and the one who is eating snacks (khādanaṃ khādāno) goes. Because of the meaning "he will travel the path," the one who will travel the path (maggaṃ carissaṃ), the one who is traveling the path (maggaṃ caranto), the one who is traveling the path (maggaṃ caramāno), and the one who is traveling the path (maggaṃ carāno) goes. Because of the meaning "he will beg for alms," the one who will beg for alms (bhikkhaṃ bhikkhissaṃ), the one who is begging for alms (bhikkhaṃ bhikkhanto), the one who is begging for alms (bhikkhaṃ bhikkhamāno), and the one who is begging for alms (bhikkhaṃ bhikkhāno) goes.
