1294. Aniyatakāle gamādito ṇī. When the time is not fixed (indefinite), the suffix ṇī is applied after roots such as "gam." A teaching that leads to the enlightenment called the four paths (sambodhagāmī). A man who enjoys sensual pleasures (kāmabhogī).

1295. Chadādito to. The suffix ta is applied after roots such as "chada." The suffix ta occurs after these roots: chada, cinta, su, nī, vida, pada, tanu, yata, yati, ada, yuja, vatu, mida, mā, pu, kala, vara, vepu, gupa, and dā. Thus: umbrella (chattaṃ), mind (cittaṃ), discourse (suttaṃ), eye (nettaṃ), purity (pavittaṃ), bowl/wing (pattaṃ), thread (tantaṃ), effort (yattaṃ), effort (yantaṃ), food eaten (attaṃ), rope (yottaṃ), conduct/vow (vattaṃ), friend (mittaṃ), measure (mattā), son (putto), wife (kalattaṃ), thong/fiber (varattaṃ), cane (vettaṃ), lineage (gottaṃ), and sickle (dāttaṃ). In the Pali Canon (pāvacana), forms such as "chatra" and "gotra" are never seen; however, in the word "gotrabhū," because it is in a compound, the letter 't' reaches the form of 'tr', or similarly in words like "atrajō."

1296. Traṇ ti ca garū. Teachers say that the suffix traṇ is also applied after roots such as chada and cinta. In their view, forms such as chatraṃ, citraṃ, sotraṃ, netraṃ, pavitraṃ, patraṃ, tantraṃ, yatraṃ, yantraṃ, atraṃ, yotraṃ, vatraṃ, mitraṃ, matrā, putro, kalatraṃ, varatraṃ, vetraṃ, gotraṃ, and dātraṃ are formed.
348:
1297. The suffix ṇitta is applied to roots such as vada in the sense of a group. A group of those who play instruments is called vādittaṃ. Similarly, a group of those who practice, or a collection of cāritta precepts, is called cārittaṃ. A group of those who restrain, or a collection of vāritta precepts, is called vārittaṃ. And so forth.

1298. The suffixes tti and ti are applied to roots such as mida. Metti (love/friendship), patti (attainment or foot soldier), ratti (night), tanti (expansion, lute string, or Pali text), and dhāti (nurse) are thus formed.

1299. The suffixes ḍḍha and ṭṭha are applied to the roots usu and rañja. Uḍḍho (agitation/heat), raṭṭho (country/kingdom). In the phrase "May the country also be destroyed," the word raṭṭha is of the neuter gender.

1300. In the opinion of other teachers, there is a statement that the root daṃsa should be changed to daḍḍha. Daḍḍho. The occurrence of the word daḍḍha is well-known only through the power of the root daha in the sense of "burning to ashes," and not through the power of the root daṃsa.

1301. The suffix tha is applied to the roots su, vu, and asa. The ū, u, and asa of these roots are changed to a. Satthaṃ (weapon), vatthaṃ (cloth), attho (meaning).

1302. The suffixes dha, da, idda, ka, and ira are applied to roots such as rañja, udi, and idi. In some instances, ja and da are elided. Randhaṃ (cavity/hole), samuddo (ocean), indo (Sakka or lord), cando (moon), mando (dull person), khuddo (hungry person), chiddo (hole), ruddo (the god Rudra or Maheśvara), daliddo (poor person), sukkaṃ (semen or merit), pakkaṃ (cooking or ripening), vajiraṃ (thunderbolt weapon or lightning), and so forth.

1303. The suffixes a and iya are applied to the root hara preceded by paṭi. The vowel of the letter ha is changed to e, ī, or ā. It is called pāṭiheraṃ because it removes opposing factors. Similarly, pāṭihīraṃ and pāṭihāriyaṃ are also formed.
349:
1304. In the opinion of other teachers, the root ha preceded by paṭi is replaced by heraṇ and hīraṇ. For example: pāṭiheraṃ, pāṭihīraṃ.

1305. The suffix ka is applied after roots such as kaḍa, ghaṭa, and caḍa. Kaṇḍo (arrow/section), ghaṇḍo (bell), vaṇḍo (stalk), karaṇḍo (casket), maṇḍo (ornament/essence), saṇḍo (group/grove), kuṭṭho (leprosy/cutting), bhaṇḍaṃ (goods), paṇḍako (eunuch), daṇḍo (stick/punishment), raṇḍo (oppression), vitaṇḍo (sophist), isiṇḍo (subduing), caṇḍo (fierceness), gaṇḍo (boil/cheek), aṇḍo (egg), laṇḍo (excrement), meṇḍo (ram/goat), eraṇḍo (castor oil plant), khaṇḍo (fragment/piece), and other such words are also formed.

1306. The suffix ka is applied after roots such as khāda, and the root khāda is changed to khandha. It is called khandha because it is "bitten" (oppressed) by the sufferings of the round of rebirths, such as conception, aging, and death.

1307. In the opinion of other teachers, the roots khāda, ama, and gama are replaced by khandha, andha, and gandha, and the suffix ka is also applied; such a rule along with its commentary exists. Examples in this rule are: khandho, andho, gandho; similarly, khandhako, andhako, gandhako. Among these, the words andha and gandha can also be established by the power of the roots: "andha - in the sense of removing sight, gandha - in the sense of informing or slandering."

1308. The suffix ala is applied after roots such as paṭa, kala, and kusa, as well as after collective nouns. Because it is capable in paṭa, it is paṭalaṃ (mass/clouding); similarly, kalalaṃ (mud), kusalaṃ (merit/capable of cutting), kadalaṃ (banana/capable of intoxicating), bhagaṇḍalaṃ (fistula), mekhalaṃ (girdle), vakkalaṃ (bark garment), takkalaṃ (resin), pallalaṃ (pool), saddalaṃ (green sward), mūlālaṃ (lotus stalk), bilālaṃ (support/black salt), vidhālaṃ (as one likes), caṇḍālo (outcaste), pañcālo (Pañcāla country), vālaṃ (tail hair/hair), vasalo (low-born), pacalo (slimy person), macalo (thief), musalo (pestle), gotthulo (jackal), potthulo (broad person), bahulo (abundant person), bahulaṃ (abundantly), maṅgalaṃ (auspiciousness), bahalaṃ (thickness), kambalaṃ (blanket).
350:
sambala, bilāla, aggala, and other such words also exist.

1309. The stem putha is replaced by puthu and paṭha. Puthavī (earth), paṭhama (first), or pathavī (earth).

1310. The vowel u of the substitute uva becomes a. Puthavī.

1311. The vowel u of the word putha also becomes a, and the letter tha becomes dha. Padhavī.

1312. The suffix ama is applied after the word paṭha, which is a substitute for putha. Paṭhamo so parābhavo (That is the first cause of ruin).

1313. The suffixes tu and du are applied after roots such as sasa, daṃsa, and ada. Sattu (enemy), daddu (ringworm), addu (eating/elephant's trunk), maddu (madness/kneading).

1314. The suffix īvara is applied after roots such as ci. Cīvara (robe), pīvara (fat person), pīvara (turtle). Here, the dictionary definition should be known: "The word pīvara occurs in the sense of a turtle and a fat person."

1315. The suffix i is applied after roots such as muna. Muni (sage), yati (monk), aggi (fire), pati (lord/husband), kavi (poet/wise), suci (purity), ruci (splendor), mahāli (King Mahāli), bhaddāli (Elder Bhaddāli), maṇi (precious gem). Here, maṇi refers to: diamond, large emerald, sapphire, parakara, lapis lazuli, lotus-colored ruby, cucumber-colored ruby, kakketana, puloka, vimala, red ruby, crystal, coral, jotirasa, and gomutta (agate/cat's eye).
351:
Gomedaka (zircon), Sogandhika (ruby-colored gem), Muttā (pearl), Saṅkha (conch), Añjanamūla (antimony stone), Rājavaṭṭa (lapis lazuli), Amatamsuka, Piyaka, and Brāhmaṇī—these twenty-four are known as Maṇi (precious gems).

1316. The suffix ūra is added after roots such as vida. Examples: Veḷūriya (beryl), ballūra (dried meat), masūra (leather or lentil), sindūra (ornament or piercing of defilements), dūra (far), kūra (boiled rice), kappūra (camphor), mayūra (peacock), undūra (rat), khajjūra (date palm), kurūra (osprey).

1317. The suffixes ṇu, nu, and tu are added after roots such as hana. Examples: Hanu (jaw), jāṇu (knee), bhāṇu (light), reṇu (pollen or bamboo dust), khāṇu (stump), aṇu (atom or subtle), veṇu (bamboo), dhenu (cow), dhātu (element), setu (bridge), ketu (banner or pinnacle), hetu (cause).

1318. The suffix ṭha is added after roots such as kuṭa. Examples: Kuṭṭha (leprosy), koṭṭha (abdomen or aching), kaṭṭha (firewood or timber).

1319. The suffixes ussa, nu, si, and sā are added after roots such as manu, pūra, suna, ku, su, and ila. Examples: Manussa (human), mānusa (human), purisa (man), suṇisā (daughter-in-law), karīsa (excrement), sirīsa (acacia tree), ilisa (shaking or weak), alisa (lazy), mahisa (buffalo or a deity to be worshipped), sīsa (head), kisa (lean).

1320. The suffix tu is added after the root ara. When followed by the suffix tu, the final vowel of the root ara is changed to u. It is called Utu (season/climate) because it brings about various occurrences according to the time.

1321. The suffix ruṇa is added after the roots kara and kira. It is called Karuṇā (compassion) because it acts (karoti). What does it do? It causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble. When does this happen? It happens when there is the suffering of others. Thus, it is called Karuṇā because it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble when others encounter suffering. Alternatively, it is called Karuṇā because it removes (kirati) the suffering of others.

1322. The suffix ṇa is added after the root rudh when preceded by the word ka. When followed by the suffix ṇa, the consonant dha is elided.
352:
In this (derivation of the word Karuṇā), there is no function for the anubandha (indicatory letter). It is called Karuṇā because it obstructs (rundhati) happiness (kaṃ). Here, the word 'ka' denotes happiness.

1323. The vowel of the root is changed. It is called Karuṇā because it removes (kirati) (defilements).

1324. The suffix ṇaka is added after the root cara in the sense of afflicting (bhakkhana). In the sense of afflicting, the suffix ṇaka occurs after the root cara. It is called Cāraka because it afflicts beings who have been cast into it (the prison). Both a prison for binding thieves and the prison of Saṃsāra are called Cāraka. Although the form could be established with the suffix ṇvu, the use of the suffix ṇaka is to show that while the root cara in terms like 'desacārako' and 'cārikañcaramāno' denotes 'going' (gati)—which is not rare—this specific sense (of afflicting) is much rarer.

1325. The suffix a is added after the collective roots medha. The word 'me' occurs in the sense of taking (ādāna), and the root dhara occurs in the sense of bearing (dhāraṇa). Thus, the suffix a occurs after this collective root, similar to the term 'macchuddāna' (a collection of fish). It is called Medhā (wisdom) because it quickly takes and bears subtle meanings and the Dhamma. Therefore, it is stated in the Atthasālinī Commentary: 'It is called Medhā in the sense of quick grasping and bearing.'

1326. The suffix ṇa is added after the root midhu. The suffix ṇa occurs after the root midhu. It is called Medhā because it afflicts, harms, or destroys (medhati) intense delusion (sammoha).

By the power of the root khād, or by the power of the root khanu;
From the root khan, or from a root preceded by khaṃ;
The wise scholar of grammar should explain the derivation of the word Khandha.
In these and other ways, I have spoken of various etymologies.
Herein, these are the characteristics of the derivation of that (word Khandha).

Having spoken of the specific characteristics of the causes of formation in this section, I shall now briefly state the general characteristics and specific characteristics.

1327. Augmentation of a letter (vaṇṇāgama) occurs where appropriate.
353:
1328. Metathesis of letters (vaṇṇavipariyaya) occurs where appropriate.

1329. Transformation of letters (vaṇṇavikāra) occurs where appropriate.

1330. Elision of letters (vaṇṇavināsa) occurs where appropriate.

1331. Association with an intensity of meaning of roots occurs where appropriate.

1332. Lengthening of short vowels occurs where appropriate.

1333. Shortening of long vowels occurs where appropriate.

1334. Change of vowels to another vowel occurs where appropriate.

1335. Change of consonants to another consonant occurs where appropriate.

This should be understood respectively in examples such as 'pabbājito' and 'pabbajito'.
A long vowel does not become short, nor does a short vowel become long (arbitrarily).
In words like 'vaka' and 'baka', the letters va and ba do not interchange.
If they were to interchange, the meaning of those words would indeed be ruined.

1336. Change of vowels to consonants occurs where appropriate.

1337. Change of consonants to vowels occurs where appropriate. These are the general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa). Now, the specific characteristics (visesa-lakkhaṇa) follow.

1338. The augmentation of i-vaṇṇa (i or ī) occurs as appropriate when the roots bhū and kara follow. When the roots bhū and kara follow, the augmentation of the vowels i or ī occurs after a nominal stem as appropriate. Examples: Sītībhūto, byantibhūto, byantikato, byantiṃ akāsi, yānikatā, bahulikatā, cittīkataṃ, etc. Thus occurs the augmentation of the vowel i. However, the teachers desire the shortening of the vowel ī in the word 'yānikatā'.
354:
In the view of those teachers, only the arrival of the long vowel ī (ī-kāra-āgama) occurs, and there is no function for the arrival of the short vowel i. In our view, however, since it has been stated that the arrival of both i and ī occurs as appropriate, there is no need for the process of shortening (rassatta). The arrival of ī is seen in examples such as "sammukhībhūto" (become present), "kaddamībhūtaṃ" (become like mud), "ekodakībhūtaṃ" (become a single expanse of water), "araṇībhūtaṃ" (become a refuge), and "bhasmīkataṃ" (reduced to ashes).

What is meant by "as appropriate" (yathārahaṃ)? It refers to cases like "manussabhūto" (having become a human) and "kammakāro" (a worker). What should be understood here is: because it has reached a state where the end has departed, it is called "byantībhūto" (one who has reached the cessation of craving or evil). Evil that has been made to cease is called "byantīkato." Defilements that have been made to cease are called "byantīkatā." The forest of craving that has been made to cease is called "byantīkataṃ." Unwholesome states that have been made to cease are called "byantīkatāni." Craving that has been made to cease is called "byantīkatā." One made the defilements cease (byantaṃ akāsi) or brought about their cessation (byantiṃ akāsi). One made the defilements cease (byante akāsi) or brought about their cessations (byantī akāsi). One made evil cease, or brought about its cessation. One made evil deeds cease, or brought about their cessations. One made cravings cease, or brought about their cessations.

Because it is made in the mind, it is called "cittīkataṃ." For this very reason, it is said: "It is called a shrine (cetiya) because of the sense of being placed in the mind." It is also said to be so called because of the sense of being honored or being worthy of worship. Here, the derivation (nibbacana) is: it is called "cetiya" because it is placed in the mind or consciousness. The statement "It is called a treasure (ratana) because of the sense of being honored in the mind" is not made by way of the literal derivation of the word. If so, how is it meant? It is spoken by way of the state of being honored, which is characteristic of objects recognized as "treasures" in the world. Thus, it is stated in the Commentaries:

"Because it is honored in the mind (cittīkata), is of great value (mahaggha), is incomparable (atula), is rare to behold (dullabhadassana), and is the object of use for noble beings (anomasattaparibhoga), it is therefore called a treasure (ratana)."

In that verse, the meaning is that it is called a treasure because it is honored in the mind, because it is of great value, because it is incomparable, because it is rare to behold, and because it is used by noble beings. Here, the derivation is: just as in phrases like "gatena etaṃ palobhenti," going (gamana) is called "gata," so too, delight (ramaṇa) is called "rata." Because it causes the world to experience great delight, it is called "ratana" through the elision of the letter 'ja'. As for its manifestation, it should be understood as the gold, silver, etc., recognized by worldly people; the seven treasures that appear to a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), namely the Wheel-treasure, Elephant-treasure, Horse-treasure, Gem-treasure, Woman-treasure, Householder-treasure, and Eldest Son-treasure (Advisor); the Triple Gem of the Buddha, etc., by way of the highest distinction; and persons who are grateful and appreciative.

Some teachers say that in the term "cittīkata-ṭṭhena," it means because of the sense of being "variegatedly made" (vicittakata). That meaning should not be accepted. Why? Because the word "citta" here refers to the mind, as in the Pali passage: "Listen to me, having placed my words in your mind (cittī katvā)." Therefore, without taking that variegated meaning mentioned by some, only the meaning "placed in the mind" (citte kataṃ) should be accepted. For this reason, it should be understood that when the Triple Gem of the Buddha, etc., appears, devas and humans do not even give rise to the notion of delight in other treasures, but place only those three treasures exceedingly in their minds, respecting, honoring, esteeming, and worshipping them. This is an excellent method.
355:
Just as going is called 'gata', so too delight is called 'rata'. Because it generates delight and intense pleasure in the world, it is called 'ratana' (treasure) through the elision of the letter 'ja'. That treasure, in its essence, should be understood as: gold, silver, and so forth recognized by the common worldly folk; the seven treasures that arise for a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), such as the Wheel-treasure, Elephant-treasure, Horse-treasure, Gem-treasure, Queen-treasure, Householder-treasure, and General-treasure; the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, which are the refuges by way of the highest distinction; and persons who are grateful and appreciative.

Some teachers, regarding the meaning of 'cittīkata', say it is 'because of the sense of being variegatedly made'. That meaning should not be accepted. The reason is that in this context, the word 'citta' denotes the mind (heart), as in the Pali text: 'Listen to me, having placed [my words] in your mind.' Therefore, without accepting the meaning stated by some, only the meaning 'placed in the mind (citte kataṃ)' should be taken. This is because when the Triple Gem of the Buddha and so forth appears, devas and humans do not even give rise to the perception of delight in other treasures, but place only those three treasures exceedingly in their minds, showing them reverence, honor, esteem, and worship. This method is extremely subtle and should be well-attended to. However, in passages such as 'Behold the body variegatedly adorned (cittīkataṃ) with jewels and earrings,' the meaning 'made variegated'—which was not variegated before but is now—should be taken. This method is also subtle like the previous one. Speech, too, should be made variegated (refined).

1339. When a name is being expressed, the letters 'dha' and 'ma' of the word 'uddhamukha' are elided; the augment 'aka' comes after the vowel 'u'; and the suffix 'ala' is applied after the letter 'kha'. Because its opening is at the top, it is called 'udukkhala' (a mortar). Why is it said 'when a name is being expressed'? [Because this rule does not apply] in cases like 'He sat with his face turned upwards (uddhamukho).' 

1340. When a name is being expressed, if the word 'vāhaka' follows, the entirety of the word 'vāri' is replaced by 'vo', and the 'va' of that word 'vāhaka' is replaced by 'la'. (Because it carries water, it is called 'vārivāhaka'; that same 'vārivāhaka' becomes 'valāhaka' [a cloud] by this rule.) Why is it said 'if the word vāhaka follows'? [Because this does not happen] in cases like 'A river or ocean full of water (vāri).'
356:
The letter 'va' of the word 'vāhaka' is substituted with 'la'. Because it carries water, it is called 'vārivāhaka'; this very 'vārivāhaka' is called 'valāhaka' by this rule (characteristic). Why is the restriction 'in the word vāhaka' included? As in the example 'yathā vārivaho pūro' (like a full river/ocean), where it is called 'vārivaha' and not 'valāhaka'.

1341. When a name is to be expressed, the entirety of the word 'chava' is substituted with 'su' when followed by the word 'sayana'; the letter 'ya' of the word 'sayana' is elided, and the vowel of the letter 'sa' becomes long (dīgha). The bed of corpses is called 'chavasayana'; this very 'chavasayana' is called 'susāna' (cemetery) by this rule.

1342. When a name is to be expressed, the entirety of the root 'brū' is substituted with 'bhi' when followed by the root 'sad'; the letter 'sa' of the root 'sad' is substituted with 'sa' (s-kāra) when followed by the suffix 'ī'. Those who have increased in virtue in this world dwell here; therefore, it is called 'bhisi' (a mat/seat).

1343. When a name is intended, among many letters, the desired letters are taken, and the remaining letters undergo elision. For example: He is called 'Bhagavā' because he has vomited out (vanta) the going (gamana) in the realms of existence (bhavesu), or because he has vomited out the going into the realms of existence. An ornament like a garland for the waist that causes urine to flow is called 'mekhalā' (girdle). However, some teachers say that the root 'mekha' occurs in the sense of decorating the waist elaborately; in their view, the suffix 'ala' is applied. Because it binds water (or the life of beings), it is called 'jīmūta' (cloud).

Grammarians, however, stating the paribhāṣā rule 'pisodarādīni yathopadiṭṭhaṃ' (words like pisodara are formed according to instruction), have mentioned the fivefold method of nirutti (etymology) such as 'vaṇṇāgama' (augmentation of letters) to establish words whose rules have not been specifically prescribed, such as: pisodara, valāhaka, mekhala, jīmūta, susāna, udukkhala, pisāca, bhisi, and mayūra. Because they split the roots, 'mūlavibhujā' (trees) and so forth...
357:
To establish such words, they stated the rule 'mūlavibhujādīhi upasaṅkhyānaṃ'. In the Dispensation (Sāsana) as well, teachers expert in etymology (nirutti) have spoken of the fivefold etymology—

'Augmentation of letters (vaṇṇāgama), transposition of letters (vaṇṇapariyaya), and the other two: transformation (vaṇṇavikāra) and elision of letters (vaṇṇanāsa); and association with the excellence of the meaning of roots (dhātūnamatthātisayena yoga)—this is called the fivefold etymology.'

1344. The suffix 'kkhina' follows the root 'dā'. Because it is to be given, it is called 'dakkhiṇā' (donation).

1345. The suffix 'iṇa' follows the root 'dakkha'. Beings increase (prosper) by this gift, thus it is called 'dakkhiṇā'. Other examples not specified here should also be established by the rules already mentioned.

1346. The suffix 'ṇa' expressing the state (bhāva) occurs in the masculine gender. For example: 'pavisanaṃ' (entering) is 'paveso', 'phusanaṃ' (touching) is 'phasso', and so forth.

1347. The suffix 'ta' expressing the state (bhāva) occurs in the neuter gender. For example: 'gamanaṃ' (going) is 'gataṃ', 'supanaṃ' (sleeping) is 'suttaṃ', 'āsīsanaṃ' (wishing) is 'āsiṭṭhaṃ', 'bujjhanaṃ' (knowing) is 'buddhaṃ', 'nisīdanaṃ' (sitting) is 'nisinnaṃ', and so forth.

For the sake of the listeners' ease of understanding the meaning of words in the Dispensation of the Teacher, who has fame protected in all aspects, the arrangement of kit suffixes (kibbidhāna) has been explained.

## Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter called Kibbidhānakappa in the treatise of Saddanīti, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the paths of the language of the Tipitaka together with its Commentaries, which has nine factors.
358:
## 8. Catupadavibhāga (Analysis of the Four Types of Words)
## Nāmapada (Nouns)

From here on, I shall explain the classification of the four types of words.
Listen with a well-concentrated mind to that analysis of the four words in which speech is established.

In that analysis of the four words, there are four types of words in which speech is established: nāmika-pada (nouns), ākhyāta-pada (verbs), upasagga-pada (prefixes), and nipāta-pada (particles). Indeed, in this group of four words, all the words spoken in the Tipitaka that accomplish the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa) are illuminated. Among these four, regarding the 'nāmika-pada'—

Words together with compounds (samāsa), derivatives (taddhita), primary derivatives (kita), and all conventional names (rūḷhīnāma), which were shown below as being dependent on the verb in the sense of a kāraka (case-relation), are all spoken of as 'nāma' (noun) only.

After that, the verbal word (ākhyātika), which is endowed with the three times (tenses) and so forth, is spoken of. These two divisions, the noun and the verb, have been declared.

Even though this is so, I shall say something regarding the noun among those words.

In that context, 'nāma' is so called because it bends (namati) towards the meaning; it is also called 'nāma' because it causes the meaning to bend (nāmeti) towards itself. It refers to any word such as 'ghaṭa' (pot), 'paṭa' (cloth), etc. For such a word itself bends towards the meaning of 'pot', 'cloth', etc., because the naming of it is possible only when the meaning exists; and it causes that respective meaning to bend towards itself, because without the name, the understanding of the meaning would be impossible.

And that 'nāma' is of two kinds by way of being descriptive (anvattha) and conventional (rūḷhī). Therein—

Words such as 'Loka' and 'Buddha' are certainly and exclusively descriptive (anvattha).

Words such as 'Yevāpana' and 'Telapāyī' are certainly and exclusively conventional (rūḷhī).

A name such as 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' can be conventional (rūḷhī) because it is applied to slaves and others; or it can be descriptive (anvattha) because it is applied to a person who is a lord (issara).
359:
Names such as 'cow' or 'buffalo' are connotative names (anvatthā-nāma) because they follow the literal meaning (according to the derivation 'gacchati iti go' - that which moves is a cow). However, since actions such as moving or sleeping on the ground also occur in other animals like elephants and horses, they are also called conventional names (rūḷhī-nāma).

Similarly, names (nāma) are of two types: etymological names (neruttika-nāma) and arbitrary names (yādicchaka-nāma). Among these, an etymological name is one that is established through grammatical characteristics, by forming the verbal roots (dhātu) and suffixes (paccaya) within the designation, followed by phonetic changes such as the addition of letters (vaṇṇāgama).

An arbitrary name is one that is merely given according to one's wish, devoid of the meaning derived from the sentence structure (viggaha).

Similarly, names are of three types: connotative (anvatthā), artificial (kārimā), and metaphorical (opacārimā). Among these, a connotative name is one that depends on the etymological meaning (nibbacana). An artificial name is a designation (saṅketa) made according to one's wish. A metaphorical name is the usage of a term for something that does not inherently possess that nature, as if it did.

Similarly, names are of four types: names by consensus (samaññā-nāma), qualitative names (guṇa-nāma), given names (kittima-nāma), and spontaneous names (opapātika-nāma). Among these, the name of the king 'Mahāsammata' is a name by consensus because it was established by the agreement of the people at the beginning of the aeon. Indeed, it is called a consensus name because it exists through the general agreement (samaññā) of the people. Names derived from qualities such as 'Dhammakathika' (preacher of Dhamma), 'Paṃsukūlika' (wearer of rag-robes), 'Vinayadhara' (bearer of the Vinaya), 'Tepiṭaka' (knower of the Three Pitakas), 'Saddhā' (faith), and 'Saddho' (the faithful) are qualitative names. The hundreds of names of the Blessed One, such as 'Bhagavā', 'Arahaṃ', and 'Sammāsambuddha', are also qualitative names. The name given to a newborn child on the naming day by relatives who, after making offerings to those worthy of gifts, decide 'let this child be named so-and-so' is a given name (kittima-nāma). That which falls under former and later designations, where the ancient usage corresponds with the later usage, is a spontaneous name. For example, in the previous aeon, the moon was called 'Canda', and it is still called 'Canda' now. In the past, the sun, the ocean, the earth, and the mountain were called by those names, and even now a mountain is called a mountain. Such a name is...
360:
A spontaneous name (opapātika-nāma) means a name that has the nature of naturally attaching itself to the named object.

Similarly, names are of five types: arbitrary (yādicchaka), situational (āvatthika), sign-based (nemittika), characteristic-based (liṅgika), and conventional (rūḷhika). Among these, an arbitrary name is a designation made according to one's wish. A situational name refers to terms like 'vaccho' (calf), 'dammo' (a steer being tamed), and 'balibaddo' (an ox). A sign-based name refers to terms like 'sīlavā' (virtuous) and 'paññavā' (wise). A characteristic-based name refers to terms like 'daṇḍī' (staff-bearer) and 'chattī' (umbrella-bearer). A conventional name refers to terms like 'go-mahiṃsa' (cow and buffalo), which are designated based on a slight indication.

Furthermore, names are of six types: proper nouns (nāmanāma), primary derivatives (kitaka-nāma), compounds (samāsa-nāma), secondary derivatives (taddhita-nāma), pronouns (sabbanāma), and imitative names (anukaraṇa-nāma). Among these, proper nouns are of four types: collective (sāmūhika), individual (pacceka), conceptual (vikappa), and antithetical (pāṭipakkhika). Among these, terms like 'ghaṭo' (pot) and 'paṭo' (cloth) are collective names because they arise from a collection of many substances. Terms like 'vedanā' (feeling) and 'saññā' (perception) are individual names because they arise in dependence on a single phenomenon. Terms like 'deso' (region), 'kālo' (time), and 'okāso' (opportunity) are conceptual names because they arise through special conceptualization of non-ultimate realities (aparamattha). Terms like 'sītaṃ' (cold) and 'uṇhaṃ' (heat) are antithetical names because they arise by way of meanings that are mutually opposite. The four types of names starting with primary derivatives have been shown below. Imitative names are those such as 'yevāpano', 'yevāpanako', 'suvatthigāthā', and 'natumhāka-vaggo'.

Another method: names are of three types by way of gender: masculine (pulliṅga), feminine (itthiliṅga), and neuter (napuṃsakaliṅga). For example: rukkho (tree), mālā (garland), and dhanaṃ (wealth). They are of four types by way of general, qualitative, verbal, and arbitrary: for example, rukkho, nīlo (blue), pācako (cook), and sirīvaḍḍhano. They are of eight types by way of their endings: a-kāranta, ā-kāranta, i, ī, u, ū, e, o-kāranta, and niggahita-ending stems. All of these have also been explained below.

## The verbal part (ākhyāta) has also been analyzed in every aspect.
361:
## Section on Prefixes (Upasāra-pada)

Now I shall discuss the prefixes (upasāra). Regarding prefixes, grammarians in the treatises on grammar have established them starting with the word 'pa'. In the Dispensation (Sāsana), some teachers in the scriptural texts have also established them starting with 'pa'. However, the teachers of Nirutti (etymology), because prefixes are dependent on vowels, have established them in a different order starting with the pure vowel 'ā', which serves as a support. They are: ā, u, ati, pati, pa, pari, ava, parā, adhi, abhi, anu, upa, apa, api, saṃ, vi, ni, nī, su, and du. These twenty words are called prefixes (upasagga). Among them:

The word 'ā' occurs in the sense of facing towards, in upward action,
in the meanings of limit (mariyādā) and pervasion (abhividhi), in embracing and reaching,
in desire, in beginning, in dwelling, and in taking,
and also in the meanings of calling, proximity, and so forth.

Among those meanings, in the sense of facing towards: 'āgacchati' (he comes towards). In upward action: 'ārohati' (he ascends). In the sense of limit: 'āpabbataṃ khettaṃ' (the field up to the mountain). In the sense of pervasion: 'ākumāraṃ yaso kaccānassa' (the fame of Kaccāyana spreads even unto children). In embracing: 'āliṅgati' (he embraces). In reaching: 'āpattiṃ āpanno' (he has fallen into an offense). In desire: 'ākaṅkhā' (desire). In beginning: 'ārambho' (beginning). In dwelling: 'āvasatho' (rest-house), 'āvāso' (dwelling/monastery). In taking: 'ādiyati' (he takes/steals). In calling: 'āmantesi' (he addressed/called). In proximity: 'āsannaṃ' (near).

The word 'u' occurs in the sense of rising, in upward action,
in excellence (predominance), in existence,
in specific description, in obtaining a benefit, in power,
and in the meanings of separation and so forth.

Among those meanings, in rising: 'uggacchati' (it rises). In upward action: 'āsanā uṭṭhito' (risen from the seat), 'ukkhepo' (throwing upwards). In excellence: 'uttamo' (noble/highest), 'lokuttaro' (transcending the world).
362:
In the sense of occurrence (sambhava) — it means "this is the occurrence, this is the logic." In the sense of specification (sarūpakathana) — there is "he specifies the Sutta (Pātimokkha)." In the sense of attainment of benefit (atthalābha) — there is "knowledge has arisen." In the sense of ability (satti) — there is "he is able to go." In the sense of separation (viyoga) — there is "he is made to rise."

The word 'ati' occurs in the sense of past the end, as well as in surpassing, in excess, and in intensity, etc.
Among those senses, in the sense of past the end (atikkanta) — there is "beyond the end." In the sense of surpassing (atikkamana) — there is "he shines surpassing us," and "he has passed." In the sense of excess (atisaya) — there is "extremely skilled." In the sense of intensity (bhusattha) — there is "intense and overwhelming anger," and "heavy rain."

The word 'pati' occurs in the sense of being towards, as well as in substitution, in giving back, in prohibition, in similarity, in turning back, in taking, in requital, in dependence, in understanding, in the senses of sign (lakkhaṇa), state (itthambhūtakkhāna), and portion (bhāga), in the sense of contrary (paṭiloma), and in repetition (vicchā), etc.; thus should the wise note.
Among those senses, in the sense of being towards (paṭigata) — there is "direct (paccakkha)." In the sense of substitution (paṭinidhi) — there is "a pupil who is in place of the teacher." In the sense of giving back (paṭidāna) — there is "he gives ghee in return to the one who wants oil." In the sense of prohibition (nisedha) — there is "he prohibits." In the sense of similarity (sādisa) — there is "similar." In the sense of turning back (nivattana) — there is "he turns back." In the sense of taking (ādāna) — there is "he receives." In the sense of requital (paṭikaraṇa) — there is "requital." In the sense of dependence (paṭicca) — there is "condition (dependence)." In the sense of understanding (paṭibodhana) — there is "penetrative understanding." In the sense of sign (lakkhaṇa) — there is "lightning shines towards the tree." In the sense of state (itthambhūtakkhāna) — there is "Devadatta is very good towards his mother." In the sense of portion (bhāga) — there is "whatever portion should be mine in this distributed object, let that portion be given." In the sense of contrary (paṭiloma) — there is "against the current." In the sense of repetition (vicchā) — there is "the moon shines pervading every tree."

In the senses of variety, completion, interiority, otherness, prominence, lordship, separation, and flowing...
363:
The word 'pa' occurs in such senses as intensity, satisfaction, aspiration, and clarity.
Among those senses, in the sense of variety (pakāra) — there is "knowing in variety (paññā)." In the sense of completion (abhinipphanna) — there is "already done." In the sense of interiority (antobhāva) — there is "thrown in." In the sense of otherness (tappara) — there is "the teacher's teacher." In the sense of prominence (padhāna) — there is "excellent." In the sense of lordship (issara) — there is "the lord of the region." In the sense of separation (viyoga) — there is "one who goes to another region (one who is separated)." In the sense of flowing (sandana) — there is "the Ganges river flows from the Himalayas." In the sense of intensity (bhusattha) — there is "one with a large body." In the sense of satisfaction (tittiya) — there is "one with much wealth." In the sense of aspiration (patthanā) — there is "aspiration." In the sense of clarity (anāvila) — there is "clear water."

The word 'pari' occurs in the senses of all around, delimitation, avoidance, embracing, wearing, honoring, serving, as well as contempt, blaming, and sign, etc.
Among those senses, in the sense of all around (samantatobhāva) — there is "surrounded on all sides." In the sense of delimitation (pariiccheda) — there is "that which should be fully understood (the Truth of Suffering)." In the sense of avoidance (vajjana) — there is "he avoids or shuns." In the sense of embracing (āliṅgana) — there is "he embraces." In the sense of wearing (nivasana) — there is "he wears the robe." In the sense of honoring (pūjā) — there is "service." In the sense of serving (bhojana) — there is "he serves the monk." In the sense of contempt (avajānana) — there is "he despises or reviles." In the sense of blaming (dosakkhāna) — there is "he mutters (in blame)." In the sense of sign (lakkhaṇa), etc. — there is "lightning shines towards the tree," and so on.

The wise should know that the prefix 'ava' occurs in the senses of downward, separation, place, determination, purity, contempt, knowing, theft, etc.
Among those senses, in the sense of downward (adhobhāva) — there is "face down," and "one with downcast eyes." In the sense of separation (viyoga) — there is "one with shoes removed," and "a forest without cuckoos." In the sense of place (desa) — there is "place."
364:
In the sense of determination, there is 'avadhāraṇaṃ'; in the sense of purity, 'vodānaṃ'; in the sense of contempt, 'avajānanaṃ', 'avamaññati' (he despises; one should not despise thinking someone is young); in the sense of knowing, 'avagacchati'; in the sense of theft, 'avahāro'.

The word 'parā' occurs in such senses as taking defeat, going, effort, decline, and handling.
Among those senses, in the sense of taking defeat, there is 'parājito'; in going, 'parāyaṇaṃ'; in effort, 'parakkamati'; in decline, 'parābhavo'; in handling, 'aṅgassa parāmasanaṃ' (handling of the limbs).

The word 'adhi' occurs in such senses as excess, lordship, being above, determination, management, overcoming, learning, and attaining.
Among those senses, in the sense of excess, there is 'adhisīlaṃ'; in lordship, 'adhibrahmadatte pañcālā' (the Pañcālas are under King Brahmadatta); in being above, 'adhirohati', 'adhisayati', 'adhivacanaṃ'; in determination, 'adhimokkho'; in management, 'bhūmikammādiṃ adhitiṭṭhati' (he manages earth-work, etc.); in overcoming, 'adhibhavati'; in learning, 'byākaraṇamadhīte' (he learns grammar); in attaining, 'bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigacchati' (he attains a mass of wealth).

The wise should know that the prefix 'abhi' occurs in distinction, being towards, acting upwards, the sense of excess, noble lineage, suitability, salutation, sign, state, repetition, etc.
Among those senses, in distinction, there is 'abhidhammo'; in being towards, 'abhimukho', 'abhikkamati'; in acting upwards, 'abhiruhati'; in the sense of excess, 'abhivassati'; in noble lineage, 'abhijāto'; in suitability, 'abhirūpo'; in salutation, 'abhivādeti'; in sign, 'rukkhamabhi-'
365:
The lightning flashes with reference to the tree; in the sense of a state of being such (itthambhūta), Devadatta behaves well towards his mother; in the sense of repetition (vīcchā), the moon shines on every tree.

The word 'Anu' occurs in the senses of following, uninterruptedness, afterwards, intensity, similarity, inferiority, the sense of the third case (instrumental), sign, state of being such, portion, and repetition, etc., as should be noted by the wise.

Among those senses: in following—anveti (follows); in uninterruptedness—anusayo (latent tendency); in the sense of afterwards—anurathaṃ (after the chariot); in intensity—anuratto (intensely attached); in similarity—anurūpaṃ (suitable/similar); in inferiority—anu sāriputtaṃ paññavā (the wise one is inferior to Sāriputta); in the sense of the third case—nadimanvāvasitā senā (the army is stationed along the river); in the sense of a sign—rukkhamanu vijjotate vijju (the lightning flashes with reference to the tree); in the state of being such—sādhu devadatto mātaranu (Devadatta behaves well towards his mother); in the sense of a portion—yadettha mamanu siyā taṃ dīyatu (whatever share of mine is here, let it be given); in repetition—rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ anuvijjotate cando (the moon shines on every tree).

The word 'Upa' should be understood to occur in the senses of proximity, approaching, similarity, excess, suitability, occurrence, name, being above, fasting, blaming, preliminary action, manner of grasping, worship, intensity, and so forth.

Among those senses: in proximity—upanagaraṃ (near the city); in approaching—nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya (or should sit down near one who is sitting); in similarity—upamānaṃ, upamā (comparison); in excess—upakhāriyaṃ doṇo (a doṇa is more than a khārī); in suitability—upapattito ikkhati (sees through suitability); in occurrence—saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati (is reborn in the heavenly world); in name—upadhā, upasaggo (prefix); in being above—upasampanno (ordained/attained); in fasting—upavāso; in blaming—paraṃ upavadati (blames another); in preliminary action—
366:
Upakkamo means preliminary effort; upakāro means preliminary service. In the sense of the manner of grasping (gayhākāra), there is 'soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ' (having purity as the manifested manner). In the sense of worship (accana), there are 'buddhupaṭṭhāko' (one who serves and worships the Buddha) and 'mātupaṭṭhānaṃ' (serving and worshiping the mother). In the sense of intensity (bhusa), there are 'upādānaṃ' (firm clinging), 'upāyāso' (intense despair), and 'upanissayo' (strong cause).

The word 'Apa' is found in the senses of departure, blame, and exclusion, as well as in the senses of offense and worship, etc. Among them: in departure (apagata)—'apagato' (one who has departed); in blame (garahā)—'apagabbho samaṇo gotamo' (the ascetic Gotama is one whose rebirth is ended/blameworthy); in exclusion (vajjana)—'apasālāyā āyanti vāṇijā' (merchants come excluding the hall); in offense (padussana)—'aparajjhati' (offends); in worship (pūjanā)—'vuddhāpacāyī' (one who habitually honors elders).

The word 'Api' should be shown to exist in the senses of praise, expectation, question, and conjunction, as well as in blame, etc. Among them: in praise (sambhāvanā)—'api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati. taṇhākkhayarato hoti, sammāsambuddhabhāvako' (the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One finds no delight even in divine pleasures; he delights only in Nibbāna, the destruction of craving); and 'merumpi vinivijjhitvā gaccheyya' (he would go even piercing Mount Meru). In expectation (apekkhā)—'ayampi dhammo aniyato' (this offense also is indefinite). In question (pañha)—'api bhante bhikkaṃ labhittha' (Venerable Sir, did you receive alms?). In conjunction (samuccaya)—'itipi arahaṃ' (for this reason also, He is the Worthy One); and 'antampi antaguṇampi ādāya' (taking both the large intestine and the small intestine). In blame (garahā)—'amhākampi paṇḍitakā' (our so-called wise ones are also blameworthy).

The word 'Saṃ' is found in the senses of well and equal, combination, meeting, all around, summary, intensity, and smallness; as well as in being together, origin, inclusion, and facing; and in wandering, closing, and success, etc. Among them: in the senses of well and equal (sammāsama)—'samādhi' (well-established concentration, equal concentration). In combination (samodhāna)—'sandhi' (combination). In meeting (saṅgata)—'saṅgamo' (meeting). In being all around (samantabhāva)—'saṅkiṇṇā' (mixed all around),
367:
samullapanā (speaking all around). In the sense of summary (saṅkhepa)—samāso (compound). In the sense of intensity (bhusa)—sāratto (intensely attached), sārajjati (is intensely attached/ashamed). In the sense of smallness (appaka)—samaggho (of small value). In the sense of being together (sahattha)—saṃvāso (living together). In the sense of origin (pabhava)—sambhavo (origin). In the sense of inclusion (saṅgaha)—puttadārassa saṅgaho (supporting wife and children), puttadāraṃ saṅgaṇhāti (supports wife and children). In the sense of facing (abhimukha)—sammukhaṃ (face to face). In the sense of wandering (saṃsaraṇa)—sandhāvati (wanders/runs through). In the sense of closing (pidhāna)—saṃvutaṃ (restrained/closed). In the sense of success (samiddhi)—sampanno (endowed/successful).

The prefix 'Vi' is evident in the senses of distinction, various kinds, opposition, absence, beginning, perversion, and separation, etc.

Among them: in distinction (visesa)—vimutti (distinct liberation), visiṭṭho (distinguished). In various kinds (vividha)—vimati (various doubts), vicitraṃ (various/variegated). In opposition (viruddha)—vivādo (dispute). In absence (vigata)—vimalaṃ (free from stain). In beginning (ādikamma)—vippakataṃ (unfinished/begun). In perversion (virūpa)—virūpo (deformed/perverted form). In separation (viyoga)—vippayutto (separated).

The word 'Ni' should be known by the person seeking to extract the meaning as existing in the senses of completeness, exit, insertion, removal, absence, departure, prohibition, division, manifestation, end, decision, investigation, skill, and comparison, etc.

Among them: in completeness (nissesa)—niravasesaṃ deti (gives completely). In exit (niggata)—nikkileso (free from defilements), niyyāti (goes out). In insertion (antopavesana)—nikhāto (dug in/inserted).
368:
In the sense of extraction (nīharaṇa) — niddhāraṇaṃ (extracting and taking out), nirutti (extracting and speaking/expression). In the sense of absence (abhāva) — nimmakkhikaṃ (free from flies). In the sense of departure (nikkhanta) — nibbano (departed from the forest of craving), nibbānaṃ (Nibbāna, the state of departure from craving). In the sense of prohibition (nisedhana) — nivāreti (prohibits/prevents). In the sense of analysis (vibhajana) — niddeso (analytical explanation). In the sense of manifestation (pātukamma) — nimmitaṃ (created/manifested). In the sense of conclusion (avasāna) — niṭṭhitaṃ (finished/completed). In the sense of determination (avadhāraṇa) — nicchayo (decision/determination). In the sense of investigation (upadhāraṇa) — nisāmanaṃ (investigation/contemplation). In the sense of skillfulness (cheka) — nipuṇo (subtle and skillful). In the sense of simile (upamā) — there is the term nidassanaṃ.

A person who wishes to extract the meaning should know that the word 'ni' exists in the sense of extraction, obstruction, departure, and so forth.

Among those, in the sense of extraction (nīharaṇa) — nīharati (extracts/takes out). In the sense of obstruction (āvaraṇa) — nīvaraṇaṃ (hindrance). In the sense of departure (niggamana) — there is the expression 'My dispensation leads out (niyyānika) from the round of suffering'.

The word 'su' occurs in the sense of beauty, happiness, excellence/rightness, and prosperity, etc.

Among those, in the sense of beauty (sobhanattha) — sugandho (beautiful fragrance). In the sense of happiness (sukhattha) — sukaro (easy to do). In the sense of excellence/rightness (suṭṭhu-sammārattha) — He is called Sugato because He has gone well (suṭṭhu gato) and gone rightly (sammā gato). In the sense of prosperity (samiddhi) — there is the term subhikkhaṃ (plentiful in alms).

The word 'du' occurs in the sense of lack of beauty, absence, contemptibility, lack of prosperity, difficulty, deformity, and so forth.

Among those, in the sense of lack of beauty (asobhana) — duggandho (bad smell). In the sense of absence (abhāva) — dubbhikkhaṃ (famine/scarcity of alms). In the sense of contemptibility (kucchita) — duggati (a contemptible destination). In the sense of lack of prosperity (asamiddhi) — dussassaṃ (failed crops). In the sense of difficulty (kiccha) — dukkhaṃ (suffering). In the sense of deformity (virūpatā) — dubbaṇṇo (ugly/discolored) and dummukho (ugly-faced/sad-faced).
369:
Thus, the twenty prefixes (upasagga), having many meanings, qualify nouns and verbs.

They are called 'upasaggā' because they approach (upecca) and adhere to (sajanti/lagganti) nouns and verbs, and qualify their meanings. If this is so, why is it said in some places 'upasaggamatta' (merely a prefix)? This is true; it is said with reference to those prefixes following nouns and verbs when there is no specific meaning to be qualified. That statement is very appropriate:

Some prefixes block the meaning of the root.
Some prefixes follow the meaning of the root.
Other prefixes qualify the meaning of the root itself.
Thus, the application of prefixes is threefold.

The four prefixes pati, pari, anu, and abhi
Indeed occur at both the beginning and the end of words.
All the remaining sixteen prefixes
Occur only at the beginning.
They never occur at the end;
One should bear this method in mind.

Among these four prefixes: paṭisevati (associates/indulges), paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito (arisen from seclusion), suriyuggamanaṃ pati (concerning the rising of the sun), paribhuñjati (consumes/uses), paributtaṃ (consumed), rukkhaṃ pari vijju vijjotate (lightning flashes around the tree), anubhavati (experiences), anubhūtaṃ (experienced), anusāriputtaṃ paññavā (less wise than Sāriputta), sādhu devadatto mātaram-anu (Devadatta serves his mother well), abhibhavati (overpowers/oppresses), abhibhūtaṃ (overpowered), sādhu devadatto mātaram-abhi (Devadatta serves his mother well). These examples should be understood. This is the analysis of prefixes.

## Nipātapada (The Particle)

Now the analysis of particles will be stated. A word that expresses conjunction (samuccaya), distinction (vikappa), negation (paṭisedha), or filling (pūraṇa), and does not denote a substance (asattavācaka), is called a particle (nipāta). Here, 'sattva' refers to substance (dabba). A meaning other than substance is called 'asattva'. Conjunction and so forth are indeed 'asattva'. Because it expresses 'asattva', it is called 'asattavācaka'. Alternatively, it is called 'asattavācaka' because it does not express substance. For example, 'acandamullokikāni mukhāni' (faces that do not look at the moon).

Is it not that a characteristic should be a unique mark that does not overlap with others? Just as the earth element has the characteristic of hardness. The state of not denoting substance (asattavācaka) also exists in verbs and prefixes. If so, how can 'asattva' be the characteristic of a particle? For only the noun reaches the state of denoting substance. Therefore, there is a ground for objection that this determination is incorrect.

This mark is not constant. Even if a characteristic overlaps, if it attains a distinction in a certain thing, that overlapping characteristic is still a characteristic. Just as it is said, 'It is called rūpa (matter) because it is subject to change/deformation (ruppana)'. Deformation means the arising of different states due to the meeting of opposing causes. That deformation also exists in mental phenomena (nāma). However, the deformation of material phenomena (rūpa) is evident when encountering cold, heat, etc. Therefore, only that matter is called 'rūpa' due to the sense of deformation; similarly here, whichever word especially does not denote substance, only that word is called 'asattavācaka' and is termed a particle (nipāta). In truth, the verb denotes an action dependent on substance. The prefix also qualifies that action. Therefore, both the verb and the prefix appear as if they denote substance. The particle, however, denotes conjunction and so forth, which are far removed from substance.
370:
A characteristic (lakkhaṇa) should be something unique (not shared by many). For example, it is said, "The earth element has the characteristic of hardness." Since verbs (ākhyāta) and prefixes (upasagga) also do not denote a substance (asattavācaka), how can this be the characteristic of a particle (nipāta)? Is it not true that only nouns (nāma) denote a substance? This determination is not fixed. Even if something is shared by many, if it serves as a specificator in a certain context, it can indeed be a characteristic. For example, in the statement "It is called rūpa (form/matter) because of the sense of being deformed (ruppana)," deformation refers to the arising of dissimilar states due to the meeting of opposing causes. Although such deformation also exists in mental phenomena (arūpa), the deformation of physical phenomena (rūpa) is more evident when in contact with cold and so on. Therefore, only that physical matter is said to be "rūpa because of the sense of being deformed."

In this context as well, whichever word does not specifically denote a substance, only that word is called a particle (nipāta), which is described as asattavācaka. A verb (ākhyāta) denotes an action dependent on a substance, and a prefix (upasagga) specifies that action. Therefore, both of them appear as if they denote a substance. A particle, however, denotes things like conjunction (samuccaya) which are far removed from a substance; thus, only the particle is called asattavācaka.

Among those particles, the particle ca occurs in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya, making a group). For example: "The deity Asama and the deity Sahali and the deity Nika and the deity Ākoṭaka and the deity Vegabbhari and the deity Māṇavagāmiya," or "Friends and colleagues, and children and wives, and relatives." In these instances, the word ca occurs in the sense of conjunction. Here, conjunction means making a group, making things that are naturally different dependent on one another. How so? If one says "Asamo," it is known as a single deity of this name; but if one says "Asamo ca," the knowledge arises that there is someone else as well.

Similarly, the particle ca occurs in the senses of anvācaya (secondary conjunction with different actions), itarītarayoga (mutual conjunction with the same action), samāhāra (aggregation into a singular form), vyatireka (distinction/opposition), avadhāraṇa (emphasis/limitation), and so on. Among these, in the sense of anvācaya: "Give alms and also bring the cow," or "Give gifts and also guard your virtue." Thus, anvācaya should be understood in contexts where there are different actions.
371:
In the sense of mutual association (itarĩtarayoga): 'The recluse stands and (ca) the brahmin stands; recluses and brahmins (samaᅆabrāhmaᅆā) stand.' Thus, mutual association should be understood in the context of the same action.

In the sense of collective (samāhāra): 'Cold and (ca) heat' becomes 'cold-heat' (sĩtuᅆhaᅁ). 'The bowl and (ca) the robe' becomes 'bowl-robe' (pattacĩvaraᅁ). Thus, the collective should be understood as reaching the state of a singular noun. This point should also be noted here: secondary conjunction (anvācaya) means taking one meaning as primary and mentioning another meaning as if saying 'if it were possible.' For example: 'Give alms and bring the cow.' Mutual association (itarĩtarayoga) is found in a copulative compound (dvanda samāsa) with plural usage, such as 'samaᅆabrāhmaᅆā' (recluses and brahmins). The collective (samāhāra) is found in that same copulative compound with singular usage, such as 'ajeᄳakaᅁ' (goats and sheep).

In the sense of distinction (vyatireka): In the verse 'Yo ca buddhaca dhammaca,' the word 'ca' in this context denotes the sense of distinction. That word 'ca' refers back to the meaning previously stated. How so?

'Driven by fear, men go to many a refuge: to mountains and forests, to park-shrines and tree-shrines.
That, indeed, is no safe refuge; that is not the supreme refuge. Having gone to that refuge, one is not released from all suffering.'
This is what is called the previously stated meaning (pubbapakkha).

After that:
'But he who (yo ca) has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saᅁgha, sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths.
This, indeed, is the safe refuge; this is the supreme refuge. Having gone to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.'
This is the subsequent meaning (pacchimo attho).

In showing the sense of distinction between the previous and subsequent meanings, the intention is as follows: How? If mountains and so forth are not a safe refuge, are not the supreme refuge, and by depending on that refuge...
372:
(...one is not released from all suffering,) then what object is a safe refuge, is the supreme refuge? By going to what object as a refuge is one released from all suffering? If one asks this: 'But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saᅁgha... having gone to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.' Here, 'yo ca' has the meaning of 'yo pana' (but he who). It should be understood that here the meaning of the word 'ca' which denotes distinction is the meaning of the word 'pana.' Similarly:

'The stingy do not go to the celestial realm; fools, indeed, do not praise giving. But the wise man (dhĩro ca) rejoices in giving, and because of that, he becomes happy in the hereafter.'
In such passages, the word 'ca' denotes the sense of distinction by referring to the previously stated meaning. Here, 'dhĩro ca' should be understood as 'dhĩro pana' (but the wise man), having the meaning of the word 'pana.' The usage of the word 'ca' in emphasis (avadhāraᅆa) and so forth should be learned by attending upon teachers.

The word 'vā' is used in the sense of option (vikappana). For example: 'A warrior (khattiya) or (vā) a brahmin or a merchant (vessa) or a worker (sudda).' Similarly, the word 'vā' exists in the sense of aggregation (samuccaya), similarity (sadisa), and fixed option (vavatthitavibhāsā). Among these, in the sense of aggregation: ' Ānanda, there will be three dangers to Pāᅦaliputta: from fire or (vā) from water or from internal strife.' Here, the meaning is that it will be destroyed by fire and by water and by internal strife. In the sense of similarity: 'The fool thinks [evil] is like (vā) honey as long as the evil does not ripen.' The usage of the word 'vā' in fixed option should be learned by attending upon teachers.

The words 'na, no, mā, a, alaᅁ, halaᅁ' are in the sense of prohibition (paᅦisedhana). 'I do not (na) eat leaves; this is not (na) my food.' 'One should speak only well-spoken words; one should not (no) speak ill-spoken words.' 'May I not (mā) [be] like a crow...'
374:
In "abyākatā dhammā" etc., (the particle a-) exists in the sense of 'other'. In "amanusso" etc., it exists in the sense of similarity. In "akusalā dhammā" etc., it exists in the sense of opposition. In "arājā" etc., it exists in the sense of blame. In "abhāvo" etc., it exists in the sense of voidness. In "aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ" etc., it exists in the sense of absence. In "anudarā kaññā" etc., it exists in the sense of smallness. Furthermore, the word "a" is in some places merely a particle (nipāta). Thus, in the Gopālavimāna story, in the Pali passage "khipiṃ anantakaṃ", the letter "a" is merely a particle. There, "khipiṃ" means giving into the hand of the monk by way of making him receive it. "Anantakaṃ" refers to a worn-out cloth (nantaka).

The word "alaṃ" exists in the senses of capability (pariyatti) and decoration (bhūsana). Examples include "alametaṃ sabbaṃ" (this entire Vinaya act is capable of being an offense-free state) and "alaṅkāro" (decoration).

The sense of filling (pūraṇattha) is of two types: filling the meaning (atthapūraṇa) and filling the word (padapūraṇa). Among these two, filling the meaning refers to making the meaning more prominent by illuminating the sense already expressed by another word. Thus, even when it is said "khattiyo brāhmaṇo vesso suddo", in saying "khattiyo ca brāhmaṇo ca vesso ca suddo ca", the meaning (of the particle ca) is already expressed. This method should be applied as appropriate. However, the phrase "by another word" is not applicable in all cases, as it is unsuitable in instances such as "atthi, sakkā, labbhā".

Filling the word (padapūraṇa) refers to filling the sentence for the sake of euphony (smoothness of speech) even when there is no special meaning to be expressed. A question arises: Due to the power of the Buddha's perfections, not even a single meaningless syllable comes out of his mouth, and it is said that the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) reveals the Four Noble Truths in every word; how then can such padapūraṇa be possible? The answer is: It is true; padapūraṇa also expresses the preceding meaning by way of qualifying the meaning expressed by another word. However, because that meaning can be known through other words even without that padapūraṇa, it is simply called "padapūraṇa". Alternatively, the Buddha's teaching arises in accordance with the inclinations of those to be disciplined (veneyya). Those to be disciplined have minds permeated with worldly terms in the beginningless saṃsāra. In this world, the use of words is seen for the sake of euphony even when there is no special meaning to be understood. (For example: labbhati upalabbhati, khaññati nikhaññati, āgacchati paccāgacchati, bhavati dissati, etc.) For those to be disciplined who are accustomed to such usage, understanding the meaning through such word usage is easy. Therefore, the use of padapūraṇa is indeed appropriate.
375:
Because the meaning can be known through other words even without the padapūraṇa word, it is simply called "padapūraṇa".

Otherwise, the Buddha's teaching arises in accordance with the wishes and inclinations of those to be disciplined (veneyya). Those to be disciplined have minds permeated only with worldly words in the beginningless saṃsāra. In the world, even when there is no special meaning to be understood, the use of words is seen for the sake of euphony and smoothness of speech, such as "is obtained, is obtained; is dug, is dug; comes, comes back." For those to be disciplined who are thus accustomed, it is very easy to understand the meaning through such word usage. Therefore, the use of padapūraṇa is highly appropriate.

29. There are many varieties of that padapūraṇa. They are: atha, khalu, vata, vatha, atho, assu, yagghe, hi, ca, rahi, naṃ, ca, vā, vo, pana, have, kīva, ha, tato, yathā, sudaṃ, kho, ve, kahaṃ, enaṃ, seyyathidaṃ, ānaṃ, taṃ, and so on. We shall state the usages of these words:

Then (atha) the man should come.

Friends, the recluse Gotama, who is a son of the Sakyans, having gone forth from the Sakyan clan, indeed (khalu) (comes).

Friends, it is indeed (vata) wonderful; friends, it is indeed (vata) marvelous.

Prince Jayasena will indeed (vatha) (know) that attainment of one-pointedness of mind.

Furthermore (atho), you have compassion for me.

Not even a single person among this group of monks approaches (assu) the Blessed One.

Great King, may you indeed (yagghe) know.

That Blessed One, knowing, knows (hi); seeing, sees.

Why (rahi) is he of great wisdom?

The recluse Gotama is indeed (naṃ) of good birth.
376:
Understanding the meaning is beneficial. Therefore, using a word merely to fill the verse (padapūraṇa) is indeed inappropriate. (If the meaning is understood in a sentence without showing the grammar, it is called atthapūraṇa. If the grammar is present but the meaning is not obtained, it is called padapūraṇa.)

29. Among those verse-fillers, padapūraṇa has many varieties. They are: atha, khalu, vata, atho, assu, yagghe, hi, ca, rahi, naṃ, ca, vā, vo, pana, have, kīva, ha, tato, yathā, sudaṃ, kho, ve, kahaṃ, enaṃ, seyyathidaṃ, ānaṃ, taṃ (the words ā, naṃ, taṃ), and so forth. I shall now demonstrate the usage of these words.

Atha - At that time, the person should come.

Khalu - Friends, the ascetic Gotama, who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan, is indeed (khalu) [famous].

Vata - Friends, how wonderful indeed (vata)! Friends, how marvelous indeed (vata)! Prince Jayasena will certainly (vata) know, see, and realize that one-pointedness of mind through that renunciation. There is certainly (vata) no possibility of knowing it thus.

Atho - Furthermore (atho), please have compassion for me.

Assu - In this assembly of monks, not a single person approaches the Blessed One (assu - merely an expletive particle).

Yagghe - Great King, I urge you (yagghe), please know.

Hi - That Blessed One knows all that should be known (hi). He clearly sees all that should be seen, like an emblic myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of the hand.

Rahi - Why (kathañcarahi) is the ascetic Gotama so wise?

Naṃ - The ascetic Gotama is not of good birth (na naṃ sujāto).

Ca - Monks, for what reason (kiṃ ca) is it called form (rūpa)?

Vā - The Blessed One asked: "Is form permanent (niccaṃ vā) or impermanent (aniccaṃ vā)?"

Vā (another example) - Is that great elephant this elephant (ayaṃ vā)?

Vo - These five cords of sensual pleasure are considered happiness (ete vo sukhasammatā).

Pana - The venerable Gotama is young by birth and new to the monkhood. However (pana), being young and a new monk, why does he claim to be a Buddha?

Have - The venerable ascetics and brahmins certainly (have) encounter small and great dangers.

Kīva - Monks, as long as (yāva kīvañca) for the monks...

Ha - Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One not speak to me (mā ha pana).

Tato - And after that (tato ca), Sakka, known as Maghavā, who sees the benefit and is a giver...

Yathā - Venerable Sir, in what manner (yathā kထံ pana) is the holy life lived under the Blessed One?

Sudaṃ - At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Ginjaka abode in Nātika (sudaṃ - merely a verse-filler).

Kho - At that very time (tatra kho), the Blessed One addressed the monks.

Ve - That person certainly (ve) goes near to Nibbāna by this vehicle of the Eightfold Path.

Kahaṃ - "O only son, where are you (kahaṃ ekaputtaka)?" Thus they would beat their breasts.

Enaṃ - Because of which reason, that person (enaṃ) who lives without restraining the eye faculty...

Seyyathidaṃ - What are those five aggregates of clinging (seyyathidaṃ)? The aggregate of form as an object of clinging...

Ānaṃ - Because the fool thinks (yaṃ ānaṃ), "This person endures because he is afraid of me."

Taṃ - For what reason is that (taṃ kissa hetu)?

In those examples, in the phrase "yadānaṃ maññati", the words should be split as "yaṃ ā naṃ maññati". "Ā" is merely a particle. The meaning is "because he thinks of that person". Here, if the word "ā" were a prefix (upasagga), it would be placed before the root. Among those particles, the verse-fillers (padapūraṇa) such as atha, khalu, vata, etc., have been shown.

30. Among those particles, the particle "atha" occurs in some places in the sense of a question (pañha), sequence (anantariya), continuity (avicchinna), and another topic (adhikārantara).

In the sense of a question: "How is it (atha), you (Mahosadha), by what reason, by what cause, or for what purpose, do you free yourself from the enemy's hand?"

In the sense of continuity: Then (atha kho), the Blessed One, throughout the first watch of the night, reflected on dependent origination in forward and reverse order without interruption.

In the sense of another topic: After that (atha), the preceding vowel is elided. Furthermore, it also means "thus". Great King, after that (atha), honey...
377:
If the word "ā" were a prefix (upasagga), it would be placed before the root. Among those examples, the particles that fill the verse (padapūraṇa) such as "atha, khalu, vata" have been shown.

30. Among those particles, the particle "atha" occurs in some places in the sense of a question (pañha), sequence (anantariya), continuity (avicchinna), and another topic (adhikārantara). In the sense of a question: "How is it, you (Mahosadha), by what appearance (reason), for what cause, or for what purpose, do you free yourself (from the enemy's hand)?" In the sense of sequence: "After that, he said to him." In the sense of continuity: "Then (atha kho), the Blessed One, throughout the first watch of the night, reflected on dependent origination in forward and reverse order without interruption." In the sense of another topic: It occurs in the sense of "After that, the preceding vowel is elided," and also in the sense of "Great King, after that (atha), you will see the banyan tree with sweet fruit."

31. The particle "khalu" also occurs in the sense of hearsay (anussava). Therefore, the teachers who explain the meaning of this Pali passage, "Friends, the ascetic Gotama (is said to be thus)," stated that "khalu is a particle in the sense of hearsay." It means, "Friends, the ascetic Gotama, it is said (kira)." Likewise, the particle "khalu" occurs in some places in the sense of prohibition (paṭisedha) and emphasis (avadhāraṇa). In the sense of prohibition: "One who has finished his meal does not eat again (khalu)." In the sense of emphasis: "Yaññadatta's drinking of milk is indeed good (sādhu khalu)." Here, "sādhu khalu" means "certainly good."

32. The particle "vata" also occurs in the sense of certainty (ekaṃsa), weariness (kheda), compassion (anukampā), and thought (saṅkappa). In the sense of certainty: "In the world, wise ones certainly (vata) appear as a wonder." In the sense of weariness: "Alas (vata), this world has fallen into a state of suffering and weariness." In the sense of compassion: "Alas (vata), this lonely monk, with shaven head and wearing the robe, without mother or father, is meditatively dwelling at the foot of a tree in a pitiable state." In the sense of thought: It is the kind of thought such as, "It would be good if this pregnancy were to perish (aho vatāyaṃ nasseyya)."
378:
The particle "atho" is also used in the sense of following mention (anvādesa). For example: "Welcome, Great King; furthermore, your arrival is not unwelcome."

The particles "have" and "ve" are also used in the sense of certainty (ekaṃsa). For example: "When the phenomena certainly become manifest." "One who is unskilled in welfare cannot certainly bring about happiness by practicing for welfare." "I certainly do not eat leaves." "This youth Ānanda certainly did not know the limit." "This liquor is certainly not good."

The particle "kho" is also used in the sense of emphasis or delimitation (avadhāraṇa). Therefore, the teachers who explain the meaning of the Pali text, "The Brahmin Verañja indeed heard (assosi kho)," stated: "Kho is a particle used in the sense of a verse-filler (padapūraṇa) or in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa)." The meaning of "assosi kho" is "assosi eva" (he certainly heard).

The particle "seyyathidaṃ" is also used in an indefinite sense (aniyamita) according to gender and number, such as: "What is that?", "What are those?" (masculine), "What is she?", "What are those?" (feminine), "What is that?", or "What are those?" (neuter).

The particle "tu" is used in the sense of certainty, or as an ornament of speech (vacanālaṅkāra), or in the sense of excluding a distinction (visesanivattana). For example: "Among feelings and so forth, in a single phenomenon, the term 'khandha' (aggregate) is certainly (or as an ornament of speech) merely a conventional designation."

The particle "pana" is used in the sense of distinction (visesa), and in some places, also as an ornament of speech. In the sense of distinction, for example: In the Commentary, it is said, "Khalu, however, is a type of bird." In the sense of an ornament of speech, for example: "That which is the supreme peace is this attainment of Nibbāna." Other particles should be applied in the same way. This is the method of extracting meanings—

The word "khalu" is found in the sense of a particle and also in the sense of a species of bird.
The word "taṃ" is found in the sense of a particle and also in the sense of the objective case (upayoga).
379:
The word "assu" is found in the sense of a particle and also in the sense of tears. However, when it functions as a verb (ākhyāta), it is a plural verb. The word "vo" occurs in the sense of a particle, and also in the nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive cases.

Expletive particles that fulfill the meaning (atthapūraṇa) are of two types: those associated with case endings and those not associated with case endings. The particles "atthi," "sakkā," and "labbhā" are associated with the nominative case (paṭhamā). For example: "The fruit of giving exists (atthi), the fruit of sacrifice exists." "Monks, it is possible (sakkā) to abandon the unwholesome and to develop the wholesome." "Monks, it is possible (labbhā) to buy, sell, place, examine, or investigate the earth."

The particles "divā," "bhiyyo," and "namo" are associated with both the nominative and accusative cases. For example: "Even while it is night, they perceive it as day (divā)." "Happiness arises; beyond (bhiyyo) that happiness, joy arises." "O Buddha, the Hero, homage (namo) be to You; You are specially liberated from all [defilements]." This is how they are associated with the nominative case. "Even while it is day, they perceive it as night (rattiṃ)." "I reached a state of extreme hair-standing-on-end (bhiyyo) while dwelling in the forest." "Perform homage (namo) to the Naga (Arahant)." This is how they are also associated with the accusative case.

The particles "saha," "vinā," "saddhiṃ," "sayaṃ," "samaṃ," "sāmaṃ," "sammā," "micchā," "sakkhi," "paccattaṃ," "kinti," and the suffix "-to" are associated with the instrumental case (tatiyā). For example: "The Saṅgha may perform the Uposatha either with (saha) Gagga or without (vinā) Gagga." "Together with (saddhiṃ) a large Saṅgha of monks." "Having known by oneself (sayaṃ) with higher knowledge, whom should I point to [as a teacher]?" "Measured as equal (samaṃ) to a thousand." "Having realized the truths by oneself (sāmaṃ)." "Those who know thus, know rightly (sammā); those who know otherwise, their knowledge is wrong (micchā)." "I now know as a witness (sakkhi) the Dhamma of the Sugata, the Sage, as He teaches it." "To be known by the wise individually (paccattaṃ)." "How (kinti) shall my disciples grow in faith?" "[One should contemplate] as impermanent (aniccato), as suffering (dukkhato), as a disease (rogato), as a boil (gaṇḍato), as a thorn (sallato)."
380:
The particles "so" and "dhā" are also associated with the sense of the instrumental case. For example: "suttaso" (by way of Sutta), "padaso" (by way of words), "ekadhā" (in one way), "dvidhā" (in two ways), and so forth. The particles "tuṃ" and "tave" are associated with the sense of the dative case (catutthī). For example: "dātuṃ" (to give), "vūpakāsāpetuṃ" (to appease), "vinodetuṃ" (to dispel), "vinodāpetuṃ" (to cause to dispel), "vivecetuṃ" (to make secluded), "vivecāpetuṃ" (to cause to be secluded), "kātave" (to do), "dātave" (to give). The particles "to" and "so" are associated with the sense of the ablative case (pañcamī). For example: "Pure in conception from the mother's side (mātito) and from the father's side (pitito)." "No destruction of wealth comes to him from the king (rājato), or from thieves (corato), or from fire (aggito), or from water (udakato), or from unloved heirs (appiyadāyādato)." Also "dīghaso" (by length) and "oraso" (on this side/legitimate).

The suffix "-to" and words ending in suffixes such as "-tra" and "-tha" occur in the sense of the locative case (sattamī). For example: "ekato" (on one side), "purato" (in front), "pacchato" (behind), "passato" (at the side), "piṭṭhito" (at the back), "pādato" (at the feet), "sīsato" (at the head), "aggato" (at the tip), "mūlato" (at the root), "yatra," "yattha," "yahiṃ" (where), "tatra," "tattha," "tahiṃ" (there), "kva," "kuhiṃ," "kuhaṃ," "kahaṃ," "kuhiñcanaṃ" (where?). The particle "ko" occurs in the sense of the locative case. For example: "Where (ko) is your strength, Great King? Where (ko) is your array of chariots?"

The particles "katthaci," "kvaci," and "kvacana" are locative in sense and denote a place. "Yatthakatthaci" is a term expressing comprehensive inclusion in the locative sense. "Yatokutoci" is a term expressing comprehensive inclusion in the ablative sense. Other spatial and relational terms include: "samantā" (all around), "sāmantā" (nearby), "parito" (all around), "abhito" (within/near), "samantato" (all around), "ekajjhaṃ" (together), "heṭṭhā" (below), "upari" (above), "uddhaṃ" (above), "adho" (below), "tiriyaṃ" (across), "sammukhā" (in the presence), "parammukhā" (behind/in absence), "āvi" (openly), "raho" (secretly), "tiro" (across/beyond), "uccaṃ" (high), "nīcaṃ" (low), "anto" (inside), "antarā" (between), "antaṃ" (at the end), "antaraṃ" (in the mind/inside), "ajjhattaṃ" (internally)...
381:
... The particles bahiddhā, bahirā, bāhiraṃ (outside), oraṃ (on this side), pāraṃ (on that side), ārā, ārakā (far away), pacchā (behind), pure (formerly), huraṃ (in another place), pecca (hereafter/in the next world), and apācīnaṃ (in the west) occur in the sense of the locative case (sattami).

The particles sampati (now), āyatiṃ (in the future), ajja (today), aparajju (tomorrow), sve, suve (tomorrow), uttarasuve (the day after tomorrow), hiyyo (yesterday), pare (on another day), sajja (today), sāyaṃ (evening), pāto (morning), kālaṃ (early morning), divā (by day), ratti (at night), niccaṃ (always), satataṃ (constantly), abhiṇhaṃ (repeatedly), abhikkhaṇaṃ (frequently), muhuṃ (momentarily), muhuttaṃ (for a moment), bhūtapubbaṃ (formerly occurred), purā (formerly), yadā (when), tadāni (then), etarahi (now), adhunā (now), idāni (now), kadā (when?), kudācanaṃ (ever/sometimes), sabbadā (always), sadā (always), aññadā (at another time), and ekadā (once/at one time) occur in the sense of the locative of time (kālasattami).

The term yadākadāci is a word used in the sense of the locative of time to express exhaustive inclusion without exception.

The particles āvuso, ambho, hambho, hare, are, and he are used in addressing men in both singular and plural forms.

The particle bhaṇe is used in addressing inferiors in both singular and plural forms.

The particle je is used by masters in addressing female slaves in both singular and plural forms.

The particle bho is used in addressing both men and women in both singular and plural forms. Examples such as 'O man!', 'O fools!', 'O yakkhas!', 'O great rock, emerge!', 'O great rock, float!', and 'O housewives, go!' are all associated with case endings.

In this context, we shall say this: 'Friend (samma), come, return', 'Friend (sammā), do not speak thus', 'Friend (mārisa), I have regained my life, know thus', and 'Friends (mārisā), if fear, trembling, or hair-standing-on-end should arise in the devas who have gone to the battlefield', etc. In these instances, samma, sammā, mārisa, and mārisā are...
382:
The words mārisa and mārisā are seen as singular and plural vocative forms associated with the nominative case, but since they are not found associated with other cases such as the accusative or instrumental, they should be understood as being included among the indeclinable particles (nipāta).

Indeclinables not associated with case endings are of many kinds and occur in many meanings. The words appeva, appevanāma, and nu kho occur in the sense of doubt (saṃsaya). (For example:) "Perhaps the Blessed One might instruct me respectfully." "Perhaps this venerable one, while making use of suitable lodgings, might achieve the other (Arahatship)." "Am I? Am I not? Why am I? How am I?"

The words addhā, aññadatthu, taggha, jātu, kāmaṃ, sasakkaṃ, and jātucce occur in the sense of certainty (ekaṃsa).
