(For example:) "Friend, the Blessed One certainly knows what is to be known, and certainly sees what is to be seen." "Certainly having heard only the words of the young Brahmins." "Blessed One, the factors of enlightenment are certainly good; Sugata, the factors of enlightenment are certainly good." "I have certainly seen this happening; this is not just hearsay or oral tradition (itihītihaṃ)." "I will certainly give up my life among the Asuras." "Rāhula, you should certainly not do such a deed with such a body." "Migājina, I have never certainly conquered any relative unjustly, nor have my relatives certainly conquered me unjustly."

The words eva and iti occur in the sense of establishment (avaṭṭhāna—either as emphasis or limitation). (For example:) "Monks, formerly, even before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me."

The words kacci, nu, and nanu occur in the sense of questioning (pucchana). (For example:) "Monks, is it bearable? Is it tolerable?" "Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the Blessed One's smile to be manifested?" "Phagguna, did you not go forth from home to homelessness out of faith as a son of a good family?"
383:
The word kathaṃ occurs in the sense of asking for the means (upāyapucchana). For example: "How does one cross the flood? How does one cross the ocean?"

The words kiṃ su and kiṃ occur in the sense of asking about the object or matter (vatthupucchana). For example: "Having cut what does one sleep happily?" and "Who practicing what in this world gains wisdom?"

The words evaṃ, itthaṃ, and iti occur in the sense of indication or illustration (nidassana). For example: "Thus is your mind, thus is your mind, thus is your thought."

The words yāva, tāva, yāvatā, tāvatā, kittāvatā, and ettāvatā occur in the sense of delimitation or extent (pariccheda). For example: "As long as the body of the Blessed One remains, so long will devas and humans see him." "Monks, as far as the Kāsi and Kosala countries extend." "Ambaṭṭha, would you, merely by learning the Vedas composed by those sages, be a sage or one practicing to be a sage?" "Venerable Sir, to what extent is one a lay follower?" When asked thus, the reply is: "Mahānāma, to this extent one is a lay follower."

The words evaṃ, sāhu, lahu, opāyikaṃ, patirūpaṃ, āma, and āmo occur in the sense of acceptance or assent (sampaṭicchana). For example: "Yes, Venerable Sir," the monks replied to the Blessed One. Also, expressions of assent such as "Good," "It is no burden (easy)," "It is appropriate to the means," and "It is fit." When asked, "Friend, do you know our teacher?", the assent is "Yes, friend, I know." Also, "Yes (āmo)," having replied thus, that wise parrot, the bringer of glory, departed.

The word kiñcāpi occurs in the sense of concession or favor (anuggaha). For example: "Venerable Sir, although the Blessed One is one to be believed and trusted by me." "Monks, although he is a Wheel-turning Monarch; monks, although he is a noble disciple." "Although he performs an evil deed."
384:
The word "kiñci" occurs in the sense of favor and in the sense of blame. It means, "The King indeed still supports others; why then does the King not support his own son?"

The words yathā, yathēva, tathēva, evaṃ, evamēva, evamēvaṃ, evampi, yathāpi, seyyathāpi, seyyathāpināma, viya, iva, yathariva, and tathariva occur in the sense of similarity (comparison).

Just as a city on the frontier is well-guarded inside and out. I speak of a virtuous person who is like that. I follow only according to your words; may it be well with you. Just as it rains heavily, a person with faith and learning prepares food and is satisfied. Thus, they approach the Buddha, the peerless caravan leader who has conquered the battlefield. In that same way, you too let go of (or develop) faith. The Venerable Gotama has thus clearly expounded the Dhamma through many methods. Thus is the one who knows through path-knowledge and has a developed mind. Just as great stone mountains stand touching the sky. Monks, just as a great tree, for example. Just as a great plow-head, for example. Just as a mahout tames an elephant in rut. Just as the wind blows away fallen cotton. It is just like the Venerable Gotama; it is just like the Blessed One.

The words aho and nāma occur in the sense of blame. Friends, our being wise is indeed blameworthy. Our being very learned is indeed blameworthy. Our mastery of the three Vedas is indeed blameworthy. Ānanda, do you remain indifferent when the elder monks are being harassed? (It is unbearable). Dear Raṭṭhapāla, do we still have wealth (or) do we still have life? (It is unbearable).

The words aho, nāma, and sādhu occur in the sense of praise. Wonderful is the Buddha! Wonderful is the Dhamma! Wonderful is the Saṅgha! Wonderful is the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma! Wonderful is the well-practiced nature of the Saṅgha! Indeed, wonderful is the perfection of our Teacher! The noble gift given to the Venerable Mahākassapa is a wonderful gift.
385:
(The noble gift of the essence of ambrosia) well-established (in the Venerable Mahākassapa) is a wonderful gift. Even a disciple will have such great psychic power and such great majesty. Sāriputta, well done, well done! Just as Ānanda answers (the Gosinga Sutta) correctly, so do you answer well.

The word "sādhu" occurs in the senses of requesting and accepting. "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One preach the Dhamma to me; having heard the Blessed One's Dhamma, I shall understand it," he requested. The Puṇṇaka Yakkha, having said "Very well," and being of great wealth, departed together with the wise Vidhura.

The word "aho" occurs in the sense of wishing. "It would be good indeed if they were to anoint me as king while I am living in the forest," he wished.

The words "ingha" and "handa" occur in the sense of urging or exhorting. "Come, Ānanda, bring me drinking water; Ānanda, I am very thirsty, I will drink," He said. "Monks, now I exhort you; conditioned things are subject to decay; strive with heedfulness (to fulfill the three trainings)," He said.

The word "evametaṃ" occurs in the sense of appropriate rejoicing. "Great King, it is so as you say; Great King, it is so as you say; Great King, it is so as you say; all beings are subject to death, and have death as their end," He said.

The word "kira" occurs in the sense of hearsay and in the sense of indicating displeasure. Of these two, in the sense of hearsay: Citta the householder heard, "It is said that Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta has arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa."

In the sense of indicating displeasure: Those objects such as forms, which do not come into range of the five doors because they exist for only a brief moment and are small objects, are called "dhammārammaṇa," it is said.

The word "nūna" occurs in the senses of inference, recollection, and reflection. "That Dhamma-Vinaya is surely not inferior; that monkhood is not inferior," he inferred.
386:
Thus in the sense of inference. "That mother elephant, who is without a son, lonely, blind, and without a leader, will surely strike against a tree stump with her foot," thus in the sense of recollection. "Should I approach that person and deprive him of life?" thus in the sense of reflection.

The word "kasmā" occurs in the sense of asking the reason. "Why does the Venerable Gotama, relying on the secluded forest, practice the practice here in this forest for the sake of attaining the supreme state?"

The words "yasmā", "tasmā", "tathāhi", and "tena" occur in the sense of determining the reason. "Monks, because form is non-self (not under control), therefore form leads to affliction." "Noble sons, for that reason, the Blessed One has been invited for tomorrow's meal together with the Saṅgha of monks." "Although my house was empty, there was a matter to enter; because there was such a reason to enter, I entered."

The word "dhīratthu" occurs in the sense of blame. "The hunter with the piercing arrow is blameworthy." "That vomited poison is blameworthy." In another tradition, the word "dhī" occurs in the sense of blame. "He blames the one who strikes an Arahant Brahmin."

The word "hā" occurs in distress and in showing the manner of that distress. "O Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī! O Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī!" thus in distress. "O Moon! O Moon!" thus in showing the manner of distress.

The word "tuṇhī" occurs in the sense of not speaking. "One should look on while remaining silent."

The word "သစ္ဆိ" (sacchi) occurs in the sense of witnessing (realizing). "He realized the fruit of Arahantship."

The words "duṭṭhu" and "ku" occur in the sense of being contemptible. "Vile (duṭṭhulla)." "A contemptible son (kuputta)."

The word "yathā" occurs in the senses of excellence, suitability, repetition, order, not exceeding the meaning of the word, and illustration. "Just as this King Nimi, being wise, desires merit excessively," thus in the sense of excellence. Because of that, "yathā ayaṃ" means "this King Nimi is exceedingly wise."
387:
The word 'yathā' occurs in the sense of 'excessive'. 'Yathā paṇḍito' means 'extremely wise'. In the sense of 'suitability' (yogga), meaning to bring forward appropriately, it occurs as 'yathānurūpaṃ'. It also occurs in the sense of 'repetition' (vicchā), as in 'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ', meaning according to those who are elder. In the sense of 'order' (paṭipāṭi), it occurs as 'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ', meaning according to the seniority of the elders. In the sense of 'not exceeding the meaning of the word' (padatthānativatti), it occurs as 'yathākkamaṃ'. An example where 'ko' is changed to 'ga' is 'yathā kulūpako'. Thus, it occurs in the sense of 'illustration' (nidassana).

The words 'sādhu' and 'suṭṭhu' occur in the senses of 'acceptance' (sampaṭicchana) and 'rejoicing' (anumodana). When saying, 'Excellent, venerable sir, I shall observe [the restraint],' 'sādhu' and 'suṭṭhu' are in the sense of acceptance. When saying, 'Well done by you, well done by you,' 'sādhu' and 'suṭṭhu' are in the sense of rejoicing.

The words 'saha', 'saddhiṃ', and 'amā' occur in the sense of 'simultaneous action' (samakriyā). There is the usage: 'King Vedeha will go through the tunnel together with (saha) his ministers.' Also, 'He will go together with (saddhiṃ) me.' The new moon day, when the sun and moon dwell together, is called 'amāvāsī' day, and that night is called 'amāvāsikā' night. Because one acts together in all matters, one is called an 'amacca' (minister).

The word 'saha' also occurs in the sense of 'endowment' (sampanna). In the statement, 'He shines being endowed with clothes,' it means this body shines only when endowed with clothes, not when naked. Here, the word 'saha' does not occur in the sense of simultaneous action, but only in the sense of endowment. It is like calling a field endowed with crops 'sakhetta'.

The words 'vinā', 'rite', and 'rahitā' occur in the sense of 'separation' (vippayoga). 'Apart from (vinā) the True Dhamma, there is no other refuge in the world.' 'Without (rite) the True Dhamma, where can there be happiness?' 'A son separated from (rahitā) his mother.'

The word 'aññatra' occurs in the sense of 'exclusion' (parivajjana). 'Excluding (aññatra) the arising of a Buddha, there is no realization of the Truths.'

The words 'nānā' and 'puthu' occur in the sense of 'various kinds' (bahuppakāra). 'Trees bearing various (nānā) fruits.' 'Many (puthu) recluses and brahmins subsist on whatever food [they receive].'

The word 'nānaṃ' occurs in the sense of 'dissimilarity' (asadisa). 'Only the consonant is different (nānaṃ).'

The words 'puthu' and 'visuṃ' occur in the sense of 'non-aggregation' (asaṅghāta). 'A person who is separate (puthu) from the Noble Ones,' or 'a person who is separate (visuṃ).'
388:
The particle 'kate' occurs in the sense of 'on account of' (paṭicca). In the sentence, 'O Sakka, may the mind or body of anyone never be afflicted on account of me (maṃ kate); O Sakka, I choose this boon,' 'maṃ kate' means on account of me, or because of me.

The particle 'manaṃ' occurs in the sense of a state that has not quite been reached (nearly/almost). 'Manaṃ vuḷho ahosi' means he was almost carried away (by the current), but not quite.

The particle 'nu' occurs in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), like the word 'eva'. 'Māradiṭṭhigataṃ nu te' means 'This view of yours is indeed the wrong view of Māra.' It also occurs in the sense of the word 'nāma'. 'Yaṃ nu gijjho yojanasataṃ, kuṇapāni avekkhati' means 'A vulture (nāma) can see carcasses from a distance of a hundred yojanas.'

The particles 'puna', 'puno', and 'punaṃ' occur in the sense of 'not for the first time' (again/further). 'Puna vadāmi' means 'I shall say it again.' 'Puno pi dhammaṃ desesi' means 'He taught again the Dhamma that shows the arising and passing away of the five aggregates.' 'Na puno amatākāraṃ, passissāmi mukhaṃ tava' means 'I shall not see again your face, which is the cause for the Deathless Nirvana.' 'Nāhaṃ punaṃ na ca punaṃ, na cāpi apunappunaṃ, hatthibondiṃ pavekkhāmi' means 'I shall not enter the elephant's carcass again, nor a second time, nor repeatedly.' Here, the letter 'a' in the word 'apunappunaṃ' is merely an expletive particle without meaning.

The particle 'punappunaṃ' occurs in the sense of 'repeatedly' (abhiṇha). 'Dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ' means 'Repeated birth (rebirth) is indeed suffering.'

The particles 'ciraṃ' and 'cirassaṃ' occur in the sense of 'a long time' (dīghakāla). 'Ciraṃ tvaṃ anutappissasi' means 'You will repent for a long time.' 'Ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭhanti' means 'They remain for a long time, for a long duration.' 'Cirassaṃ vata passāmi, brāhmaṇaṃ parinibbutaṃ' means 'Only after a long time do I see a brahmin (Arahant) who is fully extinguished.'

The particles 'ce' and 'yadi' occur in the sense of 'doubt' or 'conditionality' (saṅkāvatthāna). 'Mañce tvaṃ nikkhaṇaṃ vane' means 'If (ce) you were to bury me in the forest.' 'Yadimassa lokanāthassa, virajjhissāma sāsanaṃ' means 'If (yadi) we were to miss the dispensation of this Lord of the World.'

The particle 'dhuvaṃ' occurs in the senses of 'stability' (thira) and 'certainty' (ekaṃsa). In the phrase 'nicco dhuvo sassato', it occurs in the sense of stability. In the sentence 'dhuvaṃ buddho bhavāmahaṃ', it occurs in the sense of certainty, meaning 'I shall certainly become a Buddha.'

The particle 'su' occurs in the sense of 'speed' (sīgha). It is used in contexts such as eating or going quickly.

The particles 'sotthi' and 'suvatthi' occur in the sense of 'aspiration' (āsīsa). 'Sotthi hotu sabbasattānaṃ' means 'May all beings be free from danger and be happy.' 'Etena saccena suvatthi hotu' means 'By this truth, may there be well-being.' Here, some...
389:
“I see the well-being of beings,” and “I have arisen with well-being.” In this way, the word *sotthi* is seen to have two variations by way of the accusative (*upayoga*) and instrumental (*karaṇa*) cases without dropping the case endings. When these two variations of the word *sotthi* are seen, the word *suvatthi* is also seen to have two variations because it follows the same pattern.

If this is so, a question may arise: Should these not be included among the indeclinable particles (*nipāta*) because they contradict the statement: “That which is the same in the three genders, in all cases, and in all numbers, and does not change, is called *avyaya* (indeclinable)”? It is true; however, since they do not change in relation to the remaining cases, they should indeed be included among the indeclinable particles as *avyaya*. This method also applies to other similar instances.

The word *yadi* in some places carries the meaning of the word *vā* (or). For example: “Whichever assembly he approaches, whether an assembly of nobles (*khattiyaparisā*), or an assembly of brahmins (*brāhmaṇaparisā*), or an assembly of householders (*gahapatiparisā*),” and so on. Here, the meaning of “*yadi khattiyaparisā*” etc., should be taken as “or an assembly of nobles,” etc. If it is asked how the word *yadi* is known to have the meaning of *vā*, it is known because in some passages of the Pāḷi, the word *vā* occurs in conjunction with the word *yadi*, as in: “Whether this person’s word is true or (*vā yadi vā*) false,” and so on.

In the Dispensation, some words with the same meaning occur together. For example: “*Hatthī, kuñjaro, nāgo*” (all meaning elephant); and “Life is as short as a hundred years; it exists now (*idāni etarahi*)”; and “At that time (*tena samayena*) the Buddha, the Blessed One.” Thus, by considering the logic consistent with the Dispensation, the word *yadi* is known to have the meaning of *vā*. Otherwise, what would be the use of such logical consideration? Indeed, in the commentary on the *Vattha Sutta*, the teachers of the commentary explained the meaning of “*yadi nīlakāya... yadi pītakāya*” etc., as “or for the sake of a blue color,” etc...
390:
The commentators have explained the meaning; following that explanation, it should be understood with certainty that in phrases such as “*yadi khattiyaparisā*,” the word *yadi* also carries the alternative meaning of the word *vā*.

The particle *yadi* in some Pāḷi contexts also carries the meaning of the word *yadā* (when), in the sense of the locative of time (*kālasattami*). For example: “When (*yadi*) the children, Jālī and Kaṇhā, see the fruit-bearing trees in the great forest.”

The phrase *kismiṃ viya* is used in the sense of showing a shameful manner (*sajjanākāra*). For example: “To return home empty-handed is like something shameful (*kismiṃ viya*).” Here, *kismiṃ viya* means it is like a shameful manner, or like a defilement or suffering.
(Note: In *sajjanākāra*, I think it should be *lajjanākāra* (shameful manner), but I have kept it as it is in the Nīti.)

The particle *tu* is used in the sense of certainty (*ekamsa*). For example: “A wise enemy is better, but (*tu*) a friend devoid of wisdom is certainly not better.”

The word *yañce* is used in the sense of negation (*paṭisedha*). For example: “A wise enemy is better; the compassion of a fool is *yañce*—not better.” Also, “Sons who do not obey words are *yañce*—not better.” Also, “To live without you is *yañce*—not better.”

The suffix *dhā* is used in the sense of division (*vibhāga*). For example: *ekadhā* (one part), *dvidhā* (two parts), *tidhā* (three parts).

The suffix *kkhattuṃ* is used in the sense of times or frequency (*vāra*). For example: *ekakkhattuṃ* (once), *dvikkhattuṃ* (twice), *tikkhattuṃ* (thrice).

The particles *ve* and *handa* are used in the sense of relinquishment or exertion (*vavassagga*). For example: “Wherever people have faith, there they give freely (*ve*), according to their faith.” Also, “*Handa*—now I shall give up (the home) and depart.”

The word *kintu* is used in questioning a slight distinction (*appamattavisesapucchā*). For example: “How are the results? Is it a distinction (*nānākaraṇaṃ*)?”

The phrase *nanu ca* is used in absolute contradiction (*accantavirodha*). For example: “O Teacher, should it not be (*nanu ca*) that the meaning conforms to the grammatical order?”

The particle *pana* is used in the sense of highlighting a distinction (*visesajotana*) and as a verbal ornament (*vacanālaṅkāra*). In places like “In the commentary, however (*pana*), it is said,” and “In the sub-commentary, however (*pana*), it is said,” it is used to highlight a distinction. In a place like “Why, then (*pana*), was this said?” it is used as a verbal ornament.
391:
The word *itihi* is used in the sense of making a determination, meaning “just so.” “A wise man, established in virtue, developing the mind (concentration) and wisdom (insight), an ardent and sagacious bhikkhu (or person), he should disentangle this tangle (of craving).” Thus (*iti hi*) it was said. The words *hi* and *tathā hi* are used in the sense of strengthening or confirmation (*daḷhīkaraṇa*). It is said as “*vuttañhi*” (for it was indeed said) and “*tathā hi vuttaṃ*” (for so it was said).

The word *eva* is used in the sense of showing association and so on (*sapaṭiyogitā*). Thus:

How is the word *eva* that distinguishes the meaning of an object?
It excludes non-association (*ayoga*), association with another (*anyayoga*), and absolute association (*accantayoga*).
Its usages are stated in order, as it is joined with the qualifier (*visesana*), the qualified (*visesaniya*), and the verb (*kriyā*).

“The sun *only* (*eva*) dispels darkness” (qualifier), “The Buddha *alone* (*eva*) dispels darkness” (qualified), “The blue lotus *just* (*eva*) exists” (verb); these three phrases should be understood.

From here on, because they are very well known, I shall not mention the usages.

The word *kathañci* is used in the sense of difficulty.
The word *īsakaṃ* is used in the sense of a little.
The word *saṇikaṃ* is used in the sense of slow (feeble).

The words *khippaṃ, araṃ, lahuṃ, āsuṃ, tuṇṇāṃ, aciraṃ, tuvaṭaṃ* are used in the sense of speed.
The words *musā, micchā, alikaṃ* are used in the sense of untruth.

*Api ca kho, api tu khalu, yathānāma, tathānāma, yathāhi, tathāhi* are clusters of particles.
The word *yathā ca* is a cluster of particles (conjunction/*samuccaya*) in the sense of similarity.
392:
The suffixes *tuna*, *tvāna*, and *tvā* occur in the sense of effort (*ussukkana*). The sense of effort is indeed the sense of exertion (*ussāha*). That meaning which is not complete by a single word alone but expects the meaning of another word is called the sense of effort (*ussukkana*). For example, when "having seen" (*disvā*) is said, there must be a connection such as "he said thus" or "he did thus."

*Passituna*, *passitvāna*, *passitvā* (having seen); *suṇituna*, *suṇitvāna*, *suṇitvā* (having heard); *samphussa*, *samphusitvā* (having touched); *labhitvāna*, *labhitvā*, *laddhā*, *laddhāna* (having obtained); *viddhitvā*, *viddhitvāna*, *viddhā*, *viddhāna* (having shot/pierced); *bujjitvā*, *bujjitvāna*, *buddhā*, *buddhāna* (having known); *disvā*, *disvāna*, *diṭṭhā*, *diṭṭhāna* (having seen); *dassetvā* (having caused to see); *sāvetvā* (having caused to hear); *phusāpetvā* (having caused to touch); *labhāpetvā* (having caused to obtain); *vijjhāpetvā* (having caused to shoot); *bodhetvā* (having caused to know); *dattuna*, *datvā*, *datvāna* (having given); *dāpetvā* (having caused to give); *upādāya* (having clung); *viññāya* (having known); *viceyya* (having investigated); *vineyya* (having removed); *nihacca* (having oppressed); *samecca* (having realized); *ārabbha* (having begun/concerning); *āgamma* (having arrived); *āgaccha* (having come); *āpuccha* (having asked leave); *katvā*, *karitvā*, *kacca*, *adhikacca* (having done); *khādituna*, *khāditvāna*, *khāditvā*, *khādiya*, *khādiyāna* (having eaten/chewed); *parivisiya*, *parivisiyāna* (having served); *anubhaviya*, *anubhaviyāna* (having experienced); *abhivandituna*, *abhivanditvāna*, *abhivandiya*, *abhivandiyāna* (having paid homage). Other words should also be applied in this manner.

Among the eight particles (*nipāta*)—*ca*, *vā*, *na*, *no*, *amā*, *alaṃ*, and *halaṃ*—which occur in the senses of conjunction (*samuccaya*), distinction (*vikappa*), and negation (*paṭisedha*), the particle *amā* (*mā*) falls only at the beginning of a word; it does not fall in the middle or at the end of a word. This is as in "the unseen" (*adiṭṭhaṃ*), "the unheard" (*asutaṃ*), "do not boast" (*mā akatthā*), and so on.

The particles *ca* and *vā* fall at the end of a word and also in the middle of two coordinate terms; they do not fall at the beginning of a word. How is this so? *Samaṇo ca brāhmaṇo ca* (the ascetic and the brahmin); *samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā* (the ascetic or the brahmin); *eso ca samaṇo sādhurūpo* (this ascetic is also of good nature); *eso ca brāhmaဏo sādhurūpo* (this brahmin is also of good nature); *eso vā samaṇo saṅgahetabbo* (this ascetic should also be supported); *eso vā brāhmaṇo saṅgahetabbo* (this brahmin should also be supported).

Venerable Sir, is it not the case that the word *vā* is seen at the beginning of a word in rules such as "*vā paro asarūpā*" and "*vā ṇappacce*"? It is true; however, such a specific grammatical arrangement is established in the *Akkharasamaya* treatise by adopting the views of grammarians.
393:
...placed at the beginning. In truth, such a grammatical trend does not exist in the Magadhi language or the Sanskrit language. Therefore, in our view, the rule "*paro vā asarūpā*" is established in accordance with the Magadhi language. Even so, if one says, "Venerable Sir, the word *vā* is also seen at the beginning of a word; for in the word '*vānara*', it is found as '*vānara*' because it is like a man (*narena sadiso*)," that is not so. The word *vā* expressing the sense of similarity stands only at the end of a word, as in "*madhuṃ vā maññati bālo*" (the fool thinks it is like honey).

Furthermore, this word "*vānara*" is not an *avyayībhāva* compound preceded by the sense of a particle, like the word "*nimmakkhikaṃ*." Therefore, without entering the wrong path, jumping and running is called "*vāna*"; because of having that "*vāna*," it is called "*vānara*." It should be understood in the same sense as "*kuñjā hanu assatthīti kuñjaro*" (it is called *kuñjaro* because it has a small jaw). Thus, they are called particles (*nipāta*) because they fall (*nipata-*) at the beginning, middle, and end of words as appropriate. These include *ca*, *vā*, etc., as well as *atha*, *khalu*, *vata*, etc. Words such as *katvā* and *vatvā*, being indeclinable (*avyaya*) and included among the particles, are also called particles.

The particles *na* and *no* fall at the beginning and at the end of a word; they do not fall in the middle of a word. How is this so? *Na ve anatthakusalena* (it is certainly not good for one skilled in what is harmful); *atthacariyā sukhāvahā* (the practice of welfare brings happiness); *no hetaṃ bhante* (it is not so, Venerable Sir); *pamatto puriso puññakammaṃ karoti na* (a negligent man does not perform meritorious deeds); *evampi me no* (even so, it is not for me), and so on.

The particles *alaṃ* and *halaṃ* fall at the beginning and at the end of a word; they do not fall in the middle of a word. *Alaṃ puññāni kātuṃ* (it is fit to do meritorious deeds), or *puññāni kātuṃ alaṃ*; *halaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ* (it is not fit to reveal now), or *pakāsituṃ halaṃ*.

In this treatise, in accordance with the Commentaries, the word *pi* should also be desired among the particles. The word *api* should also be included in the class of particles when it does not occur before a word expressing action (verb). How is this so? *Api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati* (even in heavenly sensual pleasures, he finds no delight); *rājāpi* (the king also); *devopi* (the deity also); *itipi so bhagavā* (thus indeed is that Blessed One), and so on. Among those words, the word *pi* falls in the middle and at the end of a word. The word *api*, however, falls at the beginning, middle, and end of a word.
394:
It may also fall at the end of a word. He stands, he sits, he walks, he lies down, and he also disappears in between. In filling out a sentence, particles such as *atha*, *khalu*, *vata*, and so on, should be applied as appropriate.

Now, I shall extract the meanings of those particles as appropriate. Among those particles, the word '*evaṃ*' has many different meanings such as comparison, instruction, approbation, reproach, acceptance of a word, manner, illustration, and determination.

Indeed, this word '*evaṃ*' occurs in the sense of comparison (*upamā*) in such passages as: "Just as (one might make many garlands), so a mortal, once born, should perform much merit."

It occurs in the sense of instruction (*upadesa*) in such passages as: "Thus you should advance; thus you should retreat."

It occurs in the sense of approbation (*sampahaṃsana*) in such passages as: "It is so, O Blessed One; it is so, O Sugata."

It occurs in the sense of reproach (*garahaṇa*) in such passages as: "This low woman praises the virtues of that shaven-headed ascetic in such a way, wherever she may be."

It occurs in the sense of acceptance of a word (*vacanasampaṭiggaha*) in such passages as: "'Yes, Bhante,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One."

It occurs in the sense of manner (*ākāra*) in such passages as: "Bhante, in this manner I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One."

It occurs in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*) in such passages as: "Go, young man, to the ascetic Ānanda; having approached him, in my name, ask the venerable Ānanda whether he is free from illness, free from affliction, active, strong, and living at ease. Say, 'The young man Subha, son of the brahmin Todeyya, asks the venerable Ānanda whether he is free from illness... and so on.' And say this: 'It would be good if the venerable Ānanda would come to the house of the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, out of compassion.'"

It occurs in the sense of determination (*avadhāraṇa*) in such passages as: "What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome? They are unwholesome, Bhante. Are they blameworthy or blameless? They are blameworthy, Bhante. Are they censured by the wise..."
395:
"...or praised by the wise?" When asked, they replied, "Bhante, they are censured by the wise. When these things are fully undertaken and observed, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? How does it appear to you in this case?" They replied, "Bhante, when these things are fully undertaken and observed, they lead to harm and suffering; it is just so that we view it in this case." In such passages from the Aṅguttara Nikāya and others, the word '*evaṃ*' is used in the sense of determination (*avadhāraṇa*). Thus:

In comparison, in instruction, in manner, in approbation,
In acceptance of a word, in reproach, in illustration,
In determination and so forth, the word '*evaṃ*' occurs.

Among those particles, the word '*antarā*' occurs in the senses of cause, moment, mind, interval, opening, and so on. The word '*antarā*' is used in the sense of cause (*kāraṇa*) in such passages as: "Who but the Tathāgatas would know that cause?" and "People meet and whisper; they do not know what the cause is regarding me and you."

It occurs in the sense of a moment (*khaṇa*) in such passages as: "Bhante, a certain woman washing pots saw me in a flash of lightning."

It occurs in the sense of the mind (*citta*) in such passages as: "Within whose mind (internal) anger does not exist."

It occurs in the sense of an interval (*vemajjha*) in such passages as: "He reached the end in the interval (before reaching the fruit of Arahantship)."

It occurs in the sense of an opening or gap (*vivara*) in such passages as: "This Tapodā river flows through the gap between two great hells." In other places, the sense of 'middle' or 'interval' is intended. Thus:

In cause and in mind, in a moment and in an opening,
In meanings such as interval, the sound '*antarā*' is established.

Among those particles, the word '*ajjhatta*' is seen in four senses: *gocarajjhatta* (the object of meditation such as a kasina), *niyakajjhatta* (one's own internal aggregates), *ajjhattajjhatta* (the six internal sense bases), and *visayajjhatta* (the attainment of fruition).
396:
“Ānanda, that monk should establish the mind internally in that same previous sign of concentration.” In this sentence and in sentences such as “Delighting internally, with a concentrated mind,” this word *ajjhatta* is evident in the sense of *gocarajjhatta* (internal as an object). In sentences such as “Internal clarity” and “He dwells contemplating the Dhamma in the Dhammas internally,” it is evident in the sense of *niyakajjhatta* (internal as one's own). In sentences such as “The six internal sense bases,” it is evident in the sense of *ajjhattajjhatta* (the truly internal). In sentences such as “Ānanda, this dwelling has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely, dwelling by entering the internal emptiness due to the non-attention to all signs,” it is evident in the sense of *visayajjhatta*, meaning in the place of sovereignty. Indeed, the attainment of fruition is called the place of sovereignty for the Buddhas. Thus, the analysis of the indeclinables is completed.

If a person desires great proficiency in the Pariyatti Dhamma, which has a vast essence of meaning, is analyzed in many ways, and is adorned with the four types of words included in the speech;
That person should constantly and repeatedly apply effort; by applying effort with great proficiency, that person can attain [that Pariyatti Dhamma].

## Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, called the Analysis of Words Included in Speech (Vācogadhapadavibhatti), in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the ways of the three Piṭakas together with the Commentaries, which have nine factors.

## 9. Compendium of the Methods of Pali, etc.

I shall hereafter describe the compendium of the methods of Pali, etc., which expands wisdom and increases joy and gladness.

In that compendium of the methods of Pali, etc., four methods are intended: the Pali method, the Commentary method, the Sub-commentary method, and the Other treatises method. Among them, the Pali method is the way of the Pali in the Word of the Buddha within the three Piṭakas. The Commentary method is the way of the words appearing in the Commentaries. The Sub-commentary method is...
397:
...the way of the words appearing in the Sub-commentaries. The Other treatises method is the way of the words appearing in other treatises besides the Pali, Commentaries, and Sub-commentaries. Among those ways of words, I shall present a summary of the Pali method, etc., by taking the sixfold phrasing (byañjanachakka) and the sixfold meaning (atthachakka) as primary in the way of the Pali, along with the appropriate conclusions on the way of the words occurring in the Commentaries, Sub-commentaries, and so forth.

Among those sixfold phrasings, etc., there are six components of phrasing (byañjanapada): syllable (akkharā), word (pada), phrasing (byañjana), mode (ākāra), linguistic analysis (nirutti), and exposition (niddesa). There are six components of meaning (atthapada): explanation (saṅkāsanā), illumination (pakāsanā), opening up (vivaraṇa), analysis (vibhajana), making clear (uttānīkaraṇa), and description (paññatti). These six beginning with akkharā and the six beginning with saṅkāsanā are also called the sixfold phrasing and the sixfold meaning.

Among those, regarding the phrasing-words, a syllable (akkharā) is to be taken here as an individual letter included within a word that expresses meaning, according to the statement: “One who is taught ‘Form is impermanent’ recites ‘Ru’ in unison.” Alternatively, a single-letter word that expresses meaning, like the letter ‘Yo’ in the verse ‘Yo pubbe...’, is to be taken here as a syllable. Also, an individual letter in an incomplete word, like the initial letter ‘Sa’ uttered by a denizen of hell who intended to say ‘Saṭṭhivassa sahassāni’, is to be taken as a syllable.

By the method taught in this Dhammapada verse: “One who is free from craving, without clinging, skilled in linguistic analysis and words, should know the combination of syllables and their sequence,” a collection of syllables ending in an inflection (vibhatti) that expresses meaning is called a word (pada). It is like the word ‘Sīle’ in the phrase ‘Sīle patiṭṭhāya’. A collection of words ending in a demonstration of the connection of meaning is called phrasing (byañjana), like “Cattārome bhikkhave satipaṭṭhānā.” The manner of analyzing the phrasing is called mode (ākāra), like “Monks, what are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body...” and so forth. The derivation of a word demonstrated by the mode is called linguistic analysis (nirutti), like “It is contact (phassa) because it touches; it is feeling (vedanā) because it feels.” The exhaustive and detailed explanation of the derived meaning is called exposition (niddesa), like “Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; it is pleasant (sukha) because it causes ease, it is painful (dukkha) because it causes suffering, it is neither-painful-nor-pleasant because it causes neither suffering nor ease.” These six are called the components of phrasing (byañjanapada).
398:
Exposition (Niddesa) is the complete and detailed explanation of the grammatical analysis, such as: "Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling [Abhi-1, 1]. It is called pleasant (sukha) because it causes pleasure. It is called painful (dukkha) because it causes pain. It is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant (adukkhamasukha) because it causes neither pain nor pleasure" [Abhi-a 1, 84], and so forth. These (syllable, word, phrasing, manner, terminology, exposition) are the six aspects of phrasing (byañjanapada).

Among the aspects of meaning, showing briefly is called Indication (Saṅkāsana). Here, "showing" (kāsanā) means illuminating (dīpanā); it means illuminating the meaning in brief. For example: "Monks, one who clings is bound by Māra; one who does not cling is free from the Evil One" [Saṃ-2, 61], and so forth.

Showing first is called Manifestation (Pakāsana). It means illuminating the entire meaning to be spoken later by the very first statement. For example: "Monks, all is burning" [Saṃ-2, 251; Vi-3, 44], and so forth.

Opening up and making clear the detail of the meaning shown through Indication and Manifestation by means of a sequence of words is called Explanation (Vivaraṇa). For example: "Monks, one who clings to form is bound by Māra; one who does not cling is free from the Evil One" [Saṃ-2, 61], and so forth; or "And what, monks, is the all that is burning? The eye, monks, is burning; forms are burning" [Saṃ-2, 251; Vi-3, 44], and so forth.

Making the very meaning that has been opened up appear before the intellect through many aspects is called Classification (Vibhajana). For example: "And what, monks, is form? The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements" [Saṃ-2, 48], and so forth; or "With what is it burning? It is burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion; with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair" [Saṃ-2, 251; Vi-3, 44], and so forth.

Accomplishing the classified meaning by expanding it and by providing similes and successive explanations is called Clarification (Uttānīkaraṇa). In that (form)...
399:
What are the four great elements? The earth element, the water element, and so forth.

Monks, suppose there were a river flowing down from a mountain, carrying everything along, traveling far, with a swift current. On both banks of that river, kāsa grass might grow, and it would hang over and cover the river. Kusa grass might also grow, and it would cover the river. Pabbaja grass might also grow, and it would cover the river. Bīraṇa grass might also grow, and it would cover the river. Weak trees such as castor-oil plants might also grow, and they would cover the river. A man being carried away by the current of that river might grasp the kāsa grass, but it would break off and come away with its roots, and he would come to ruin and destruction because of that breaking of the kāsa grass. He might grasp the kusa grass, or the pabbaja grass, or the bīraṇa grass, or the weak trees, but they would break off and come away, and he would come to ruin and destruction because of that breaking of the plants.

In the same way, monks, an uninstructed worldling who has no regard for the noble ones, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who is undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has no regard for true men, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of true men, who is undisciplined in the Dhamma of true men, regards form as self (like the light and the flame), or self as possessing form (like a tree and its shadow), or form as in self (like a scent in a flower), or self as in form (like a ruby in a casket). For him, that form disintegrates, and he comes to ruin and destruction because of that disintegration of form. He regards feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as self (like the light and the flame), or self as possessing consciousness (like a tree and its shadow), or consciousness as in self (like a scent in a flower), or self as in consciousness (like a ruby in a casket). For him, that consciousness disintegrates, and he comes to ruin and destruction because of that disintegration of consciousness, and so forth.

Making known in various ways is called Description (Paññatti). It means making the meaning known by causing delight in the listeners through various ways and by making the intellect sharp. For example: "Rāhula, whatever form there is, whether internal form belonging to oneself, or various..."
400:
Making known in various ways is called Paññatti (designation). It means making the meaning known by causing delight to the listeners in many ways and by sharpening their wisdom.

"Rāhula, whatever form (rūpa) there is—whether internal, belonging to oneself, hard, harsh, and clung to (by craving, conceit, and views)—what is it? It is: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, gorge, dung. Furthermore, Rāhula, whatever other form there is—whether internal, belonging to oneself, hard, harsh, and clung to—this is called the internal earth element (pathavīdhātu). Both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element. This should be seen as it actually is with correct insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with correct insight wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and detaches the mind from the earth element," as stated in such passages.

And as stated in such passages as: "Among those forms, what is past form? Whatever form has passed, ceased, changed, disappeared, vanished, and having arisen has passed away; what is past and is counted as belonging to the past. The four great essentials (mahābhūta) and the derived form (upādārūpa) dependent on the four great essentials—this is called past form. Among those forms, what is future form? Whatever form is not yet born, not yet become, not yet produced, not yet arisen, not yet manifested, not yet appeared, not yet arisen, not yet well-arisen, not yet stood up, not yet well-risen; what is future and is counted as belonging to the future. The four great essentials and the derived form—this is called future form. Among those forms, what is present form? Whatever form is being born, becoming, being produced, arising, manifesting, appearing, reaching the three sub-moments, being well-arisen, standing up; what is present and is counted as belonging to the present."
401:
"The four great essentials and the derived form dependent on the four great essentials—this is called present form," and so forth. These are the six terms of meaning (atthapada).

Among those terms of meaning, the Blessed One indicates briefly by letters (akkhara), displays first by words (pada), opens up by phrasing (byañjana), analyzes by aspects (ākāra), makes clear by definitions (nirutti), and designates by descriptions (niddesa). Or else, having indicated briefly by letters, He displays by words; having opened up by phrasing, He analyzes by aspects; having made clear by definitions, He designates by descriptions. Or else, having opened the door of meaning by letters and displaying by words, He disciplines the person of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū); having opened up by phrasing and analyzing by aspects, He disciplines the person who understands through expansion (vipañcitaññū); having made clear by definitions and designating by descriptions, He disciplines the person who needs guidance (neyya). The meaning is that He develops the respective teachings by considering what is appropriate for the place, time, and those to be led, and by the power of the inclinations, latent tendencies, characters, and dispositions of those beings to be led.

In terms of meaning, what is the sixfold phrasing (byañjanachakka) and what is the sixfold meaning (atthachakka)? The vocal sound together with its communication (viññatti), which is the cause for understanding the meaning when the Buddha, the Blessed One, is teaching the Dhamma, is called the sixfold phrasing. The Dhamma together with its characteristics (lakkhaṇa), functions (rasa), etc., which is to be realized through that sound, is called the sixfold meaning.

Thus:
Letters, words, and phrasing,
Aspects, definitions, and descriptions—these six
Are called the sixfold phrasing
By the wise who know the meaning of phrasing.

Brief indication, display, opening up,
Analysis, making clear,
And designation—these six
Are called the sixfold meaning.

Therein, the sixfold phrasing is called the phrasing-term (byañjanapada),
And the sixfold meaning is called the meaning-term (atthapada);
Thus it should also be noted.
402:
The distinction in this matter is as follows: In the sixfold phrasing (byañjanachakka), a letter (akkhara) refers to each individual character such as "rū" which is included within a word that clarifies the meaning, as in "rūpaṃ aniccaṃ" and so forth; or a single character that clarifies the meaning such as the characters "yo" and "so" in "yo pubbe karaṇīyāni, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ" and so forth; or characters such as "sa" uttered by those who wish to speak each verse, as in "saṭṭhivassasahassāni" and so forth—all these should be taken as "akkhara".

In the view of the grammarians (akkharacintaka), however, in the scope of the designation of letters, the vowels starting with 'a' and the consonants starting with 'ka' should be taken as "akkhara". In the scope of the designation made by the general public, in such passages as "the letter (name) Mahāsammata first arose," a collection of characters that forms a word and clarifies the meaning should be taken as "akkhara". In the Jātaka Commentary also, in the explanation of the passage "kiṃ te'ttha catumaṭṭhassa," it is said that the phrasing (byañjana) of this Pali portion is beautiful, but the meaning of the letter (the meaning of 'fox') is not beautiful; thus, even a collection of characters that forms a word and clarifies the meaning should be understood as being called by the names "byañjana" and "akkhara".

Similarly, in the sixfold phrasing, a word (pada) should be taken as a group of letters that ends in an inflection (vibhatti) and clarifies the meaning, like the word "sīle" in the phrase "sīle patiṭṭhāya". In the view of the etymologists (neruttika), however, a collection of letters that clarifies the meaning, whether ending in an inflection or not, as well as a single letter of that nature, prefixes (upasagga), and particles (nipāta), should all be taken as "pada".

Similarly, in the sixfold phrasing, phrasing (byañjana) should be taken as a collection of words that ends in a teaching connected with a meaning, as in "cattārome bhikkhave satipaṭṭhānā" and so forth. In the view of the grammarians, however, in the scope of the designation of consonants, each individual character starting with 'ka' that is devoid of pure vowels starting with 'a' and is without a vowel should be taken as "byañjana". Similarly, in the view of the teachers who are experts in the Pali Canon and know the True Dhamma...
403: "The sithila (relaxed) letter, the dhanita (aspirated) letter, the dīgha (long) letter, the rassa (short) letter, the garu (heavy) letter, the lahu (light) letter, the niggahita (nasalized) letter, the sambandha (connected) letter, the vavatthita (distinct) letter, and the vimutta (released from nasalization) letter—the classification of consonants is tenfold according to the knowledge of sound." In this context, the group letters starting with 'ka' along with vowels, the characters starting with 'a' which are vowels, conjunct syllables, non-conjunct syllables, non-group letters, the bindu (dot), the joining of words, the separation of words, and the virāma word uttered with a released effort—all these should be understood as 'vyañjana' (consonant/expression). Similarly, in the sixfold group of consonants, the etymological derivation (nibbacana) such as "it is called phassa (contact) because it touches" is known as 'nirutti'. It is also preached thus: "Monks, they construct, therefore they are called saṅkhāra (formations)." The sound (abhilāpa) that is uttered with its cause by extracting such a derived word (nipphanna) is called 'nirutti'. In the Nirutti-piṭaka, however, the nature of things (dhamma-jāti) expressed by these ten terms—saṅkhā, samaññā, paññatti, vohāra, nāma, nāmakamma, nāmadheyya, nirutti, vyañjana, and abhilāpa—is called 'nirutti'. In its essence, that nirutti is simply the sound (cittaja-sadda) accompanied by intimation (viññatti). In the view of some teachers who comment on the lineage of the Commentaries, in the sixfold group of meanings, nāma-paññatti (designation of names) and upādā-paññatti (derivative designation) are called 'paññatti'. It should be understood as the manifestation of meaning by causing delight to listeners through various methods and by sharpening the intellect. In the Paññatti-duka, however, the nature of things expressed by the ten names already mentioned, such as "saṅkhā, samaññā," etc., is called 'paññatti'. That paññatti also, in its essence, is simply every sound accompanied by intimation. In the view of some teachers who comment on the lineage of the Commentaries, it should be understood as nāma-paññatti and upādā-paññatti. Knowing this definition, I have explained it here. A wise person should apply usage (vohāra) well, and not incorrectly (carelessly).
404: A wise person, desiring proficiency in all aspects of the sixfold group of consonants and the sixfold group of meanings, should keep this Nīti (guide) in mind. That proficiency (kosalla) is of sixteen types by way of classification. How? They are: skill in grammar (sadda), skill in letters (akkhara), skill in collection (samuccaya), skill in gender (liṅga), skill in inflection (vibhatti), skill in sequence (pubbāpara), skill in euphonic combination (sandhi), skill in compounds (samāsa), skill in expansion (byāsa), skill in etymology (nibbacana), skill in increase (āya), skill in decrease (apāya), skill in substitution (ādesa), skill in learning (gahana), skill in retention (dhāraṇa), and skill in accomplishment (sappaṭipādana). In the Pali Canon, however, five types of proficiency are mentioned according to the person endowed with them. How? Skill in meaning (attha-kusala), skill in the text (dhamma-kusala), skill in language (nirutti-kusala), skill in phrasing (vyañjana-kusala), and skill in sequence (pubbāpara-kusala). Among those five, one who is proficient in the Commentaries is called 'attha-kusala'. One who is proficient in the Pali Canon is called 'dhamma-kusala'. One who is proficient in etymological statements is called 'nirutti-kusala'. One who is proficient in the classification of letters is called 'vyañjana-kusala'. Thus, one who desires these five types of proficiency—attha-kusalatā, dhamma-kusalatā, nirutti-kusalatā, vyañjana-kusalatā, and pubbāpara-kusalatā—should also keep this Nīti in mind. Now, listen to the Nīti which is based on the Pali methods and the like, which is like a pair of scales in the Buddha's Dispensation, which brings benefit to the monks who bear the scriptures within the Dispensation, which increases joy and gladness, and which brings about the abundance of mindfulness and wisdom. The word 'eva' (only/certainly) found in the first phrase should also be applied to the second phrase and others where appropriate. For example: "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, quite secluded from unwholesome states," "Only in this teaching is there a recluse (Sotāpanna), here the second, here the third, here the fourth," and so on. In the context of the masculine gender, when the meaning 'identical' is intended, the word 'ekā' should be used. Thus it is seen in the Pali: "Let both the Pañcāla king and the Videha king be as one (ekā)." Here, 'ekā bhavantu' means...
405: ...let them be identical, just as the water of the Ganges merges with the water of the Yamunā. Similarly, in the masculine context, when the meaning 'identical' is intended, if one says 'eke' instead of 'ekā', it would mean 'some people', and thus the meaning would be ruined. When a man speaks a simile, placing himself in the position of the object of comparison, the simile should be expressed in the masculine gender. Thus it is seen in the Pali: "Like a bull elephant (nāga) having broken its bonds, I dwell without taints (anāsava)." When a woman speaks a simile, placing herself in the position of the object of comparison, the simile should generally be expressed in the feminine gender. Thus it is seen in the Pali: "Like a cow elephant (nāgī) having broken its bonds, I dwell without taints," and, "Those who have bathed and have beautiful skin, though they are widows, they consider themselves fortunate; they forcibly drag away one who does not desire them, just as crows (vāyasa) surround an owl (ulūka)," and, "Just as a forest cow elephant follows the forest bull elephant as he wanders through mountain gorges, level ground, and uneven ground, so too I shall follow you, taking our sons behind. I shall be one easy for you to support, I shall not be one difficult for you to support." Why is it said 'generally'? Because of instances like: "I shall serve my husband and sons day and night, being diligent, with matted hair and living the holy life, just as a young student (māṇava) serves his teacher (ācariya)." (In this case, a feminine simile is not used). When one considers only the feminine gender status without regarding the nature of the meaning, and looks for gender agreement, the simile is expressed in the feminine gender. As in this verse from the Saccasaṅkhepa: "As long as the shore is not seen in the middle of the ocean, the sea-bird (sāmuddasakuṇī) [remains on the mast]; so too the mind remains fixed on the characteristics of the faults [of formations] as long as it does not see the shore [of Nibbāna]."
406:
Without regarding the feminine gender, a metaphor is stated in the masculine gender by looking only at the nature of the meaning.

"For one who has well-discerned formations and well-investigated the three characteristics, while he remains equanimous, insight reaches its peak. It proceeds for as long as it takes to focus on the nature of formations, just like a shore-sighting bird [circles] as long as it does not see the other shore."

This is as found in the verse from the Paramatthavinicchaya.

Because meanings shown in the masculine gender are the meanings of feminine words, in some places, those meanings are indicated in the feminine gender. As in the following sentences: "Visākhā, in this world, a woman is one who has well-arranged work, has well-supported attendants, conducts herself to the liking of her husband, and protects the wealth accumulated." What is meant by "in some places"? It is like the instance: "Mallikā, in this world, some woman is prone to anger."

Because meanings shown in the neuter gender are the meanings of masculine words, those meanings are indicated in the masculine gender. This is as in the instance: "Five hundred Paccekabuddhas have lived for a long time on this Isigili mountain," and also as in: "That counselor-gem of the Wheel-turning Monarch admits those known and excludes those unknown."

For men who should be indicated in the masculine gender, by looking only at the gender, they are indicated in both masculine and feminine genders.

"Yakkha, you are one who desires my benefit. Devatā, you are one who desires my welfare. I shall follow your word; you are my teacher."

This is as in this instance.

From the three genders, by way of being in the same grammatical relation with those three genders, the term "seyyo" (better/noble) is generally used for indication.
407:
"An enemy endowed with wisdom is better," "This worship alone is better," "Living for even a single day is better," and so on. Why is it said "generally" (yebhuyyena)? Because it is said: "O Lord of men, even some woman is better (therefore, cherish her)."

Where "pānīya" should be said, there is the reading "pānī". As in: "The water drunk by them is like extremely hot chaff." Where "khattiyā" etc. should be said, the indication is "khatyā" etc. As in: "At that time, a hundred warriors..."; "Thus the sectarians speak diversely"; "And the blossomed lotuses"; "I desire to be free from affection," and so on. Where "disvā" should be said, the indication is "diṭṭhā". As in: "I have seen Ummādantī."

Some words are verbs in some places and nouns in others. "The attendants associated with me existed; they gave me flowers then." "This suffering is not [true] suffering; that suffering is [true] suffering." "He who goes does not return." "Desiring to discipline my son, I shall go," and so on. In these examples, "aduṃ" means "adaṃsu" (they gave). Again, "aduṃ" means "taṃ" (that).

There are words with unelided case endings and words with elided case endings. For example, the word "manasikāro". It is called "manasikāro" without eliding the case ending, as in "manasmiṃ kāro" (making in the mind). It is also called "manasikāro" because it produces a cognitive process (vīthi) that is distinct from the preceding life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

There are words that end in the singular and not in the plural. "That Bhāradvāja goes," "is great," "practices," and so on.

There are words that end in the plural and not in the singular. As in "Venerable ones (āyasmanto)," "The two venerable ones (āyasmantā)."

Some words are singular in some places and plural in others. "The angry worldling kills." "Crying out, they kill with sharp weapons."
408:
Among those sons, [they kill] the fat and the best. Knowing and seeing, I dwell. The one who knows tells the one who does not know. "O venerable ones, do you dwell knowing and seeing?" In this case, it should be understood as vacanavipallāsa (reversal of number).

In some contexts of meaning, a word may end in the singular; in other contexts, it may end in the plural. "This person comes, prospering with various successes." "This king, being the lord, delights in successes." "May these venerable ones come." "He is peaceful, tamed, certain, and a practitioner of the holy life." "In the world, virtuous people are manifest."

Some words may end in the plural in prose (cuṇṇiya), but when reaching a verse (gāthā), they may end in the singular in some places. "Kings are indeed wise."
"At that time, I was a Naga king of great power, named Atula, meritorious and possessing splendor,"
and so on. Why is it said "in some places"? Because in places like "possessing power, possessing splendor, possessing beauty, possessing fame," [the plural is maintained even in verse].

This method should be understood by the wise even in places not yet mentioned. Although stated briefly, it can be understood by the discerning. If one says "whatever much wealth" or "whatever various wealth" in the singular, and then says "those riches" [in the plural], there is no fault. Likewise, if one says "whatever great multitude (mahājana)" and then says "that great multitude (mahājanatā)" or "those people (te janā)", or if one says "whatever group of people (janatā)" and then says "those people (te janā)", there is no fault. Here, we shall state a small portion of the Pali text:

"Unfortunate people strive and accumulate whatever much wealth. Whether one is skilled or unskilled, the fortunate one enjoys those riches."
409:
In verse lines (gāthā-pāda), a line with extra syllables is not to be criticized when it is associated with terms such as *ariya*, *araha*, *cariya*, and so on. For instance:

"The practice that burns away defilements and the holy life,
Seeing the Four Noble Truths,
The realization of Nibbāna,
These four things are the highest blessing."

"O Prince Temiya, who has been entreated, it is fitting for you to follow these words of mine, Sunanda," and so forth.

Venerable Sir, in the context of the Pāḷi Canon, is it not true that a verse line with extra syllables is beyond reproach in every way? If so, why is this stated? In the Canon, lines such as "*Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ*" and "What evil have these beings done, those people who experience such intense, harsh, and bitter suffering?" and so on, even with many extra syllables, are not to be criticized but are indeed worthy of honor.

True, but this statement is made with reference to the poetic convention (*kavisamaya*) regarding verse lines composed by teachers within the Dispensation (*sāsanika*). Thus, in poetic convention, a verse line with extra syllables composed by teachers within the Dispensation, when associated with terms like *ariya* and so on, is not to be criticized but is indeed worthy of honor. For example: "I bow my head to that Noble Saṅgha, which is the field for virtuous people who desire merit," and so forth.

When a verse line is not complete with words such as "*nāgarukkho*" or "*sīhahanuttama-labhī*," those syllables are discarded and other extra syllables are added for the sake of verbal ornamentation (*vacanālaṅkāra*). For example: "Trees named after elephants (*vāraṇavhayanā rukkhā*)" and "He obtained the great mark of the lion-like jaw (*sīhahanu*)."

In some places, another specific name is inserted for the sake of verbal ornamentation. "*Jalajuttaranāmino*" means "*Padumuttaranāmino*" (the Buddha Padumuttara).

It should be understood that a name well-known from a previous mention, when spoken in a general sense, refers to a specific instance. For example: The Elder Tissadatta, who was wise and confident in the Vinaya, and his disciple, the Elder Sumana, who was of great wisdom and well-known by the name Sumana. Here, the name of that Elder Sumana was mentioned in a previous verse. That name mentioned previously should be taken. That name Sumana, like the name of Princess Sumanā, is a metaphorical application to a person based on the name of the jasmine flower (*sumana-puppha*). Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "*Pupphanāmo'ti vissuto*" (Known by the name of a flower).

It should be understood that although certain meanings are numerous and should be expressed in the plural, they are often referred to in the singular because they are identical in essence. For example: The very qualities that are superior and distinct from the Sutta texts are the meaning. The meaning of the superior and distinct qualities... kamma...
410:
"The Elder Tissadatta, wise
And confident in the Vinaya;
His disciple of great wisdom,
Known by the name of a flower."

In this context, the name of that Elder Sumana was previously mentioned as 'Sumana'; that name should be understood as the name of the Elder mentioned in the previous verse. That name Sumana is a metaphorical application to a person based on the name of the jasmine flower, just as the name 'Sumanā' was given to the daughter of King Kosala because it rained jasmine flowers at the time of her birth. It is not a metaphorical application to a person based on a name of the mind (*citta*), but rather based on the name of the jasmine flower. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: '*Pupphanāmo'ti vissuto*' (Known by the name of a flower).

It should be understood that although certain meanings are numerous and should be expressed in the plural, they are often expressed in the singular because they are identical in essence. For example, the term '*dhammātirekadhammavisesattho*', where the meaning is the very qualities that are superior and distinct from the Sutta texts. Excluding the *kamma-paccaya* (kamma condition), in the remaining twenty-three conditions, many phenomena constitute each single condition. "All humans became food for the ogre," and so forth. Why is it said 'mostly'? Because in the phrase '*paccayā honti*', the singular is not used.

It should be understood that although a noun exists in one gender (*liṅga*), when referring to persons and so on, it may take another gender different from its original one. For example: The Buddha named Paduma (masc.), the woman named Padumā (fem.), the hell named Paduma (masc./neut.), the householder named Citta (masc.), the woman named Cittā (fem.), and so forth.

There are words that can be called 'compound words' (*samāsa-pada*) and 'non-compound words' (*asamāsa-pada*). For example: Seeing the Teacher (*satthudassanaṃ*), the Dispensation of the Teacher (*satthusāsanaṃ*), the indication of the agent (*kattuniddeso*), the winning of both benefits (*ubhayatthakaṭaggāho*), and so forth. Among these, *ubhayatthakaṭaggāho* refers to both the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life.
411:
Both benefits are called 'ubhayattha'. Taking the win of those two benefits is called 'ubhayatthakaṭaggāha'; in this way, it is a compound word (samāsapada). In this context, the word 'ubhaya', like the word 'ubho', only ends in the plural; it never ends in the singular. Taking the win in two places is called 'ubhayatthakaṭaggāha'; in this way, it is a non-compound word (asamāsapada). This same method applies to words such as 'ubhayatthakaliggāho'.

There are words that are exclusively compound words and never non-compound words. What are they? They are words such as: 'satthāradassanaṃ' (seeing the Teacher), 'kattāraniddeso' (indication of the agent), 'satthāraniddeso', and 'amātāpitara saṃvaḍḍho' (one who was not raised near their parents).

There are words that, by way of usage in a sentence, are exclusively non-compound words and never compound words. What are they? They are words such as: 'satthu sāsanassa ca guṇaṃ āroceti' (he announces the virtues of the Teacher and the Teaching) and 'pitumātu cāhaṃ catto' (I am abandoned by my father and mother). If this were a compound word in this context, the reading would have to be 'mātāpitūnaṃ'.

There are words that appear as meaningful terms to those skilled in the Magadhi language, but do not appear as meaningful terms to grammarians (akkharacintaka). What are they? They are words consisting of verbal suffixes such as 'eyya', 'eyyuṃ', and 'eyyāsi'.

There are words that appear as meaningful terms to grammarians by way of convention (saṅketa), but to those skilled in the Magadhi language, they appear as terms whose meaning must be taken in another way. What are they? They are words such as 'so', which is formed by changing the 'si' suffix to 'o', and the practice of calling 'a', 'i', and 'u' as 'ayu', and so forth.

There are words that are both euphonic combinations (saṃhitāpada) and non-euphonic combinations (asaṃhitāpada). What are they? They are words such as 'āpatti pārājikassa', and so forth.

There are words whose meaning is to be taken as being endowed with inherent power (satti), and there are words whose meaning is not to be taken as being endowed with inherent power. Between these two, in the former case, there is the usage: 'seto dhāvati' (the white one runs). Here, the intended meaning is as follows:
412:
Who runs from here? The female dog runs from here. What color is the one running? The white one runs. In that statement, 'seto' should be analyzed as 'sā ito'. 'Sā' refers to a female dog. In every sense, it means 'the white female dog runs from here'.

It should be known that there are words with one intention, words with two intentions, words with three intentions, words with four intentions, and words with many intentions. Among them, a word with one intention is 'sacakkhuko' (one with eyes), and so forth. Such words with a single intention are not rare. A word with two intentions is 'hīnasammataṃ' (regarded as low), and so forth. In the word 'hīnasammataṃ', it is called so because it is regarded as low (hīna) in the world. Alternatively, it is called 'hīnasammataṃ' because it is regarded as good by low beings. It is like dung-eating creatures regarding dung as good. Likewise, 'sādhusammato' (regarded as good), and so forth.

What is a word with three intentions? For example: it is called 'cakkhubhūto' because it is like an eye in the sense of leading to seeing. Or, it is 'cakkhubhūto' because it has become like an eye. Or, it is 'cakkhubhūto' because one has reached the eye of wisdom. Such are the examples.

What is a word with four intentions? For example: it is 'ekāyano' because it is a single path; 'ekāyano' because it is a path to be traveled by one alone; 'ekāyano' because it is the path of the Sole Buddha; 'ekāyano' because it is a path that exists only in the noble Dispensation. In this regard, the Pali text says: 'Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, for the realization of Nibbāna—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.'

Words with many intentions are 'puthujjana' (worldling), 'bhagavā' (the Blessed One), 'tathāgato' (the Tathagata), and so forth. Among them:

One is called a 'puthujjana' because of reasons such as generating many defilements. Or, because one is included among the many folk, or because this person is distinct from the Noble Ones, they are called a 'puthujjana'.
413:
That person is called a worldling (puthujjana) because of such reasons as generating many and various defilements and so forth. He is called a worldling because he generates many defilements for as long as he has not attained the Path. They are called worldlings because those who possess self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) that has not yet been abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry are numerous. They are called worldlings because they look up to the faces of many teachers. They are called worldlings because they are unable to rise above all five destinations (gati). They are called worldlings because they perform various volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). They are called worldlings because they are swept away by the various four floods (ogha). They are called worldlings because they are tormented by various torments. They are called worldlings because they are burned by various fevers. They are called worldlings because they are attached, greedy, infatuated, intoxicated, strongly clinging, entangled, fastened, and obstructed by the many cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). They are called worldlings because they are hindered, obstructed, enveloped, blocked, concealed, and covered by the many five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) [Khuddaka Nikāya 7, 113-4]. Alternatively, they are called worldlings because they are included among the countless people who have turned their backs on the Noble Dhamma. Alternatively, he is called a worldling because he stands apart and distinct from the Noble Ones (ariya) who are endowed with such qualities as virtue (sīla) and learning (suta). Regarding the remaining terms, the meaning should be understood by observing the sequence of the Commentaries. Although there are other decisions to be stated in this Saddanīti treatise, we do not state them for fear of making the text too extensive. The wise can understand those unstated methods according to the methods already stated; therefore, only a summary of the methods is shown here.

This point should also be noted in this treatise [taken from the Kathāvatthu-anuṭīkā]. There are three types of discourse (kathā): vāda, jappa, and vitaṇḍā. Among these three, vāda (debate) is the adoption of one's own side and the opposing side, which is accomplished through valid logic (pamāṇa-takka) [in many versions it is samāna-takka], involves proof and refutation, is not contrary to one's own tenets, and is endowed with the five members. (Nyāya-darśana 1.2.1). Regarding one's own side and the opposing side...
414: It consists of establishing one's own side and refuting the opposite side; such a practice is called vāda. Only those views that are mutually contradictory regarding the same object are called one's own side (sakapakkha) and the opposing side (parapakkha). For example: 'The Tathāgata exists after death' and 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death'. However, even if they are mutually contradictory, if the objects are different, they are not called one's own side and the opposing side. For example: 'Form is impermanent' and 'Nibbāna is permanent'. The endeavor to establish one's own side and refute the other's side through chala (equivocation), jāti (futile rejoinders), and nigghahaṭṭhāna (grounds for defeat) is called jappa (wrangling). In this jappa, the word 'endeavor' (ārambha) is used to show that there is only the effort and no successful realization of the goal. The endeavor only to refute the opposing side (the other's side) through chala, jāti, and nigghahaṭṭhāna is called vitaṇḍā (cavilling). Among those terms, chala (equivocation) is the destruction of another's speech by devising alternative meanings. For example: 'This man has a new blanket' (or 'This man has nine blankets'), 'The king is not our witness', and so forth. The types of speech that tend to destroy another's words are called jāti (futile rejoinders); it means they are pseudo-responses.
415:
A sentence (vākya) is a group of words consisting of five components: proposition (patiññā), reason (hetu), example (diṭṭhanta), application (upanaya), and conclusion (nigama). Among these five, the indication of the thesis to be established is the proposition (patiññā); for example, "There is fire in this place." The indication of the reason that establishes the thesis is the reason (hetu); for example, "Because there is smoke." Stating the common characteristic between the thesis to be established and the reason is the example (diṭṭhanta); for example, "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen." Applying the observed common characteristic to the subject under discussion is the application (upanaya); for example, "There is smoke in this place too." The restatement of the proposition is the conclusion (nigama); for example, "Therefore, there is fire in this place." Combining all these five components, it should be understood thus: "There is fire in this place, because there is smoke. Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen. There is smoke in this place too. Therefore, there is fire in that place."

There are thirty-two methodological principles (tantayutti). They are: adhikaraṇa (subject matter), yoga (construction), padattha (meaning of words), hetuttha (meaning of the reason), uddesa (enunciation), niddesa (exposition), upadesa (instruction), apadesa (specification of reason), atidesa (extension), paṭidesa (re-extension), apavagga (exception), vākyasesa (ellipsis), atthāpatti (presumption), vipariyaya (reversal), pasaṅga (contextual relevance), ekanta (certainty), anekanta (uncertainty), pubbapakkhā (objection), niṇṇaya (conclusion), anumata (assent), vidhāna (arrangement), anāgatāpekkhaṇa (anticipation), atītāpekkhaṇa (retrospection), saṃsaya (doubt), byākhyāna (explanation), anaññā (deliberation on effort), sakasaññā (technical term), nibbacana (etymology), niyoga (injunction), vikappa (alternative), samuccaya (aggregation), and ūhanīya (deduction).

1. The five components—proposition, reason, illustration (example), application, and conclusion—are also presented in the Nyāya-darśana (1, 1, 32) and the Takkasaṅgaha. They should also be consulted in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā, Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā, Visuddhimagga, and their respective sub-commentaries (ṭīkā).

2. These 32 methodological principles can also be found in the Suśruta Saṃhitā (Uttaratantra, Chapter 65) and the Arthaśāstra. In the Caraka Saṃhitā, however, they are mentioned as 35 or 36 principles.

3. There are variant readings for vākyasesa as vākyadesa or vākyadosa. 4. There is a variant reading for pasaṅga as pasagga. 5. The term anaññā seems to be redundant; it is not found in the other four texts.
416: (1) In that treatise, the subject matter that is being discussed is called adhikaraṇa. (2) The unification of words, whether near or far, which are spoken in their proper sequence is called yoga. (3) The meaning that is established through the connection of preceding and following words in the sutta passages is called padattha. (4) The reason that establishes the stated meaning is called hetuttha. (5) A brief statement is called uddesa. (6) A detailed statement is called niddesa. (7) An indication such as "Thus" is called upadesa. (8) An indication such as "Because of this cause" is called apadesa. (9) Establishing what is present by means of what has passed is called atidesa. (10) Establishing the meaning of what is present by means of what is to come is called paṭidesa. (11) Exclusion after a general application is called apavagga. (12) The unstated word by which a sentence is completed is called vākyasesa.
417: (13) An unstated meaning that follows by implication is called atthāpatti. (14) The reversal of a word's meaning within the context it was established is called vipariyaya. (15) A meaning that is similar to that in another treatise is called pasaṅga. (16) A meaning that remains the same in all instances is called ekanta. (17) A meaning that occurs in a different way in some instances is called anekanta. (18) A meaning stated to remove the doubt of listeners is the objection, called pubbapakkhā. (19) The answer to that objection is the decision, called niṇṇaya. (20) Not refuting the view of another is called anumata. (21) Arrangement according to the sequence of the treatise is called vidhāna. (22) Looking forward to what is to come, such as "I shall say thus," is called anāgatāpekkhaṇa. (23) Referring to what has already passed, such as "It has been said thus," is called atītāpekkhaṇa.
418:
(24) Showing two types of reasons is called saṃsaya (doubt).
(25) A detailed exposition is called byākhyāna (explanation).
(The deliberation on the origin of beings and so forth is called anaññā.)
(26) A technical mark or sign pertaining to oneself is called sakasaññā.
(27) Stating a meaning that is well-known in the world is called nibbacana.
(28) Connection with an illustration is called nidassana.
(29) A mandatory injunction such as "Only this" is called niyoga.
(30) A deliberation such as "It could also be this" is called vikappa.
(31) A concise statement is called samuccaya.
(32) An unstated meaning that must be understood by penetrating it with wisdom is called ūhanīya.
## These are the thirty-two methodological principles (tantayutti).
419:
1. Showing two causes is Doubt (Saṃsaya).
2. Detailed exposition in that context is Exposition (Vyākhyāna).
3. Detailed exposition in that context is Exposition (Vyākhyāna); for example, the exposition of the twenty-five principles of the Person (Purisa) in this text. In other Ayurveda texts, there are investigations starting with the nature of the elements (Bhūta), etc.
4. A sign that is not common to other beings but pertains only to oneself is Specific Designation (Sasaññā). ... It is a well-known example or meaning in the world.
5. A word that is determined is Definition (Nibbacana).
6. That in which the meaning is established by an illustration is Illustration (Nidassana).
7. The constant application "Only this must be done" is Injunction (Niyoga).
8. The consideration "It could also be like this" is Option (Vikappa).
9. The combination "This and this" is Conjunction (Samuccaya).
