In another view, a collection of letters that expresses meaning, whether it has an inflectional ending or not, or a single such letter, as well as prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta), should be understood as a 'word' (pada). Similarly, in the group of six phrasings, a collection of words ending in an instruction connected with meaning, such as 'Monks, these foundations of mindfulness are four,' should be understood as 'phrasing' (byañjana). In the view of grammarians, however, in the place of the name 'byañjana,' each individual letter such as 'ka' without a vowel, excluding pure vowels such as 'a,' should be understood as 'byañjana.' In the view of the Great Elders who are experts in the Pali and have realized the Sublime Dhamma, the varieties of 'byañjana' should be understood through ten types of knowledge. These are: laxly recited letters (sithila), forcefully recited letters (dhanita), long-recited letters (dīgha), short-recited letters (rassa), heavily recited letters (garu), lightly recited letters (lahu), letters recited with pressure (niggahita), letters recited connectedly (sambandha), letters recited distinctly (vavatthita), and letters recited released from pressure (vimutta). In this context, all letters of the groups (vagga) such as 'ka' occurring with vowels, vowels (vaṇṇa) such as 'a,' conjunct words (saṃyutta-pada), non-conjunct words (asaṃyoga-pada), non-group letters (avagga), the dot (niggahita), euphonic combination (saṃhitā), separation of words (asaṃhitā), and words recited with a stop (virāma) should also be understood as 'byañjana.' In the group of six phrasings, the analytical definition such as 'It is called phassa because it touches' is called 'nirutti.' The words of the Buddha such as 'Monks, they are called saṅkhāra because they process' are also similarly determined, and the term spoken together with its reason is called 'nirutti.' In the Nirutti Pitaka, the nature of things expressed by these ten terms: name (saṅkhā), designation (samaññā), concept (paññatti), usage (vohāra), name (nāma), naming (nāmakamma), nomenclature (nāmadheyya), etymology (nirutti), phrasing (byañjana), and expression (abhilāpa) is called 'nirutti.' That nirutti, in its essence, is merely sound produced by the mind (cittaja-sadda) occurring together with communication (viññatti). In the view of some commentators, name-concepts (nāma-paññatti) and derivative-concepts (upādā-paññatti) are called 'paññatti.' By showing meaning through various divisions, it causes delight and sharpens the wisdom of the listeners. In the Paññatti-duka, the nature of things expressed by the ten names mentioned above is called 'paññatti,' and it too is merely sound. Knowing this distinction, the wise should make designations well. The wise person who wishes to be fully proficient in the six phrasings and six meanings should contemplate this Nīti. That proficiency (kosalla) is of sixteen types. They are: proficiency in grammar (sadda), letters (akkhara), suffixes (paccaya), gender (liṅga), inflection (vibhatti), sequence (pubbāpara), euphonic combination (sandhi), compounds (samāsa), sentence expansion (byāsa), etymology (nibbaccana), increase (āya), decrease (apāya), substitution (ādesa), learning (gahana), retention (dhāraṇa), and accomplishment (sampaṭipādana). In the Pali, five types of proficiency are mentioned according to the power of the person endowed with them: proficiency in meaning (attha-kusala), proficiency in the text (dhamma-kusala), proficiency in etymology (nirutti-kusala), proficiency in phrasing (byဉ္ဇန-kusala), and proficiency in contextual sequence (pubbāpara-kusala). One who desires these five types of proficiency should also contemplate this Nīti. Now, listen to the Nīti which is like a balance in the Dispensation, which brings benefit to the monks who bear the scriptures, and which increases joy, rapture, mindfulness, and wisdom. The word 'eva' (only/just) attached to a preceding word should also be attached to the second word and so on where appropriate. For example: 'secluded from sensual pleasures only, secluded from unwholesome states only,' and 'in this Dispensation only is the first recluse (Sotāpanna), in this Dispensation only is the second recluse (Sakadāgāmi),' and so on. In the masculine gender, the word 'ekā' is used in the sense of 'being united and equal.' For example, in the Pali: 'Let the King of Pañcāla and the King of Videha be one (ekā),' it means equality like the mixing of the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. If one says 'eke,' it means 'some,' and the meaning would be lost. A man who uses a metaphor by placing himself in the comparison is given a metaphor in the masculine gender. For example: 'Just as a bull elephant (nāga) lives having broken its bonds, so shall I live free from taints (āsava).' A woman who speaks comparing herself is given a metaphor in the feminine gender. For example: 'Just as a female elephant (nāgī) lives having broken its bonds, so shall I live free from taints.' It is stated in the Pali: 'As crows surround an owl, as they drag an unwilling huntress, as a female elephant calls her young and follows the bull elephant, so shall I, Maddī-devī, take my son and daughter and follow King Vessantara; I shall be one who is easy to support.' Maddī-devī spoke this by comparing herself using the feminine gender.

For what reason? Because it is stated in the Buddha's word (pāvacana) as 'nānāratne ca māṇiye' and so forth. One should not think that these words are spoken by taking the method from the Sanskrit (Sakkata) language. For what reason? Because the Blessed One, who is skilled in the designation of all phenomena and who knows all phenomena, did not speak by taking the method from the Sanskrit language. Indeed, He spoke and taught the Dhamma only through the natural linguistics (sabhāvanirutti) known as the Magadhi language (Māgadhabhāsā). Ancient teachers have also said: 'The Buddha did not teach the Dhamma by discarding the Magadhi language; even the grammarians analyze only the Magadhi language.' Therefore, it is called 'Māgadhikā bhāsā'. Usages such as 'uccate' and 'uttaṃ' are words spoken by taking the method from the Sanskrit language. Other such linguistic variations should also be closely and comprehensively observed.

48. Furthermore, this method of Nīti should be well-considered in this treatise for the purification of other words that are not of the Magadhi language but are brought into the scriptural tradition (pariyatti-sāsana). How should it be considered? In words like 'nātho', only the verbal forms like 'nāthati' were spoken. Names such as 'so dhanañjayo', though not appearing in the Pāḷi Canon, are indeed of the Magadhi language. Those words do not appear simply because they do not occur in the Pāḷi, not because they should not be spoken. It should be understood that words like 'uttaṃ' and 'uccate' do not appear because they should not be spoken. This mode of understanding is the domain only of the great Arahants (khīṇāsava) who have reached the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), not the domain of worldlings (puthujjana). However, relying on the Pāḷi method, worldlings also understand this mode to a small extent.

49. When words such as sīha, vyaggha, usabha, kuñjara, and nāga stand after a word in the masculine gender, that word expresses excellence. Examples are: Sakyasīha (the Lion of the Sakyans, the Buddha), purisavyaggha (an excellent man), uragūsabha (an excellent serpent/nāga), gajakuñjara (an excellent elephant), purisanāga (an excellent man), and so forth.

50. Between the words pavara and vara, the word pavara usually precedes, and the word vara usually follows. Examples are: pavararājā (an excellent king), rājavaro (an excellent king). Words like uttama occur in both positions: uttamarājā, rājuttamo, seṭṭharājā, rājaseṭṭho, and so forth. The word haṃsa also follows the word rāja: rājahaṃso (a king of swans), haṃsarājo (a king).

51. In this regard, this decision should also be noted. Names with a single meaning for each are Cātumahārājikā, Yāmā, Tusitā, and so forth. To show a single name with various meanings, the words dhamma and samaya are mentioned. Examples of different names having the same meaning are Tāvatiṃsā and Tidasa (the Tāvatiṃsa devas); Sabbaññū, Sugato, and Buddho (the Buddha); Sakko, Indo, and Purindado (Sakka).

52. In this regard, meaning is twofold: etymological meaning (nibbaccanattha) and denotative meaning (abhidheyyattha). Among them, the etymological meaning is taken by the power of the root's meaning. For example, one is called 'rājā' because of the meaning 'he shines' or 'he pleases'. The denotative meaning, however, is taken in connection with convention (saṅketa). How? A 'rājā' is understood as one who has received consecration, who rules the land, and who disciplines for the welfare of all people.

53. When a location (ṭhāna) is considered such that the located object (ṭhānī) cannot exist without it, and if that location exists, the located object certainly exists, such an occurrence of the located object due to the location is called tadanantarika (inseparable association). For example, when someone desiring ghee is told, 'Bring the pot,' if that man brings the ghee, he brings it along with the pot in which the ghee is placed. Or he brings it along with whatever object, such as another vessel or a leaf, serves as the container for the ghee. Thus, when the ghee, which is the content (ādheyya), is brought, even if it is not said to bring the container like a pot, it is already brought. Why? Because it is inseparable from the ghee. This meaning will be shown by the words stated in the Subhasutta-ṭīkā: When the mundane direct knowledges (abhiññā) are accomplished, they cannot be completed without the mastery of the fourteen modes of mind in the eight attainments (samāpatti). Therefore, when the direct knowledges are taught, the formless absorptions (arūpajhāna) are also already taught. This is because they are inseparable from the occurrence of direct knowledge.

54. Thus, in this treatise, according to the sequence of the table of contents (mātikā) set below, we have shown the roots starting with bhū, the forms of those roots, the divisions of sandhi, nouns, etc., along with the sutras, the analysis of the four types of words, and the Pāḷi methods, etc., adorned with Pāḷi passages that complete the meaning in between. All these methods of Nīti, which we have set forth to the best of our ability and strength, should be learned and maintained by clansmen (kulaputta) endowed with faith for the sake of the long endurance of the Buddha's Sāsana.

55. Those wise ones who always study this Saddanīti treatise will obtain the noble meaning in the beautiful and noble Pariyatti Pāḷi through subtle methods. Having obtained the noble meaning in the noble intention of the Buddha, which is the proper foundation for mundane and supramundane happiness, those wise ones, without fear, will roar like a lion with noble and unfailing speech like a lion's roar.

Who among the virtuous, who desires the noble and peaceful Nibbāna and has a mind associated with welfare, would not listen to this treatise, which performs what is beneficial, pleases the wise, always dispels doubt, and is like an exceedingly sharp sword? It should indeed be listened to.

This treatise, which is for the benefit of the virtuous who seek the true noble meaning, which is accompanied by well-spoken Pāḷi passages, and which is well-constructed by relying on the various views of the wise, should be kept in the mind, which is the foundation of wisdom.

Having entered into the ninefold Sāsana consisting of Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Jātaka, along with the Commentaries, and having adorned it with the doctrines of various teachers that are truly free from defilement, this treatise named Saddanīti is completed. O virtuous ones, this treatise is like black agallochum among root-fragrances, like red sandalwood among heartwood-fragrances, and like the great jasmine (malli) among flowers.

Just as the Mañjūsaka tree bears various land and water flowers, so too this Nīti-mañjūsaka treatise bears various flowers of methods. Just as the ocean is the repository of various jewels, so too this Nīti-samuddara (Ocean of Nīti) is a collection of jewel-like methods. Just as the stars in the sky are endless and immeasurable, so too the methods in the Saddanīti treatise are immeasurable. Just as the ministers and chaplains of Dhamma-protecting kings rely on the Nīti treatises to make decisions, so too in the Sāsana of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, let the wise rely on the Saddanīti to make decisions. Just as the sun rising on the eastern horizon dispels great darkness while causing much joy and rapture to all beings, so too may this Saddanīti treatise dispel the darkness of doubt for students in the Buddha's Sāsana while causing noble joy.

## The twenty-eighth chapter, called the Collection of Pāḷi Methods in the Ninefold Pāḷi Scriptures, is finished.

I have composed this treatise only for the sake of Pariyatti, Paṭipatti, and Paṭivedha. Therefore, this treatise should indeed be listened to. If it is asked whether Pariyatti or Paṭipatti is the root of the Buddha's Sāsana, it should be shown that Pariyatti alone is the root. The Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, who caused the Sāsana to endure for five thousand years, spoke these words: 'As long as the Suttantas endure, as long as the Vinaya shines, for that long light will be seen as when the sun remains. When the Suttantas no longer exist, and when there is negligence in the Vinaya, darkness will occur in the world as when the sun sets.' When the Suttanta is guarded, the Paṭipatti (practice) is guarded. A wise one established in Paṭipatti does not fall away from the fruit of Arahantship. Indeed, Pariyatti alone is the root of the Sāsana. Paṭivedha (realization) and Paṭipatti sometimes occur and sometimes do not. At one time, monks who carry the realization are many; at another, a monk is such that he can be pointed to with a finger, saying, 'This monk is a worldling.' Those who fulfill the practice are also sometimes many and sometimes few. Thus, for the long endurance of the Sāsana...

When it is asked whether the fundamental root of the Sāsana (Dispensation) is pariyatti (learning) or paṭipatti (practice), it is shown that pariyatti alone is the fundamental root. The Exalted One, of the Solar lineage, who ensured the endurance of the Sāsana for five thousand years, declared: 'As long as the Suttas remain, as long as the Vinaya shines, the light of the Sāsana will be seen, just as the light is seen when the sun rises.' If the Suttas no longer exist, or if the Vinaya disappears, it will be as if darkness overwhelms the world when the sun sets. If pariyatti is protected, paṭipatti is already protected. A wise person established in paṭipatti does not fall away from Nibbāna.

In truth, pariyatti alone is the fundamental root of the Sāsana. Paṭivedha (realization) and paṭipatti (practice) may or may not exist at certain times. Sometimes, monks who possess paṭivedha are numerous, but at other times, they are so rare that one might point and say, 'This monk is a worldling (puthujjana).' Those who fulfill paṭipatti are also sometimes many and sometimes few. Therefore, for the long-term endurance of the Sāsana, pariyatti is the primary standard. Only when a wise person hears the teachings of the Buddha from the Tipiṭaka can they fulfill both paṭipatti and paṭivedha.

Just as a herd of cattle, though numbering in the hundreds or thousands, cannot endure if there is no cow to continue the lineage, so too, even if there are hundreds or thousands of monks practicing dhutaṅga, if pariyatti disappears, paṭivedha (realization of the Dhamma) can no longer occur. Alternatively, just as it cannot be said that treasure pots are lost as long as the inscriptions carved on stone slabs to identify them remain, so too, as long as pariyatti remains, it must be said that the Sāsana has not yet disappeared. Just as it cannot be said that water does not remain if the embankment of a large lake is firm, and if there is water, it cannot be said that lotuses will not bloom; likewise, if the words of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka, which are like a firm embankment, exist, it cannot be said that there are no noble sons (kulaputta) to fulfill paṭipatti, which is like water, nor can it be said that there is no paṭivedha, which is like the lotus. Thus, pariyatti is the primary measure. Therefore, it must be said that the Sāsana has not yet disappeared as long as at least the two Pātimokkhas are still known by heart. If pariyatti disappears, even one who practices well cannot realize the higher Dhamma. Only when pariyatti does not disappear is the realization of the higher Dhamma possible.

Therefore, I have composed this treatise for the benefit of all three aspects of the Sāsana. By the power of the noble merit gained from composing this treatise, may all beings in this world attain the bliss of the supramundane (lokuttara). May all the devas guarding the stūpas receive ever-new happiness. May my guardian devas, relatives, and all donors (dāyaka and dāyikā) attain happiness. May the deva Mātali, the Four Great Guardian Kings, Sakka, Sahampati Brahma, and the Bodhisatta Metteyya protect the Sāsana. May the great elders, junior monks, and middle-ranking monks, possessing pure virtue, protect the Sāsana for a long time without hardship. May all kings rule justly. May the rains fall seasonally in all places at all times. May I, the author of this treatise, attain the noble Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) in the future and liberate all beings from the bonds of saṃsāra. This treatise was composed by the teacher Aggavaṃsa, whose fame is as evident on earth as the sun and moon are in the sky.

Thus ends the Saddanīti treatise, composed by the teacher Aggavaṃsa, who resided in the city of Bagan (Arimaddana), whose speech was faultless, who was a knower of the Dhamma, who bore the name Agga, who was the nephew and pupil of the Mahā-aggapaṇḍita teacher, and who received his ordination from that teacher who was perfect in all aspects of grammar and meaning. This treatise is completed in summary with seventy bhāṇavāras and over seven hundred verses.

The Catu-pada-vibhāga-ādi Saddanīti Nissaya is finished. At the invitation of the Chief Queen of the Great King Mahādhammarāja, the supporter of the Sāsana who founded the royal capital of Amarapura for the second time, the teacher Cakkindābhisīri Saddhammadhaja Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru, who traveled from the Great Maung-mye-bon-san Brick Monastery of Ratanapura to Amarapura and resided in the Maṅgalā-bon-kyaw Monastery, composed this Saddanīti Nissaya. It was completed on Sunday, the 2nd waning day of the second month of Vaso, in the year 1203 of the Burmese Era, at the time when the shadow measured five foot-breadths past noon.
